transcripts: OUR SEABOARD ISLANDS ON THE PACIFIC. BY JOHN E. BENNETT. THERE are upon the southwest extremity of the United States, and distributed along the coast for three hundred miles, from the latitude of San Francisco to that of San Diego, certain islands, nine in number and of various areas, about which neither geography nor history has much to say. These are the only seaboard islands on the Pacific belonging to the United States, if we do not consider those of Alaska, and those numerous tiny aits or eyots in the waters of the Sound country, not the Hawaiian group. There are from the Golden Gate to the British line a few rock reefs or single cones sitting like black stacks here and there in the sea, and at greater or less distances from the bluffy shores; but these have no claim to be spoken of as islands; that dignity belongs alone to those insular elevations in the ocean lying south of the thirty-eighth parallel, and ending, for us, at the Mexican boundary. Nature, however, taking no note of political division-lines, has not stopped at this point the southern trend of her island deposition, but she has carried them on across the line, along the mountainous coast of Lower California, where they are found under the names of San Marten, San Geronimo, Cerros, Los Lobos, and so on, to the equator. None of these are large, and the entire aggregate area of the nine belonging to us does not exceed three hundred and fifty-one square miles, or less than two hundred and twenty-five thousand acres. Separately they grade in size from one hundred and seventy-six square miles, which is the area of Santa Catalina, to less than two square miles, which is that of both Santa Barbara and the largest of the Farallones. The others, measured in square miles, are Santa Cruz, 115; Santa Rosa, 112; San Miguel, 183; San Clemente, 72; San Nicolas, 36; and Anacapa, 12. They lie in the arid region, at an average distance of thirty miles from the mainland, and they are uniform in their aspect of desolation. For the most part their surfaces present the characteristics of table-lands; some are rounded hummocks; but Santa Catalina is formed of two mountains, which pinch into sharp peaks three thousand feet high, and spread below them a jumble of ridges and ravines, the broken surface occasionally interrupted by small plateaus. The Farallones group is a granitic dike, but the others are mostly lava. It is a heavy black basalt that lies massed in its hardened meltings, and shows a Surface often of smooth rounded lumps or semi-spheroids, revealing the contracting effects of the extrusion of heat. Sometimes along with the basalt there is country rock such as is found on the mainland. This rock has, by the action of the weather, become degraded, and often at the mouth of a canyon on the lee side of the island there is spread a pleasant level of land. It has been formed by the detritus borne down from the higher areas by the canyon's stream. This has been deposited here, and it has built up the ocean floor beside the roots of the island. As it arose, the sea was pushed back, until a little flat was made, and it stands there now covered with its scrub oak, its juniper, or its wild gray grass, and meets the water with a crescent shore, upon which the little wavelets of softly lap as they rock in from the stilly bay. But upon the opposite side of the island, where the southwest winds, sweeping over the broad field of the Pacific, throw the blue waters against the black gaunt rocks, the wild elements war and play havoc. The white-frothed breakers roll and boom and burst, and the feathery spray is flung high against the scowling cliffs, until their face is varnished with a bath of spume. And all along the cliffy coasts of those sea-girt islands there have been hewn by the waves' resistless action great caverns, with high arches above the entrances, and burrowed deeply by successive chambers into the bowers of the islands. Santa Cruz abounds with these wonders of marine erosion, the largest of which is Painted Cave. It is a succession of arches, the outermost the highest, the others grading down as depth in penetration is attained. Branching from either side of this range of compartments are other openings, so that a labyrinth of recesses appears. For fifteen hundred feet into the interior of the Painted Cave the light will enter, and there can be seen upon the walls and ceilings the infinite brilliant frescoes, red, green, yellow, and their blends, deposited by the oozing mineral waters from above. On the lee side of the islands there grottos are floored with the stillest, softest, serenest waters. The sea about the sheltered coasts is intensely blue and, when under the shade of a bluff or beneath the roof of a cave, where the calms allay the waters into glassy sheets, your boat will appear to be sitting upon the top of a neither world, which spreads with innumerable population of fish and other life. Far down gardens of maidenhair, algae, and sea-ferns are seen, curved or laced by paths of white sand, against which goldfish, the mackerel, sheep's-head and the yellowtail show their floating bodies in repose, or moving slowly with rhythmic motion of gills and tail. And over all that scene there is an atmosphere pellucid, balmy, soft as the cloudless azure which overhangs it, and the sea is a shimmering breast of sunshine. The breeze brushes your cheek like silken velvet, fans you into dreamy moods, or suffuses you with gentlest slumbers. But on the weather side of the islands the water is rough, and the agitation of the surface impairs your vision into the abyss below: a tapestry of froth edges the line of shore, and the surging, ebullient billows drive in from the sea, plunge into the caves, explode, roar, and fill them with their fury. But the results of the erosion of the sea at the base of these island rocks are not more curious than those of the rain and sun upon the cliffy faces of the lava. The patient artists of nature have worked upon a surface scarified into strange devices by the contraction of the heated mass, and the wild scheme of embellishment has been accentuated and elaborated in remarkable details. What primarily were depressed lines have become deep gashes; smooth rounded bulges have been worn into jagged protuberances, sharp points, and keen hatchetlike blades of enormous size. Much of this fantastic sculpturing strikingly resembles the effects of architecture. The castellated style predominates, and you are impressed with the profusion of spires, turrets, and towers, and parapets edging the outline of the tops with merlons and crenelles. And then there are Byzantium domes and Grecian columns, the entire filigreed with the tracery of the arabesque. And not alone have wave erosion and that of water from the clouds in their processes of island degradation wrought marvels in nature-carving, but the wearing action of the wind has been scarcely less effective. On San Nicolas, more perhaps than upon any other of the islands, is this phenomenon observable. Upon this island there is a singular subsidence, forming a canyon some hundreds of feet deep and half a mile across. It contains many little peaks of cerulean slate draped with vari-colored foliage and sitting upon a ground of white sand which has been blown thither by the winds. These winds at some seasons strike strongly over the islands, and effects of their exertions are everywhere presented. Now such is seen in a broad pebbly surface swept clean, the mosaics smoothly polished; again the feathery tiles have rasped the hard dark rocks, gouged them with the emaciated hollows, ofttimes threatening the very security of their posture. The sharp fine particles give teeth to the blasts, and these gnaw at the structure of whatever interposes. At the Farallones the erosive agents have worked with queer caprice. This rock being granites, has been acted upon by the sea at all levels, and throughout the long period when it has been rising out of the watery depths. Through a long narrow hole, slanting, and communicating with the ocean, there comes at intervals a terrific stream of air, forced by the spasmodic heaving of the waves against the lower orifice. The government, which uses this island for light-house purposes, enclosed the upper end with the nozzle of a fog=horn, and every few seconds there was blown an ear=splitting brawl, which was heard far out at sea and above the din of the breaking rollers. It was allowed to roar only in foggy weather, but it was eccentric in that it would only sound at high tide. When the tide was low, although the weather might be very thick, the thing was silent. For lack of its warning a ship went ashore upon the island rocks, and then it was that the government abandoned its location on the wind hole and erected a steam-siren, or mechanical fog-horn, which has since very faithfully performed the necessary service. Another singular perforation in this island rock is a passageway about two hundred feet long, interested by several globose enlargements. One enters it on hands and knees, proceeds eighty feet, when it suddenly widens into a chamber about thirty feet in breadth and six or seven feet high. On the farther side the channel again contracts, proceeds, branches, becomes labyrinthine, and finally emerges to the surface in small unexplored holes. As though a ghastly circumstance was needed to make this boring grimly interesting, it is related that the first white person who entered this globular apartment found in it the skeleton of a woman. Her bones were delicate, and her teeth were freshly white. Who she was, how she came there, and for what reason, all this was sealed to the discoverer of her remains. These were withdrawn into the open and interred beneath a cairn of stones. There is but little vegetation upon the islands, and that much of the same character as is found upon the mainland. Santa Catalina, however, differing from the others in the numerous springs of fresh water(--)a circumstance which has been availed of to make it a resort(--)has considerable verdure and may groves of trees. Among these is the Lyono thamnus, a tree not found elsewhere than upon the islands. It has a stout branched trunk, and bears white blossoms in June. This island is also decorated with various charming and refreshing flowers(--)white lilacs, tree-poppies, and lavender, with ferns and lichens draping gloomy walls or weaving a carpet over the broken surface. Santa Cruz also has a good stream of water, which allows the growth of considerable vegetation. But upon the other islands there is little else than a bleak desert, a waste of sand and cacti, the latter interspersed with blackthorn, the glistening fleshy ice-plant covering terraces and terraces of bluffs, which rise step by step to the plateaus above. A sparse growth of grass brought up by the winter rains heightens the tawny aspect to a light faint green, but the immense herds of sheep with which all these places are populated soon eat off this back to the bare brown earth; or if it is not devoured while green, it dries into an ashy herbage(--)scant fodder for the hungry mouths. These winter rains also supply the chief water sources of the islands. They are caught in holes in the rock surface called water-pots; in these the fluid collects, and for several months after the lapse of the humid season it may remain sufficiently fresh to be palatable: but after it stagnates or evaporates there is little of potable moisture accessible, and vegetation would soon perish were it not for the heavy fogs, which during the three months of spring are so dense upon the islands and deposit such heavy dews as to amount almost to showers. On San Clemente there is a well from which a brackish liquid is pumped, and on the Farallones there is a mineral spring(--)pure water agreeably impregnated with iron and sulphur. But beyond this the water-supply is not material, and frequently, in periods of long drouths, with feed all consumed and water scarce, great sacrifices are made in sheep life by the owners of these animals. There are in all perhaps sixty thousand sheep maintained upon the islands, and the number has a constant tendency to increase in excess of the possible food-supply. When such a condition is conceived to have been reaches, a flat of wholesale execution goes out, and then it is that matanzas, or great abattoirs, are erected, in which thousands of sheep are killed merely for their pelts, tallow, and glue. In 1875, on Santa Cruz Island, twelve thousand were thus slaughtered, and in 1887 twenty-five thousand were in like summary manner taken off. The few persons who herd these sheep comprise the populations of the islands. An exception to this is presented by Santa Catalina, which, being a resort, has several thousand inhabitants, gathered principally into its village, Avalon. The owners of the islands are the proprietors of the sheep. In the early fifties, when these lands were taken possession of, in some instances by the parties who now own them, they were stocked with about two hundred sheep apiece. Fenced in by their fluid barrier, there was no possibility of the animals' escaping, and small danger of the preserved over being invaded by thieves. The stock was left to their own shift, and their owners concerned themselves with other affairs in divers parts of California. But soon the sheep had so multiplied that the island principalities came to be veritable El Dorados. Thousands of dollars of annual income were derived from them, and are to-day, through when first seized upon the islands were covered with heavy growths of rich grasses, which had accumulated upon them through successive years of unmolestation, and which it took even a large number of animals a long time to eat off, and the areas would then support larger flocks than now. In those days, too, which were the early period of California's settlement, the prices of wool and mutton were much in excess of present quotations; so that a very few years of the earlier returns which these gentlemen acquired through their island estates made them comfortable rich. Of animals ferae naturae upon these islands there are several species(--)wild hogs on Santa Cruz and Santa Rosa, wild goats on Santa Catalina and San Clemente. Both of these were placed there by whites, though the year of their introduction is not known. Originally domestic, they have returned to a state of nature through neglect. Rats and mice are also upon the islands, having been cast thither by vessels wrecked upon their rocks; there are also a small red fox and a skunk, which are indigenous mammals; but there are neither serpents, frogs, not poisonous insects, these noxious things never having been transported thither. The tourist exploring the interior of the island caves will experience an unpleasant shock when, after proceeding far into the grotto, he discovers that the place has inhabitants; and the splash, panic, and roar which follow tell him that the occupants are sea-lions. Quickly her must needs speed out, for they will plunge straight toward him, dive under him, and he must be wary, else they will upset his boat, and once he is in the water they will attack him, with possibly fatal results. Sea-lions are abundant about all of the islands. At Anacapa there is an enormous kelp-bed, where they breed and have their metropolis. These carnivora are not fur-bearing, but are covered with hair which grows upon a thick, unelastic hide. The hide has few uses, and the flesh is not palatable, though Indians find many services for the former, and the latter has furnished immeasurable meals to both whites and natives. About Anacapa, too, there is a variety of shell-fish, the most notable of which is the haliotis, or abalone. It is a univalve, which seizes hold of a rock with its strong, muscular foot, and floats idly upward upon the surface, its broad scooped shell shielding its body like a dark umbrella. When disturbed it will suddenly contract, collapse, and its shell will be drawn over the body tightly against the rock. These abalone are much sought, and their fisheries sustain a numerous population of Italians and Chinese. The shell is iridescent, the macre being variegated blue and green or pink and white; they are exported to London, where they are worked up into mother-of-pearl of commerce, and so employed in the manufacture of buttons and ornaments. The flesh of the animal is dried, and becomes a hard, soap-colored ball as large as a woman's fist. It is sent to Chins, where it is used as food. The shells bring $30 per ton, while $90 is paid for a like quantity of the desiccated meat. Upon San Nicolas, the farthest seaward of the islands, lying about sixty miles off shore, there are innumerable remnants of an aboriginal population. Evidences appear upon all the islands of their having been the abode of a race of people who have passed; but at San Nicolas appear all the specimens that are found elsewhere, and many that have not been duplicated by any other spot. Immense mounts of abalone shells, some half an acre in extent, are among these curiosities, revealing the sites of periodic feasts of the islanders upon this fish. Among these piles are scattered the shells of the limpey, mya, mussel, and other mollusks, whole stone mortars and pestles, implements of bone and ornaments of teeth, are both numerous and curious. On a knoll two miles from the island beach is an Indian burial-ground. A dozen or more grim skeletons with their whitened skulls lie upon the shore, denuded of the sand in which they were once interred. The wild winds have swept it away, and the rains and fogs and the bleaching suns have been striving to dissolve and eradicate them, but they still remain. Some of the skulls show evidences of the tragic manner in which their owners met their deaths. The Innuits, it is said, coming down from the Alaskan archipelagoes, fell upon these harmless children of the south, massacred the man, and after a little while abandoned the women and the young, and carried off all they could steal. This was long after 1542, when Cabrillo, the Spanish navigator, visited the islands, and found them tenanted by a mild and vigorous people, who, reveling in the soft ether of their climate, found their sustenance in the plentitudinous spontaneity of nature. After the invasion of the Innuits and their departure, those who remained managed to maintain themselves until 1835, when the Franciscan friars went to the islands, and gathering them all into boats, took them to the mainland, where they were mingled with the neophytes of the missions. It is related that after the last boat had pushed off from San Nicolas a woman screamed for her child, which, in the excitement of the movement aboard the transports, she had forgotten. She humped out of the vessel and sped away to seek it. The boat continued its passage, and the woman was left to her fate. The baby died, but the lone and miserable creature remained the solitary inhabitant of the place for many year. In her old age she was rescued and brought to Santa Barbara, where she died soon after her arrival. Of all the several islands the Farallones are the most remarkable, for the fact that they comprise the rookeries of vast numbers of sea-fowl, which assemble there and breed. These lie opposite the bay of San Francisco, and they are used by the government for a light-house station. The maintenance of this requires the residence upon the island of a small colony of persons who in the service of the government consent thus to banish themselves from society. The light-house steamer visits them every three months, then restocks their larder. Aside from this their only communication with civilization is by an occasional tag which may stop there to allow its captain to spy abroad from the light-house tower for incoming craft. Sometimes such a landing is not possible, owing to the height of the sea, and weeks may pass before the waters will subside so such can be effected. At nearly all times a strong cool wind prevails, and often in the afternoon it is sifted through with fog. A light board fence has been erected to protect the vegetation in the tiny patch of the light-house-tender's garden from being uprooted by the wind. But even with that, plant life does not thrive(--)or rather it thrives excessively, so that foliage becomes rank, and the fruit is a failure through growing too fast. Cabbages spring up, rush quickly into an abundance of green heavy leaves, but will not head. Onions and potatoes become immense in stalk and foliage, but will not "bulb" or "tuber" The cause of this is the strong guano soil in which the plants are grown; and the guano is deposited by the wild sea-fowl, which infest all the Farallones, three in number, making of them, in the opinion of ornithologists, the greatest bird islands in the world. There are eight varieties of these birds. They are the guillemot, commonly called the murre, the gull, the auk or auklet, the sea-pigeon, the shag or cormorant, the ashy petrel, the tufted puffin or sea-parrot, and the rock-wren. The first of these, the murre, dominates in number and importance upon the island. It is a kind of duck, with a black head, white breast, and bluish back, and sits upright like a penguin. Its food is vegetable, dissection never having revealed the presence of fish. Its eggs are valuable for food, and until recently and for many years they were extensively gathers and sold in the San Francisco market, about fifteen thousand dozen yearly being disposed of there, purchased mainly by restaurants and boarding-houses, at an average price of twenty five cents per dozen. The egg is about twice the size of that of a hen, is white or bluish-green, and flecked with brown. When fresh it is indistinguishable from the hen product, but it soon develops a fishy taste. The murre lays one egg upon a nest of roots or grass, and proceeds to incubate the next generation. At night, when she is off duty, the male succeeds her. If unmolested, the nest will this be covered until the young is hatched, when it will be guarded for a few weeks, then escorted off into the indefinite distance of the sea. But if the murre is disturbed by an egg-hunter and its single egg taken, it will return and replace its successively stolen ovum until eight have been laid. It is loath to leave its nest even when the despoiler approaches, and when he comes up she leans away from him and moves over to the far side of the nest. But presently, yielding to the alarm within her breast, she emits a sudden squawk and flies off, flushing the entire rookery as she moves toward the sea, leaving the pickers to fill their pouched shirts with the booty. They must hurry the work, for as soon as the eggs are uncovered the gulls hover close and become thick upon the scene. These then men much fight off, for they brazenly interpose themselves and battle with the humans for the possession of the eggs. The opportunity being open, the gull sweeps down upon the murre egg, seizes it in its mouth and goes sailing aloft; cracks it in its bill and gobbles what of its contents it can, the residue falling on the rocks below; then it takes another swoop away the balances itself to spy out a new egg. The gull's egg also is palatable. It is slightly smaller than that of the murre, whitish and speckled, three eggs being a litter. The eggs of the other birds are worthless for human uses, but their nests are raided by gulls and by each other. The albuminous fluid of the cormorant egg will not coagulate, and the puffin's egg has a repulsive fishy flavor. This bird has black plumage, with red beak and feet, while the cormorant is a large light blue bird, and flies in pairs. The sea pigeon is dark slate with some white in its wings; it has red feet and lays a light blue egg. The auk is as large as a pigeon, and is nocturnal in its habits. The patrel has a musky small, by the odor of which its nest is easily traceable. The murres make their nests high up, and often in the open, but the other hide theirs in the crevices of the rocks. Their note is loud, shrill, not pleasing to the ear; all except the cheery little rock-wren, whose liquid warble is a sweet, harmonious solo in the concern of shrieks and screams which ascend form the thousand of feathers throats. That these islands were a great repository of edible eggs became known in the early fifties. At the time of the discovery of this fact provisions were scarce and gold was plentiful in San Francisco, and the rookery eggs offered in the markets of that city brought one dollar a dozen. The opening of this new and free opportunity to acquire wealth precipitated numbers of people upon the islands and in the business of egg-gathering. Quarrels ensued between the competitors as to their respective "rights" in the premises, with the result that a company was formed among a number of the pickers, which bought out the claims of the others. This company managed to hold on to its advantages for some years, not, however, without experiencing contests and encroachments, until the bickerings ultimately grew so fierce as to attract the attention of the United States district attorney at San Francisco. He sent a detachment of government soldiers there and deported every egg-picker. Following this the murres and gulls were permitted for a season to lay and hatch in safety; but later, the government revealing no desire for revenue from the eggs, those on the island allowed them to be picked on shares. This introduced a company of about eighteen Greek and Italian egg-pickers into the nidue-robbing enterprise; but disputes soon again arose, and ultimately to re-establish peace upon the islands it became necessary to forbid permanently any traffic in the eggs. This has accordingly been done by a recent order from Washington. Avalon, Santa Catalina. ON THE NORTH COAST OF SANTA CRUZ ISLAND. THE TWO CAVES AT VAL DEZ HARBOR, SANTA CRUZ. The larger opening affords the only landing-place from the harbor, and the smaller one the only way to the beach. LOOKING INTO VAL DEZ HARBOR. ON THE NORTH FARALLONES. THE INTERIOR OF SANTA CATALINA ISLAND. SANTA CRUZ ISLAND(--)THE MAIN RANCH. ONE DAY'S CATCH. Jew-fish, a shark and small fry. SHEEP-SHEARING. THE GREAT MURRE, SOUTH FARALLONES. AN EGG-PICKER'S CABIN. transcripts: MRS. ROBINSON CRUSOE (--) BY WiLLiAM CROSBY BENNETT She lived, isolated, for eighteen years on San Nicolas(--)off our Southern California shores. When they rescued her she withered and died in the discomfort of our cramped civilization THE origlnal of Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe was, as everyone knows, a sailor named Alexander Selkirk, who, from 1704 to 1709, was marooned on the island of Juan Fernandez, 300 miles west of Chile, and from this bare record the author made his masterpiece of in[genuity, _________, and adventure](--)a shrine destined to live as long as youthfulness exists in the world; but few are aware that a century and a half later, another forlorn creature dwelt alone on an uninhabited island, off our California coast. And to make matters worse, this time it was a female Crusoe. Against Selkirk's five years' isolation, this poor thing lived in solitude for eighteen. without even a man Friday for company, and she probably would have ended her life on this rugged crumb of land in the Pacific Ocean, unknown and unsung, had it not been for a chance discovery of her presence there. It was on a sunny day in July, 1853, that a party of otter men from Santa Barbara anchored their schooner off the northeastern coast of the island of San Nicolas, some eighty or ninety miles distant, and established a camp on shore. The party consisted of Capt. Nidiver, a man named Brown, an Irish cook and a crew of mission Indians. The evening after their arrival the captain and Brown strolled a mile or so down the beach, enjoying their pipes and making plans for their work. It was a moonlight night, almost as bright as day, with the stars shining large and clear from a low sky. As they were about to retrace their steps toward the camp Nidiver stopped suddenly, looked hurriedly around, and then knelt on his knee to examine the ground. Plainly outlined on the shore was the print of a slender, naked foot! "My God!" the captain exclaimed. "There is a woman on the island!" At dawn the next day he and Brown returned to the spot and found a basket of rushes hanging from a tree. It contained bone needles, thread made of sinews, shell fish-hooks, ornaments and a partly completed robe of birds' plumage, the feathers pointing downward, and so skUlfully matched as to seem one continuous sheen of changeful luster. Nidiver proposed leaving the things untouched, but Brown scattered them about, saying that if they were picked up it would be proof the owner was alive and had visited the place. Extending their search inland. they discovered several circular, roofless inclosures, made of woven brush. Near these shelters were poles, with dried meat hanging from elevated cross-pieces. In the fissures of the rocks, near a spring of fresh water, were wedged dried fish and seal blubber; but there was no sign of the near presence of the one to whom the provisions belonged. After several days' search the men abandoned the task and started hunting the otters. This lasted for weeks and the well-loaded schooner was preparing for the return trip to Santa Barbara when Capt. Nidiver proposed further search for the woman. "If she is alive we ought to find her," he said. "If dead, we will look for her body even if we have to scrape the island inch by inch." The captain ordered preparations made and the entlre crew started on what the Irish cook called a woman-ghost hunt. Near the head of the island they came across a bone house, skillfully interlaced with rushes. An olla and stove-in basket were near the door, but all around the weeds were untrampled and the whole place had a deserted look. Still Nidiver urged his companions on. After several days' march, a dangerous climb over slippery rocks brought them to a spot where there were fresh footprints made by the same slender naked foot. These were followed up the cliffs until they were lost in the thick moss that covered the ground. Brown, walking on ahead, sighted a moving object " long way off on the hllls. At first glance it appeared like a bird, but it moved about in such a singular manner that he advanced stealthily to find out what it really was. Drawing nearer, he was dumfounded to discover it was the head of a woman, barely visible above the low woven-brush sides of her roofless retreat in the bushes. As the sailor approached nearer, a pack of tamed wild dogs, crouching at the woman's feet, began to growl; but without looking around she uttered a peculiar cry which immediately silenced them, and they ran away to the hllls. Brown halted within a few yards of her and, himself unseen, watched every movement within the hut. Inside the inclosure was a mound of grass, woven baskets filled with various articles and a rude knife made of a piece of iron hoop, thrust into a wooden handle. A fire smoldered near and a pile of bones lay in the ashes. The complexion of the woman, he noted, was much fairer than the ordinary Indian, her personal appearance pleasing, features regular, her hair thick and brown, falling about her shoulders in a tangled mat. From the time he arrived within hearing, she kept up a continual talking to herself. She was leaning forward, shading her eyes with her hand, watching the men from the schooner crossing the flat land far below her dwelling. After looking at them for a while with marked anxiety on her face, she crouched in terror, but immediately started up as if to run. The men on the flat had not seen her, and Brown, putting his hat on the ramrod of his gun, lifted and lowered it to attract their attention, and when he had done so, intimated with signs that the woman was found, and that they should spread out in order to catch her if she tried to escape. Before the men reached the cliff, Brown stepped around in sight and spoke. She gave a frightened look, ran a few steps, but instantly controlling herself, stood still, and addressed him in an unknown tongue. She seemed to be between 40 and 50 years of age, in fine physical condition, erect, with well-formed neck and [a]rms and unwrinkled face. She was dressed in a tunic-shaped garment, made of the satiny plumage of the green cormorant, low in the neck, sleeveless, and reaching to the ankle. The dress was similar to the one found in the tree. As the men came up, she greeted them each in the way she had met Brown, and with a simple dignity, not without its effect on both Indians and white men, made them welcome and set about preparing [f]ood for them from her scanty store. There were several dialects spoken by the Indian crew, but none of them was able to converse with the strange woman, or understand a word she uttered, and they were obliged to let her know by signs that they were going to take her with them. Brown went through the motion of packing her things in baskets, shouldering them and walking in the direction of the beach. She understood instantly and made preparations to go with them. One of the heaviest loaded baskets she swung without any unusual effort over her back, and, taking a burning brand from the fire, followed after the men who were carrying her other possessions. Upon reaching the boat, she entered without hesitation, going forward to the bow, kneeling and holding to either side. When the schooner was reached, she went aboard without any trouble and sat down near the stove in the cabin and quietly watched the men at their work. To replace her feather dress, which was subsequently sent to Rome and placed in the Vatican Museum, Brown made her a petticoat of ticking; and with a man's cotton shirt and gay handkerchief, her semi-civilized dress was completed. While Brown Was sewing, she watched him closely and laughed at his manner of using a needle. She showed him that her way was to puncture the cloth with her bone needle and then put the thread through the holes. She signified that she wished to try a threaded needle and Brown gave her sewing materials, but she could not thread the needle. Brown did it for her and gave her an old coat of Capt. Nidiver's to mend, and while she took her first sewing lesson she told by signs portions of her life on the island. From time to time she had seen ships pass, but none came to take her off. She watched as long as she could see them, and, after they were out of sight, she threw herself on the ground and cried, but after a time she walked over the island until she forgot about it and could smile again. She had seen people on the beach several times. But she was afraid and hid until they had gone and then wept because she had not made herself known. She intimated that Brown had taken her by surprise and she would not run because she liked his face and felt he had been sent to take her to her people, who had gone away on a ship with white men. The sailor understood by her signs that at one time she had a nursing baby, which she represented by sucking her finger and placing her arm in the position of holding an infant at the breast. She waved her hand over the sea to indicate the ship sailed away, and then that she could not find her child and wept until she was very ill and lay prostrate for days in a bed of plants. She had nothing to eat but leaves. When she somewhat revived, she crawled to a spring and after a time, as her strength returned, she made a fire by rubbing a pointed stick she showed him along the groove or a flat stick until a spark was struck. Who was this mysterious woman? This was the question that Brown asked himself, and one that naturally arises in our mind. In order to answer it in part, at least, it will be necessary to begin quite far back in history. The Santa Barbara Islands, on one of which this strangest of strange romances was enacted, lie to the southward of the Santa Barbara Channel, the nearest of the group being some twenty-five miles distant from the mainland. The islands are named Anacapa, Santa Rosa, San Miguel, Santa Cruz, Santa Catalina, Santa Barbara and San Nicolas. In the year 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo, the credited discoverer of California, landed on what is now known as San Miguel and christened it Isla de Posesion. He died on the island the following year and is buried in its sands, although his grave has never been located. But delving still further into our research we find that even berore Cabrillo's time the mainland and islands were inhabited by a populous people, the origin of whom however, is unknown. San Nicolas, on which the scenes of this wild romance are laid, was the outermost of the group. It was at one time the abode of a people differing in Customs and modes of life from those on the mainland and neighboring islands. A scientist, named De Cessae, engaged in collecting archeological specimens for the French government, left a well authenticated record that the relics found on San Nicolas were more elaborate and showed a superior workmanship to those he examined on the other islands and the mainland. He also found on San Nicolas articles of warfare and domestic use which evidently belonged to a northern tribe and were similar to those found by him on the coast of Alaska. Hence he draws the inference that the island was at one time the dwelling place of the north country tribes. It is also recorded that a ship from Boston, commanded by a Capt. Whitmore, brought down from Sitka, Alaska, a company of Kodiaks for the purpose of otter hunting on San Nicolas. These were left as permanent settlers upon the island and years of feud resulted in a massacre, in which every male islander was killed by the powerful and well-armed Kodiaks. The women were taken by the victors, lived with them and bore children. As the years passed San Nicolas faded away strangely and rapidly, so that in 1830 less than twoscore men, women and children remained. It was not until 1835 that the schooner Peor es Nada, commanded by Capt. Williams, collector of the port of San Pedro, was sent by the church fathers to fetch the benighted people of San Nicolas and place them under their spiritual guidance. On the way over a severe storm suddenly overtook the ship and a landing on the island was made with extreme difficulty. To make matters worse the wind continued to increase in fury. No time was to be wasted. The islanders, some twenty in number, were hurried in boats to the schooner and she immediately set sail. In the excitement and confusion it was not realized that an infant had been left behind on the island, but not many moments passed before the frantic mother made that fact known to the captain and with gestures implored him to return. But on account of the storm and the fear of wrecking his vessel he dared not comply with her request. Finding it was useless and the ship was heading out to sea, the mother became desperate and in spite of all attempt to detain her, threw herself into the water and started to swim toward the shore. It was impossible to attempt to save her and, as she soon vanished from sight in the terrific surf, she was supposed to have perished. After a rough passage, the schooner finally reached San Pedro, where the islanders were sent to San Gabriel Mission, fifteen miles away. It was the intention of Capt. Williams to return immediately to San Nicolas as soon as the storm abated, to see if the woman or child were living, but the schooner received orders from the owners [t]o proceed at once to Santa Barbara and thence to San Francisco. She never reached the latter port, but was wrecked at the entrance to the Golden Gate. Fifteen years passed and the uncertain fate of the woman and child was forgotten apparently by everyone but the tender-hearted mission fathers. Vessels were scarce, but in 1850 they managed to persuade one Thomas Jeffries, who had come into the possession of a small schooner, to visit the island and search for them. On his return he reported no sign of human life there. But evidently the woman did not perish, although her infant did, and on this sea-girt isle she lived a solitary life for eighteen years. On arriving at Santa Barbara, Capt. Nidiver placed the woman in the care of his wife. The news of her arrival and her strange life spread rapidly, and the house was crowded with visitors. When the ship Fremont came into port soon after, the captain offered Nidiver half of all he would make if he would allow him to exhibit the woman in San Francisco. The offer was coldly refused. Nidiver said that neither he nor his wife would for a moment consider that the friendless creature should be made a show of for the curious. The strange woman was bitterly disappointed when none of her kin could be found. She was patient and cheerful, however, looking eagerly into every new face for recognition, and sometimes singing softly to herself. Soon she began to droop under civilization, probably missing the outdoor life of her island camp. After a time she became too weak to walk and was carried to the porch, where she dozed for hours in the sunshine. Believing that a return to the old diet might help her, Mrs. Nldiver procured seal meat and roasted it in ashes, but when it was presented to her she could not eat the food. One day she fell from her chair and immediately lapsed into unconsciousness. It was soon evident that she was reaching the end of her life. Father Sanchez, a Catholic priest, was summoned and, after christening the nameless creature "Juana Marie," he administered the last rites of the church to the dying woman. Within the walled cemetery at the old Santa Barbara Mission, under the shelter of its tower, the heroine of San Nicolas was interred and, to this day, should you ask, the Franciscan brothers will point out her grave. BROWN HALTED WITHIN A FEW YARDS OF HER, AND, HiMSELF UNSEEN, WATCHED EVERY MOVEMENT . . . .

transcripts: [...] About eighty miles southeast of Santa Barbara is a small island, some eight miles in length by three in breadth, named San Nicolas, which once supported a dense population. As artificers in stone and bone they excelled the inhabitants on the other islands, and those on the mainland. The finest specimens of aboriginal workmanship I have seen in California came from this island. But little is known of the people who inhabited San Nicolas island, except the records of the industry represented by these specimens. Owing to its distance from the mainland it seems not to have been discovered by Cabrillo, Vancouver, nor by any of the early or intermediate explorers. It was visited by the early American fur traders, however, and was called by them "Sea Otter Island." In the summer of 1835 a schooner was dispatched to this island to bring off the remnant of its inhabitants, now reduced to seventeen or eighteen individuals. The cause of their declination is enshrouded in as great mystery as that of the other islanders. When all were supposed to be ready to sail, and the ship was about to weigh anchor, one of the women requested permission to return for her child, which she had left in a cañon nearby. But during her absence a heavy wind commenced blowing and drove the vessel from the island. In due time the schooner reached San Pedro in Los Angeles County, where the Indians were landed, and she was immediately ordered north by her owner, but in attempting to enter the Golden Gate, at San Francisco, was capsized and lost. There being no other large craft on this portion of the coast, no attempt was made to rescue this unfortunate woman. Indeed no effort was made to learn her fate for seventeen years afterward, although it was well known that she had been abandoned on the island. In 1851 the place was visited by a small schooner in quest of the eggs of waterfowl, when human tracks were discovered in the sand, which seemed to be those of a woman, but before search could be initiated a strong wind arose and drove the party from the inhospitable island. The following year the island was again visited by this party, who on going ashore found a large basket, woven from a species of grass, containing a gown made of bird's skins, a sinew rope, bone knife, fishhooks of shell, and other things, covered with the skin of a seal, but a second time they were driven from the island by the wind. In the summer of 1853 the island was visited for the third time by this party, who succeeded in making a thorough exploration, finding the object of their search seated in a low circular enclosure of sage brush. Within the enclosure was a smoldering fire, while without was a large pile of bones and another of ashes, showing this to have been her abode for several years. She was engaged in recovering the blubber from a seal skin, in which she employed a rude knife. She did not seem frightened, but met her rescuers with a smile and a bow. She wore a dress or gown made of bird skins, the feathers outside and pointing downward. Her hair was bleached by long exposure to a reddish brown, and hung down to her shoulders. Her features were regular and her complexion fairer than the Indians on the mainland. Though supposed to be about fifty years of age, her face was remarkably free from wrinkles. She willingly accompanied the party on board their vessel, and to the mainland. During her eighteen years of exile she seems to have entirely forgotten her language. Indians of various dialects were sent for, but none could understand her, nor she them. The change of diet to which she was subjected induced sickness, of which she died four weeks after reaching Santa Barbara. She made her rescuers understand by signs that she did not find her child but that it had been killed by dogs, a peculiar species that became extinct on this island but recently. [...]

title: "Santa Barbara. A Visitor's Views Regarding Its Climate and Attractions"
tropes: Wild Child; Vanishing Indians; Noble Savage
author: Blanco
transcripts: <hi rend="bold">SANTA BARBARA.</hi> <hi rend="bold">A Visitor's Views Regarding its Climate and Attractions.</hi> [From the Indianapolis Sentinel] SANTA BARBARA, Feb. 5th, 1882. Somebody once said that the climates of Heaven and Santa Barbara were similar. This statement may be a little strong, but there is no denying the fact that Santa Barbara has among the finest, if not the finest, climate in the United States. It is between cold, foggy, windy San Francisco and hot, oppressive San Diego, and strikes a happy medium, having all the good qualities of those places and very few of the bad ones. For the past month or six weeks it has been remarkably cold for this place, and on one occasion we awoke one morning to find the mountains covered with snow and the tops of the foot-hills slightly sprinkled with that same beautiful (?) substance. This had never occurred before within the memory of the oldest inhabitant, as many of the school children (and also some few of the grown up) had never before seen snow, they were wild with delight, and some of the more hardy boys went to the top of the hills and brought a load into town. Then they engaged in one of the chief delights of the Eastern boy, a good old-fashioned snow ball fight. An Indianapolis boy would have smiled to see the rapture with which the Santa Barbara boy patted and fondled the dirty white mixture they called snow. In the East it would have been called "slush." However, the youngsters enjoyed it hugely, and for the last time, unless they emigrate to a colder climate. They will probably never have the same chance again in sunny Santa Barbara. Flowers are very plenty at this time of the year, but during March, April and May is the time to see them in their glory. Roses bloom here all the year round, and for size and beauty of coloring I defy the world to produce their equal. From a single Gloire de Dijon bush in our front yard my sisters clip enough buds every morning to decorate the entire house. Some of our Eastern people may feel inclined to be a little skeptical, but when I tell them that the bush is about fifteen feet in hight [sic] and several inches in diameter at the base, maybe they will feel more like believing. An Eastern person who has never seen it has no idea of the profusion with which flowers grow in California, and especially in the Southern part. In the Ojai Valley, a beautiful valley in the mountains, about forty miles south of this place, I believe that wild flowers reach their perfection. In the spring and summer months the valley and hillsides are literally covered with these little volunteers of nature. The poppies are particularly noticeable for their variety of shades and great size. The situation of Santa Barbara could not be improved upon. It has a magnificent frontage on the Santa Barbara Channel, and is flanked on the northeast by the lofty Santa Ynez Mountains, and on the northwest by a range of foot-hills, making a triangular-shaped valley for Santa Barbara, "The Beautiful," to nestle in. Across the channel are the rugged Channel Islands, at a distance of from twenty to sixty miles. Scribner's Monthly a few months ago, [sic] published an account of an Indian woman who was left, during a storm, upon one of these islands, and roamed for over twenty years over her rocky fastness, and when found had forgotten her native language and become thoroughly wild. In the meantime her tribe had died out, and no one could be found who could understand her broken sentences. She did not live long after she was brought to Santa Barbara, but soon succumbed to civilization. The old Captain who found her still lives in this place, and is always ready to tell the story in his own graphic manner. The greatest drawback that Santa Barbara had to contend with is the fact that it has no railroad. Several times it has been on the eve of having one built, but every time something interferes. The Atlantic & Pacific people were just ready to build at one time, but the Central Pacific monopoly gobbled it, and as it was not to their interest to let Santa Barbara have a road, why, they did not let her have one. In time, after the C. P. Railroad is crushed, Santa Barbara will get a railroad,but [sic] in my opinion,not [sic] before. The C. P. has a way of controlling things in this country, and making things work around for their benefit. The people are getting awful tired of it,and [sic], before a great while, something will probably drop, and great will be the fall thereof. While I am on the subject I might as well say that California is controlled by monopolies. The China and Australian Steamship Company is a monopoly. The Central Pacific is a gigantic monopoly. The cities are run by monopolies. Trade is carried on by monopolies. The stock market is dictated to by monopolies, and in fact almost every branch of business on this coast is operated by a monopoly. Any body can get rich in California if they only can get into a monopoly, but the trouble is you can't get into that desired position. This State [sic] is not named right. It should be called Monopolifornia. That name would fit it like a glove. When I started out I intended to write about Santa Barbara, but when I get started on "monopolies" I don't know when to stop, so please pardon the digression. Santa Barbara is well off in the matter of hotels, three are now running, and all seem to be full. The "Arlington" is the best, and for solid comfort and convenience is not equaled south of San Francisco. The others are good houses. Three steamers per week arrive from San Francisco, and every one comes loaded down with health and pleasure seekers for this point. The fact is rapidly becoming known that this place cannot be [b]eaten on the American continent for enjoyment of life. You know what that means—good health and contentment. Living is not expensive. At the Arlington the price is only $15 per week, and keeping house is as cheap in proportion. For ten cents you can get a ridiculously large quantity of vegetables. Meat is twelve and a half cents per pound. Washing is done by the Chinese at so much per week, say $1.25 for a family of five. House rent is rather high, but not nearly so much as in Los Angeles or San Diego. When you come to the luxuries, you have to pay for them, that is, all except horses. For $30 one can get a very good riding animal, and for $75 or $80 a very fair roadster can be obtained. I am the fortunate or unfortunate possessor of a mustang, a real thoroughbred. Before I came to this country I always understood that a mustang was next door to a devil, but such is not the case. The mustang is nearer human than any other breed of horses, and will behave exactly as it is used to being treated. If it has been abused, it looks upon mankind as its natural enemy, and is always on the lookout for a chance to get a little revenge. But, on the contrary, if it has been owned by a whit[e] man and kindly treated, no animal [wi]ll be gentler and safer. My little horse has always been well treated, and a better or kinder horse cannot be found, and, remember, she is a pure bred mustang. As a rule, mustangs are smaller than American horses, but are stronger in proportion to their size. I suppose it is because they have less weight to carry, and are just as muscular. When I first came to this State [sic] I would not use a Spanish saddle, but clung to the English wafer style. I soon got out of that notion, and now use a regular "sia" the most pronounced of Spanish saddles. One of these saddles is a rather ungainly object to look at, but it is mighty comfortable riding. Hereafter, for ease and comfort, commend me to a Spanish saddle. Mrs. Helen Hunt Jackson, of the Century Magazine, is now here, writing up the California missions. Santa Barbara glories in a grand old mission, built over 100 years ago by the Franciscan monks. It is situated back of the town on the foot-hills, and is the first object which strikes the eye on landing from the steamer. It is a large building and can be seen for miles. The building is constructed of adobe, and is roofed with tiling. There was not a nail used in building, the rafters being tied with thongs of rawhide, which are as strong now as the day they were first put up. There are several heartrending statues and paintings in the chapel, one being a life-size representation of Christ on the cross. It is a most lifelike thing, and is calculated to give nervous people the nightmare for a week. The expression of agony on the face and the contortions of the limbs are most horrible. They used to have a statue of some saint that would cry, real tears running down the cheeks. This was a great marvel to the ignorant people until it was discovered that there was a cup of water inside the head, that worked by a string. Since then the statue has disappeared. The graveyard attached to the Mission reminds one of the graveyards seen in Europe. It is enclosed by a high wall, and is so full of bodies that bones stick out all over the ground. It is not used any more [sic]. Santa Barbara has one daily and two weekly newspapers. The evening PRESS has a circulation of about 1,000 copies. It is a good, live paper. Mr. C. F. McGl[a]shan, the genial editor and proprietor, is just the man for the place, and does Santa Barbara a power of good. This paper has also a weekly number. The weekly <emph>Independent</emph> is a good paper. Santa Brabara's population is 5,000, and is growing. Good stores, fine churches and handsome residences are numerous. We have a daily mail from San Francisco, Los Angeles and the East. I am very much afraid that I will have to go home in the spring; I don't want to, but reasons over which I have no control compel. I have been in California just long enough (two years) to be infatuated with its climate, and if it were not for my father I believe I would like to live here; but the fiat has gone forth, and I must obey. The sun is just setting, and the tints on the mountains are lovely. Nowhere, with the exception of Italy, do they have finer sunsets than here. A gentleman, who has traveled all over the world, told me that, and I take his word for it. They are good enough for me, any how. I saw Henry Talbot in San Francisco just before he sailed for Japan. He was looking as jolly as ever. Indian people are not very plentiful in this part of t[h]e country, but when I find one I freeze to him. Here, I have strung this out into quite a letter, but I did not mean to when I started. I will wind up by saying that Santa Barbara is the sanitarium of the United States, and any body who is afflicted with any one of the ailments that flesh is heir to had better come here and get cured. SENOR BLANCO.

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">The Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island.</hi> BY STEPHEN BOWERS, PH. D. Editor of the VENTURA OBSERVER, Ventura, California, December 20, 1892. About eighty miles south of Ventura is a wind-swept island which has the appearance of having been gently lifted from the depths of the ocean. Its altitude is about 800 feet above the sea level. It is surrounded by comparitively low banks, with gradual acclivity until terminating in abrupt escarpments, the surface of the island being comparitively level. This island has a mean length of about nine miles and an average width of about four miles. The longer axis is nearly east and west. Geologically speaking it is of recent origin. The fossils, which are numerous in some places, are of Quaternary age, except some found in the south-eastern portion which may probably be classed as Pliocene. At the present time the island is treeless. It contains neither tree or shrub, except a small species of thorn and the tree cactus, neither of which obtain a height of more than two or three feet. But it has not always been so, for there are evidences existing which indicate that it was once covered with timber. Capt. Nidever, who frequently visited the island, speaks of trees, bushes and moss, forty years ago. Much of the surface is covered with dead land shells—<emph>helix</emph> (<emph>euparypha</emph>) <emph>trioni</emph> and <emph>helix</emph> (<emph>arionta</emph>) <emph>gabbi</emph>. When they flourished there must have been much vegetation on the island. Their large size and vast numbers are noticeable. We speak of the island as being "wind-swept," but this is only at certain seasons of the year, while at other times it is calm and serene. During the season that wind prevails it is difficult to land and more difficult for vessels to remain at anchor. The writer spent three weeks on the island in Oct., 1889, and several times during his stay saw the sea lashed into fury, the waves and spray rolled up thirty feet high, and dashed against the rock-robbed shore with a noise like thunder, and seemed to cause the very atmosphere to tremble. Never before had we witnessed such wild and fierce struggle of the waves, though for many years accustomed to the ocean. One whole day and two nights we could not leave our tent, which was securely anchored to the side of a hill, because the high wind and drifting sand. When Cabrillo sailed up this coast three hundred and fifty years ago, he seems not to have discovered San Nicolas island; nor was it seen by Vancouver during his voyage a hundred years ago. The earliest voyagers who visited the island, of which we have an account, named it "Sea Otter Island," because of the great number of sea otters found there. They are still found to a limited extent; also seals, sea lions and numberless aquatic birds. Several species of land birds are found here, and a small fox, <emph>vulpus littoralis</emph>. The skeletons of two species of dogs are numerous on the island. They were living as late as 1853 and were domesticated by the natives. The island was once thickly inhabited as the vast shell heaps—kjökkenmöddings—indicate. The relics found are generally of superior workmanship to those found on the other islands and on the mainland, and indicate contact with northern tribes. The barbed spear points of which remain, are not found on the other islands of the Santa Barbara channel group. They fashioned many singular implements from stone and bone, the use of of which [the use of which] is a puzzle to archæologists. The opinion has long prevailed that there was a somewhat higher civilization, if such it could be called, here than was found on the mainland and the other islands, and it is said that the inhabitants were of a superior physical mould, the women were tall and handsome and of lighter complexion than other natives of this region. In an early day the Russians were in the habit of visiting San Nicolas island in quest of the valuable fur of the sea otter. They brought with them natives from Alaska whom they taught the use of firearms. It is said that they left some of these on the island to continue the work of capturing otters while the Russian vessels sailed north. While absent these Alaskan Indians took possession of the women on the island, and in the conflict which followed all of the men and male children were killed. When the Russian ships returned and took them away the women were abandoned to their fate. This was sometime previous to the year 1835. In some way the news reached the Mission fathers, and in the above named year they secured a schooner, the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph>, to go to the island and bring away the remaining inhabitants. The vessel was chartered by Lewis F. Burton and Isaac J. Sparks of Santa Barbara, and was commanded by Charles Hubbard. The crew with two of three exceptions were Kanakas. An American known as Bill Williams accompanied the vessel. They sailed to the island about the first of August, 1835. After collecting the Indians on the beach ready for embarking, one of them made signs that her child had been left behind, and she was permitted to go in search of it. While absent a strong wind arose which threatened the safety of the schoooner, when the officers and crew were compelled to set sail leaving the unfortunate woman and her child behind. They ran before the wind to San Pedro where the Indians were landed, soem being taken to Los Angeles and others to San Gabriel Mission. The vessel, which was owned in Monterey, was ordered north to take a load of lumber from that place to San Francisco. In attempting to enter the Golden Gate the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> was capsized and lost. There being no other craft larger than Indian canoes on this portion of the coast, no effort was made to rescue the woman, and there being no communication with the island from the mainland, the fact of her being left alone gradually passed out of mind. In 1851 Capt. John Nidever of Santa Barbara sailed to the island in quest of the valuable fur of the sea otter. He landed on the lower or eastern end of the island, when he and a man named Jeffries walked for several miles along the north shore line and discovered human tracks, and some other evidences of life. Before midday, however, a strong wind began to blow, and compelled them to return to their schooner. This continued for several days when they weighed anchor and left the island. In the winter of 1852 Capt. Nidever made a second visit to this island, having seen a large number of otter on his previous visit. He was now accompanied by a man named Brown and two Indians. He and Brown walked along the shore, as he had done on the occasion of his first visit, but discovered no signs of human occupancy of the island until near evening when they found a basket in the crotch of a small tree. Removing the sealskin covering they discovered a dress or gown made of bird-skins cut in squares, a sinew rope, bone needles, abalone fish-hooks, etc. They remained for several days but failed to see the woman to whom these things afterward proved to belong. About the fifth day a strong southwest wind began to blow which increased to a gale. Waiting for several days, for the wind to calm, they with difficulty got away from the island and sailed to San Miguel island. In July 1853 Capt. Nidever again sailed to San Nicolas island, and with the avowed purpose to thoroughly explore it in search of the lost woman. His crew consisted of Charles Brown, one Irishman and four Mission Indians. They anchored at Coral Harbor on the north side of the island. Here is a small bay that is entered by passing through a rift in the rocks about twenty feet wide. At that time it probably offered good anchorage, but is now filling with drifting sand. From this place the party went to the western portion of the island, where Brown discovered human footprints, but they were unable to find the woman. They renewed the search next day and discovered her in a wickeup or circular enclosure made of brush somewhat westward of the center of the island. When they came upon her she was removing the blubber from a seal. She arose with dignity, saluting the men with a smile. She was dressed in a gown made of bird skins, the feathers pointing downward. It was cut low at the neck and came down to her ankles. Her hair was a yellowish brown, probably caused in part from exposure. The woman was apparently about fifty years old. After roasting some nuts for her guests, and of which they partook with a relish, they made signs for her to accompany them to the vessel, which after being understood she did without hesitancy, each carrying some of her meager effects. The party remained on the island for a month, the woman proving helpful in bringing wood and water. She gave evidence in various ways of having seen much suffering during the eighteen eyars of her isolation, but was very cheerful and remained so until the last. After the schooner set sail for Santa Barbara a storm came on, when the rescued woman fell upon her knees and prayed. When the storm abated, and a patch of blue sky appeared, she pointed to it with pride as much as to say she did it. On reaching Santa Barbara she became an object of great interest to all the country around, and many visited her. Three of the Mission fathers, Gonzales, Sanchez and Jimeno came to see her, and although they were acquainted with many dialects, yet they could not understand her, nor could she understand them. Indians were brought from Santa Ynez, Los Angeles, and other places, but were unable to converse with her. While she was an object of curiosity, nearly everything she saw was curious to her. A yoke of oxen drawing an old Spanish cart greatly excited her attention. One of the first to visit her on her arrival at the residence of Capt. Nidever, was Dr. J. B. Shaw, on horseback. Several years ago the doctor narrated to the writer the circumstances of his visit. When the woman saw him riding toward her she seemed to think the horse and rider one; and when she saw him dismount her anazement was great. She came and sat beside him, felt of his clothing and seemed to look upon him as a supernatural being. The food of civilization, of which she partook to excess, did not agree with her, but brought on sickness of which she died about four weeks after landing at Santa Barbara, or two months after her rescue. While she had probably entirely forgotten her own dialect, and during the eighteen years of her weary solitude had probably consturcted another, known only to herself, yet she soon became an adept in conversing by signs. The family of Capt. Nidever, with whom she lived, became very much attached to her. She gave them to understand that when she went back for her child she found that it had been killed and devoured by dogs. She laid down and cried for a long time and became emaciated form grief, but finally recovered. She sometimes saw ships sailing on the ocean, but none came to her rescue. After her death her gown of bird skins, and various trinkets, were sent to Rome, where they may probably still be seen among the collections and curiosities of the vatican. The object of the writer in preparing and publishing this history at the present time, is in answer to certain statements that have found their way into print denying the authenticity of the story. That it is literally true there can be no doubt whatever. We received it from Capt. Nidever's own lips several years before his death. The writer was personally acquainted with him from 1874 until his death which occurred about 1886. He was much respected in Santa Barbara where he lived more than fifty years. We never heard his integrity called in question by anyone. In our visit to the islands we found much confirmatory evidence of Mr. Nidever's statements. The account may also be found in the archives of the Santa Barbara Mission fathers. We secured a translation of their record of the event to by a competent Spanish scholar some fifteen eyars ago. Dr. J. B. Shaw, an educated physician, who came from England and settled in Santa Barbara at an early day, and who saw the woman after her rescue, was well acquainted wiht the facts as related above. He is still living, and is a gentleman of unquestioned integrity. John Nidever, a nephew of Capt. Nidever, was well acquainted withe the facts under consideration, and lives in Carpinteria, Cal. Others who saw the woman and are conversant with the facts related in this paper, are still living. In short, no event that occurred on this coast forty or fifty years ago can be better established by written history and living witnesses, than the story of the Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island.

transcripts: Island woman's origins still hotly debated Alaska theory, despite support, angers experts, traditionalists By Barney Brantingham News-Press Staff Writer What would you think if the storied Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island turned out to have been an Alaskan, not a local Indian? Ho, hum? Or anger at anyone having the nerve to challenge one of our most cherished legends? Maria Daily, chronicler of the Channel Islands, felt the savage whip of scientists a few years ago. That's because she ventured to suggest in an article in "California's History" that the Alaskan scenario should be explored. After she presented a paper to archeologists meeting at the Museum of Natural History a few years ago, she got letters slamming her ideas as absurd. "People were upset. I got a bunch of letters that this was an absurd hypothesis," she said. "People don't want their bubbles to be burst. "I'm not saying she is or she isn't" Alaskan, Daily said, just that the question needs to be examined. After my recent Santa Barbara Yesterdays column, Los Olivos history buff Jim Norris also questioned the origin of "Juana Maria." That was what Santa Barbara Mission padres named the woman after she was rescued in 1853 after an 18-year solitary sojourn on the bleak island. She was accidentally left behind when all other Indians were evacuated from San Nicolas in about 1835. "No one says 'Juana Maria' was Chumash except a Harrington interviewee many years after the event." Norris said John P. Harrington was a noted local researcher into Chumash culture. "I would suggest she was Alaskan Indian left with otter hunters around 1805-20," Norris said. Norris and Michael Redmon, librarian at the Santa Barbara Historical Society Museum, also questioned the authenticity of a commonly used photo of "Juana Maria," which appeared with my column. Redmon said Southern California historians had raised questions about it. The woman pictured appears well-fed despite her many years subsisting on island fare, and younger than someone described as middle-aged. Norris is suspicious of it. "Do we have any other Santa Barbara photos from 1853?" he asked. The woman died seven weeks after her rescue, apparently as a reaction to rich foods she was offered. In her paper, Daily, of the Santa Cruz Island Foundation, raises some key points. First of all, residents of San Nicolas, one of the four southernmost channel islands, were Gabrielino Indians. Those of the four northern ones were Chumash, she said. After being brought to Santa Barbara, the woman chattered on in a language no local Indian could understand, according to accounts. Emma Hardacre, a Santa Barbaran who studied the Lone Woman legend years after Juana Maria's death, doubted that she was an island Indian, according to Daily. She behaved like a woman "who had knowledge of the amenities of life," Hardacre said, not like someone raised on a barren island. Then there were the dogs. When otter hunters George Nidever and Charley Brown, a German whose real name was Carl Dittman, rescued Juana Maria, they found wild dogs on San Nicolas. "They were about the size and form of a coyote, of a black and white color," Nidever said. "I have seen the same kind of dogs among the Northwest Indians." Nidever went back to shoot the dogs so he could run sheep there. His son later reported that Nidever told him they were "of the Alaskan breed." "Indians from the north, particularly peoples from Kodiak Island and the Aleutian Islands, participated in the California sea otter trade on and around San Nicolas during the first part of the 19th century," Daily said. Juana Maria's story was fictionalized in the 1961 book by Scott O'Dell, "Island of the Blue Dolphins."
