transcripts: By CLARENCE E. EDWORDS. ALEXANDER SELKIRK had his Daniel Defoe to immortalize him and the island of Juan Fernandez, and in every man's memory lingers the delights of hours spent with Robinson Crusoe wandering over his little empire with his man Friday and his parrot and goats, but the chronicler of the weary months and years of waiting spent by a lone Indian woman on San Clemente island, off the southern coast of California, is yet to come. It has been many years since she was found and taken to a hospitable home in Santa Barbara, and still no one has taken her wonderful experience as the theme for a novel, nor has San Clemente island achieved notice because of her habitation thereon for eighteen years in solitude. Along the southern coast of the State this island is better known as the Island of Skulls than by its geographical name, and while the peculiar features of the semi-desert bit of land have appealed to popular fancy little attention has been given to either the marooned woman or the reason why she was there. In fact, her very presence and rescue are almost looked upon as myths by the later residents who have gradually taken the places of the first population of Ventura and Santa Barbara counties. San C[l]emente's shores are bleak and drear, guarded by inhospitable coasts, where rock and wave of restless ocean serve to keep off all except those who are driven by necessity or curiousity to visit the land. High cliffs, running up thousands of feet above the water, seem to guard the secrets of the island, and there is nothing inviting in the appearance or the prospects of the land. For this reason all early navigators passed the island by, and thus it came about that the lone Indian woman finally ceased to hope for rescue, and, with the stolidity of her race, abandoned herself to her fate, thinking, if she ever thought at all, that she would end her days near where her baby had perished at the time she was left to live or die as fate willed. For eighteen long years she had lived alone, eking out an existence from the shellfish which are so abundant on these California islands, and so far had her mind wandered from the normal that when Captain Nidever happened to notice from the deck of his vessel that a human being was on the island, she fled to the interior like some wild thing, afraid of her own kind. Nor was her rescue accomplished without a long search, and then almost a battle before she could be induced to accompany her captors. Record of Adventure. There is still record of the captain's adventure, told in his own language, and from it we may learn of the conditions on the island, more than thirty years ago, when he found the solitary woman. His is a plain, blunt tale, divested of all attempt at sensationalism, simply reciting the incident as if [it] were but one of many strange happenings which came to him in his roving life on the high seas. "Light winds and calms had marked the voyage up the coast," writes Captain Nidever, "and as we came to the outer island we were carried close in shore by a current. It was a clear day with but little wind and we could see everything on the island plainly. As I looked up to the top of the high cliff which bordered the ocean I thought I saw a man, and on getting my glass I plainly made him out. He was without any clothing, and seemed to try to avoid being seen. I was sure it was some person who had been marooned and I made landing after anchoring just off shore in a little bay. I took three sailors with me and searched the island for a long time without finding any one, but I saw that some one [sic] was there, for I came upon piles of shells from clams and other shellfish. When we got over toward t[h]e interior of the island we came upon a great pile of bones, among which were human skulls and leg and arm bones. It looked as if there had been a battle and a great number of people killed. We found a trail leading into the hills near a spring, and on following it we came upon a cave. Here we found a woman so wild that she fought and scratched us when we took hold of her. She had no weapons, but used her hands and rocks. We finally overpowered her and took her to the vessel, where we gave her clothing to cover herself, as she was naked. I tried to talk to her, but she could not understand Spanish, English or any of the Indian languages which I knew. She seemed frightened at first and we could not get anything out of her, but before we reached shore she tried to make signs which we could not understand. [I] took her to my house, where she stayed until she died, about a year later." The captain did not tell the entire story, for he was not a novelist and could not see the wonderful part of the incident. To him it was but a human being rescued and cared for, and [hi]s great heart did not stop with taking the woman from her prison, but her welfare was looked after by him until she died. Remains a Mystery. Who this woman was, what her tribe, and why she was left on the island for all those years, are mysteries which will never be solved, for all who by any possibility might know something about it died long before she was taken to the mainland. Two stories have remained from the day when she was taken to the home of Captain Nidever, both, however, being surmises for she could never explain the cause of her exile. The most prevalent story, and at the same time the most improbable, is that when the Spanish owners of the land visited the island of San Clemente they found a tribe of Indians on the verge of starvation, and decided to take them to the mainland, where they could be cared for. All the Indians were taken to a vessel, and as they were preparing to set sail this woman remembered that she had left her baby behind. She rushed back after the little one and before she returned a storm arose which drove the ship to sea, and it was impossible to again make a landing. The vessel sailed for the mainland, the authorities intending to return for the woman when the weather became settled, but as time passed she was forgotten and left to her fate. According to the story the baby died from exposure and hunger, but the woman lived on shell fish. The improbability of this story lies in the fact that the Spanish who thought enough of humanity to take a whole tribe of Indians away from starvation would scarcely leave a woman to starve alone with her baby. That no tribe of Indians was taken from the island is further established by the fact that when the woman was taken to Santa Barbara the Indians of the country for miles up and down the coast and in the interior were brought to see if they could talk with her. She could understand none of the languages, nor could any of the old Indians remember anything about the incident, nor could they understand even one word used by the woman. Through the sign language she made known a few of her wants, and by signs she told of the eighteen years that had passed since she was left alone. It is extremely probable, however, that many more than eighteen years had passed, for the passage of time would be uncounted after a few years. This story is generally accepted because it is considered the most plausible by the unthinking, but to my mind the other story, even thought it be almost a legend, more readily accounts for the woman's presence on the island, as it also accounts for the numerous skeletons which are found scattered over the place. The Pirate Theory. According to this second story San Clemente island was at one time densely populated by a strong and war-like tribe of Indians which waged war on the tribes of the mainland to such an extent that all communication between them was severed. The island Indians were savage, and refused all connection with other tribes, and made a practice of eating those of their enemies who fell into their hands. It is supposed that the Seri Indians who now inhabit the Tiburón island in the gulf of California are a part of the same race, and are probably the descendants of those who were formerly the inhabitants of the Island of Skulls. In the early days, so the story runs, Russian pirates sailed down the shores of California and devastated all the towns along the coast. These pirates happened to be driven to the island where this tribe made its home, and a battle ensued, which ended only with the extinction of the savages with the exception of one woman, who hid in a cave until the invaders had departed. This story accounts for the pile of bones which is still to be seen on the island, but it, too, has the elements of the mythical, for it has been many years since Russian pirates sailed the waters of the California coast, and as there are no records of such devastation by these corsairs it must be taken as the invention of some one [sic] who desired to account for the unaccountable. It is a fact that the woman herself could not tell anything about either the reason for her isolation nor for the presence of the numerous skulls of human beings which lie scattered over a great space on one part of the island. When found the woman was strong and healthy, but good care and the confinement of civilized life did not agree with her, and she had been in the care of Captain Nidever but a few months until she sickened. It seemed as if the long life in the open air had brought about a bodily condition which resented the indoor life of civilization, and a cold soon changed into consumption, which carried her off despite all the care that could be given her. When she died she was just beginning to talk a little English, but not enough to give any account of her adventures or of the cause of the pile of skulls and bones which lies scattered over the island. This being the case, we can but speculate on these causes, and one man's theory is as good as another's. Lived on Shell Fish. According to the statements of those who found the woman, she had lost the art of making a fire, and lived entirely on raw shell fish and such berries and roots as she found on the island. There had evidently been huts on the island when the tribe was living there, but these had all been destroyed by the elements, and the woman made her habitation in a cave, or rather depression in the side of the cliff, which formed a shelter from the wind and rain. Her domestic habit remained with her, as is evidenced by an immense pile of abalone shells near where she made her home. A mass of seaweed and brush formed her bed, and, as she had no method of replenishing her clothing, she finally became naked, and it is probable that she went this way for many years. How she occupied her time, and why she did not cast herself into the sea rather than undergo the loneliness and desolation of her surroundings can be understood only by understanding the Indian mind. Her reversion to complete savagery, leaving nothing but the animal in her to fight for life against all the adverse circumstances surrounding her, was a natural sequence of the accident which marooned her, and even to the day of her death she showed a fear of other Indians, with the exception of one woman to whom she became deeply attached. The approach to San Clemente island seems barred by the high cliffs which face the sea, but as one gets closer he finds numerous little bays and inlets, and except in stormy weather the landing is easy. The hills, which rise almost from the water's edge, present a most picturesque appearance, with deep indentations traversing them in every direction. Color and form blend admirably to make a beautiful picture, and give an inviting prospect which belies the dreary aspect presented after one lands on the island and goes into the interior. All the hills seem to be covered with the softest verdure; but as one gets closer it is noticed that the coloring comes from the earth and not from growth. These cliffs rise fully a thousand feet from the sea, and are the nesting place of myriads of sea birds of many kinds. Here the murre, the tern, the gull and various other feathered inhabitants make their home, undisturbed by man or other enemy, and undoubtedly the female Crusoe, who remained so long as their neighbor, must have utilized their eggs as a part of her food supply. Not the least strange feature of the island is a peculiar formation of rock which takes on queer and weird forms, resembling to a marked degree petrifactions of trees. Those who have been in Monument Park, in Colorado, will understand the idea, for it is very similar. Like so many small tree trunks, bereft of branches, these rocks rise in every direction, ranging in size from small saplings to trees a foot in diameter. Investigation shows, however, that they are not petrifactions, but are sandstone formations which have been cut by nature's sand blast into the shapes they now present. Standing erect, as they do, in the midst of a waste of sand, they present a most drear and desolate appearance. It looks as if some mighty cataclysm had swept over the place, arresting all growth, and preserving conditions of a dead and gone age. Were one to permit his imagination to run riot, as the conditions would warrant, he might well believe that the ghosts of those who had fought the battle which left the plain strewn with skeletons, were still standing guard over the land for which they struggled. Go there on some moonlight night and the feeling changes into the uncanny, and chills chase each other up and down the spines of even the bravest men. Some of these formations take on the appearance of animals, and some of human beings, while it is easy to see gnomes working their unholy spite against mortals who dare to invade their realm. It can readily be seen why the Indians of the mainland shun this island, and why it is impossible to get any of them to go ashore. They have the hereditary fear of the cannibals who once inhabited the place handed down through generations and changed with the changing times until now they no longer understand either cannibal or enemy in their terror, but fear the spirits of evil whom they believe haunt the place where so many bones attest the death of an unknown people. So deep rooted is the fear of the island that few of the mainland Indians will even talk about it or the sights that are to be seen there. They have heard of the dead bodies and of the strange formations and are content to let it rest with the hearing. They have not been to the island nor will they ever go unless they are driven there through stress of weather when they happen to be fishing off shore and are caught in a storm. Skeletons of Humans. Lying some eighty miles southwest of the city of San Buena Ventura and away from the other islands of the Santa Barbara chain which forms the outer circle of the channel made famous because of its use by the national war ships in their trials of speed, San Clemente island is little visited and little known. There is nothing on the island to invite those commercially incl[i]ned, and its archaeological opportunities have attracted but few scientists on account of the difficulty experienced in reaching the island and the obstacles in the way of enjoying a sojourn there. For this reason, perhaps, the island is little known. What is known is of a nature to invite only the most ardent student, for outside of the queer formations mentioned but two facts are of importance. Along the mainland, from Lower California clear up to the Columbia river are to be found mounds containing what is known as kitchen-middens where vanished Indian tribes once had their homes. On San Clemente island is a kitchen-midden of most peculiar nature, in that it is composed almost entirely of red abalone shells. These shells lie scattered all over a tract of the island where the tribe evidently had its permanent domicile, and as the wind blows and the sands shift these shells, change their position, become uncovered, and are again buried in the sand. Along the shore of the island these abalones are found in great quanitities, and from the size of the pile of shells on the mound they evidently formed an important part of the provisions of the Indians. But it is to the skeletons of human beings that the island owes its greatest prominence. On the side of a sand-covered slope, extending from the sea to the interior hills of the island are found hundreds of bones of men and women, and even of little children. Skulls by the dozen are there, and while nearly all of them have the characteristics of the savage races, some have the appearance of the Caucasian, and this leads to the belief that the bones are those of the men who fell in battle between the Indians and Russian pirates. The dry atmosphere of the island has preserved the bones to such an extent that it is impossible to tell the age, or rather, the time that has elapsed since the people were killed. One of the strange features of these bones is the fact that none of them show indications of having been broken by weapons. The skulls are intact and in several instances the bones lie just as they would normally, there being no animals on the island to disturb them. It is easy to see from an examination of these bones that two races are represented, for some of them are very large, while the most of them are of people under the average size. The bones of the women and children are all of the Indian type, but among the men many are large framed and the larger skulls show a higher type of intellect. This admixture of the skeletons of two distinct people is of itself a refutation of the belief that these skeletons are of a tribe that was swept away by an epidemic of by starvation. While many utensils used in grinding corn and in cooking are found scattered among the bones, and also among the shells of the kitchen-midden, neither spear nor arrow head is to be found. Possibly such as may have been there among the bones on the field of battle were carried away by the earlier discoverers of the place, who took the relics most easily cared for. It would seem probable that with all these skeletons there would be a few evidences of a fierce fight, but, as before mentioned, no bones show marks of wounds and no remains of weapons of any character are to be found. Several well-preserved Indian mortars used in grinding corn are scattered over the ground among the bones, and also among the abalone shells, and in several places are broken bits of pottery of the crudest kind. This pottery, as well as the mortars, has evidently been brought to the island, for there are no evidences of kilns for burning the pottery, and the mortars are made of a stone foreign to the island. Another legend which accounts for the presence of these bones is that the island was sacred to a certain tribe which used it only on ceremonial occasions when they took their prisoners there and held feasts on human flesh. According to this story no people inhabited the island, but on periodical occasions this cannibalistic tribe went there, and after feasting, left the bones, which gradually accumulated. According to this theory the woman who was rescued was one of the prisoners who escaped by some means and remained hidden away for many years, even after the coming of the whites caused a cessation of the savage rites. Many things connected with the bones as well as with the island, bear out this theory, and also account for the fact that no weapons have been found, and that the bones show no evidences of injury by w[o]unds.

title: "San Nicolas Island" in "The Islands Considered Separately"
publication: An Account of the Indians of the Santa Barbara Islands in California
tropes: Vanishing Indians; Indians as Savage; No Boat Available; Indian Queen; Noble Savage; Signs Easily Interpreted
author: Gustav Eisen
transcripts: <emph>San Nicolas Island</emph>. So named on the chart of Viscaino. It is the one most distant from the mainland and one of the least fertile, poorest of the islands. It is 890 feet high and can be seen 34 miles away. The island is about 8 to 20 miles long. This island is interesting, because on it lived the last remnant of the Indians belonging to the island tribes, indeed the only Indian of whom we have a detailed account. The island was like the others once thickly populated, but little by little the number of inhabitants became less. The reason is not fully known. But it is by some believed that the natives were partly exterminated by Indians from Alaska who had been brought down to these islands to hunt seaotter. Any how it is known that already in 1811 a ship from Boston had landed some 30 Indians from Kodiak on San Nicolas and it is said that they killed all the native men, and appropriated the women. However this may be, certain it is that in 1835 the natives on the island had dwindled down to 18, and it was decided by the missionaries on the mainland to remove these Indians to the missions of the mainland. Accordingly a vessel was sent to the island of San Nicolas and the Indians gathered in. This was in 1836. But when the Indians were all embarked, one of the women missed her babe. It had been left behind in some way. The mother started to hunt for it, but remaining away very long, and on account of a sudden and very heavy wind, the small vessel had to leave and lie before the wind out to sea. In course of time the Indians were landed at Santa Barbara and probably merged in other indian tribes. The vessel which was again to visit the island in order to bring back the remaining woman, was unfortunately shipwrecked on the coast, and as there was no other vessel of sufficient size to brave the rough waters around the island, it came to pass that for 18 long years the indian woman was left to her fate on the island. It was only in 1853 that a hunter with the name of Nidever from Santa Barbara visited the island and brought the woman away. He had seen some things of her already two years previously, but was then unable to find her. During this visit Nidever had seen several small windbreaks made of branches and canes. They were in the form of a half circle and bound together with grass ropes. He had also found regular, small, pyramidal houses or Indian huts made of branches etc., but the grass growing in them, and their dilapidated condition generally indicated that they bad not been used for years. When he found the woman at last she was living in such a windbreak. We may now follow Nidevers [Nidever's] tale: "She was sitting in an enclosure, so that her head and shoulders were barely visible above it. As the white man approached, two or three wild dogs began to howl, but she gave a yell at the dogs who then disappeared. She was sitting crosslegged on some grass that coverad the ground within the inclosure and which seemed to serve as bed. Her only dress consisted of a kind of gown, leaving her neck and shoulders bare, but it was long enough when she stood up to reach to her ankles. It was made of bird (shag) skin cut in squares and sewed together, the feathers pointing downwards. Her head had no covering save a thick mass of matted hair of a yellowish brown color, and which looked as if it bad rotted off. (See the account of Cabrillo and Viscaino of the fair color of the Indians). She was engaged in stripping a piece of blubber from a sealskin. Within the enclosure was a smouldering fire and a heap of ashes. She was constantly talking to herself. When first seeing Mr Brown the companion of Mr Nidever she smiled and received him most graciously and with much dignity and selfpossession [self possession]. And when the other men came up, she greeted them in the same manner. The Indians which Mr. Brown had brought along did not understand a single word of what she said, although they knew several different dialects. From a bag she took out several roots (carcomites(?), also other roots, and roasting them on the fire she offered them to the men to eat. They found them very palatable. The visitors soon made her to understand that they wanted her to leave the island with them, and gathering up her belongings she was soon ready to start. She packed most of the things in a large basket made of rushes, while other of her things were bundled up by her visitors. She had so many things that every one of the visitors carried some of her belongings when leaving. Among her things was an extra dress made of fine birdskins and finely ornamented. She also insisted upon carrying off all the old dried blubber, and a seal's head which was so decayed that the brain was oozing out. She evidently desired to bring every thing that would sustain life. When all was ready she took from the fire a burning stick in her band and walked out. She led the party by a fine spring from which she drank, and then led them to an other spring in which she washed her face and hands. The island was inhabited by foxes and by wild dogs, similar to those which Nidever had seen among the Indians of the northern part of California. The indian woman took kindly to the food of her visitors, and evidently preferred it to the one she had been accustomed to. She was exuberant when one of the men made her a dress of calico, and observing how the man was sewing she insisted to try her hand at this too. She would push the needle in the cloth with her right hand and pull it out with her left one. At first she did not know how to thread the needle, but she learned quickly. In the hunters camp she made herself useful, in carrying wood and water. She occupied herself with making several baskets, but she worked at several at the same time, first doing a little work on one and then dropping it for another. She made the baskets watertight by placing inside several lumps of asphaltum together with some few heated pebbles. The asphaltum melting she gave the pebbles a rotary motion which soon covered the interior of the baskets with an even watertight coating, after which the pebbles were thrown out. During a storm that threatened to upset the small boat she made signs that she could stop the gale. Kneeling down on deck and facing the wind she began incantations and prayers. When the sky suddenly showed sign of clearing she pointed to it with pride as if to say "see I did it". She had never been on the mainland before, and she showed great astonishment at every thing she saw. She showed a childish delight when she saw an ox-cart, and quickly immitated the revolving motion of the wheels with her hand and arms. And when a gentleman rode down to the beach she was evidently dumbfounded by seeing him on the horse. She quickly immitated the motion of the horse by placing her first two fingers of her right hand over the thumb of her left hand, and mimicking the galloping of the horse she gave a shout of delight. She was taken care of by the family of Mr. Nidever and had every thing she wanted. She could however only communicate by signs as there was no one to understand her language. An other old indian woman was said to understand a few words (according to Hittell's History, but I do not find it mentioned in Nidever's account), but otherwise there was none who could understand her. She soon became an expert in using signs, and after a few months made herself well understood that way. She was passionately fond of fruits and would eat them constantly. This brought on a dysentery from which she did not recover. She did not survive more than four months her removal from the island. "She had a warm love, was grateful and affectionate as a child, and was of a gentle and lovable nature". After her death her belongings were gathered together and sent to Rome! except a water bottle made of rushes and covered with asphaltum, which bottle is now in the posession of the California Academy of Sciences San Francisco. It was not until a short time before she died that she understood that they wished to know some thing of her language. Only a few words of hers are now preserved : Hide = tocah; Man = nache; Sky = toygwah; Body = puoochay. From signs that she made they understood that the wild dogs had eaten her child, and that when she found it out she lay down on the ground and cried. When she at last got up and returned to the schooner it had already left. She had a generous nature and when given trinkets etc. she would soon give them away, just as did the Indians met by Cabrillo and Viscaino.

title: "H. The Lone Woman of San Nicolas"
tropes: Jump Overboard; Signs Easily Interpreted; Wild Child; Noble Savage
author: Zephyrin Engelhardt
image_description: Y--image of SBMission fathers 1889
transcripts: THE LONE WOMAN OF SAN NICOLAS ISLAND. In the latter part of the nineteenth century much was written and printed about an Indian woman said to have been rescued from one of the Santa Barbara Channel Islands. We have before us three different versions which agree on the main points, but vary in details. In brief, the story is to the effect that in 1835 the Fathers of Santa Barbara Mission had the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> (Worse is Nothing), Captain Charles Hubbard, sail over to San Nicolas Island, the farthest from the mainland, in order to bring the islanders to the coast. The weather was stormy when the vessel reached the island. The Indians, about twenty in number, were hurried into the boats, and all speed was made to reach the schooner. In the excitement a child was left behind which the mother supposed had been carried aboard in the arms of a sailor. The frantic mother implored the men to return. The captain, however, replied that he must reach a place of safety, but that later they would go back for the baby. Thereupon, the mother, a widow of about twenty-five years of age, jumped overboard and struck out through the kelpy waters for the island shore. In a moment she was lost in the seething waves. The ship with the affrighted islanders huddled together on deck staggered through the boiling waves and storm, and eventually reached San Pedro. Some of the Indians were sent to Los Angeles, others went to San Gabriel. Captain Hubbard wanted to return to San Nicolas Island, but the ship was in demand on the coast, and so the woman and her babe were forgotten. Their uncertain fate lay heavy on the kind-hearted Mission Fathers; but it was not till 1850 that Fr. González Rúbio found a man, Thomas Jeffries, who for $200 agreed to visit the island and bring over the woman and child. He made the attempt, but found no living being on the island. In the following year, George Nidever of Santa Barbara, a convert to the Catholic Faith, accompanied by Jeffries and a crew of Indians, sailed over to San Nicolas, and remained there six weeks without discovering any trace of the woman. In 1852 another unsuccessful trip was made. In July, 1853, Mr. Nidever made one more attempt in company with Carl Ditman, <emph>alias</emph> Charlie Brown, an Irish cook, and a crew of Mission Indians. This time the woman was discovered, and willingly came along to Santa Barbara, where Nidever had his family care for her in his own house. Whatever her language, no one could be found along the coast who understood her, nor could she make out what was said to her in Spanish or in any of the dialects spoken among the shore Indians. So she managed to make herself understood by means of signs. When discovered she wore a gown made of bird skins and feathers. On shore she enjoyed her new life, and displayed no symptoms of ferocity. She would go around to different homes and dance Indian dances, Mr. Nidever relates. Clothes were her especial delight. Unfortunately, change of diet cut short the life of Juana Maria; for under that name she was conditionally baptized by Father Sanchez, according to Brown. She would doubtless have lived many years, had some caution been exercised with regard to her food; but she was supplied to her heart's content with dainty foods, from which she gradually sickened and died. It was also claimed that Juana Maria after her death found her resting-place in the cemetery of Santa Barbara Mission. Such is the story in brief of the Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island. Were it not that Mr. Nidever's fame for veracity appears above suspicion, we should declare the whole story a myth, for the reason that, after a close examination of the Baptismal Registers at the Mission and at the Parish Church of Santa Barbara, we failed to discover any entry recording the woman's Baptism in either the Mission or the Parish Church. Likewise, there is no record noted of her burial in the Mission Cemetery. "That the story is literally true," writes Stephen Bowers in the <emph>Ventura Observer</emph>, December 20, 1892, "there can be no doubt whatever. We received it from Captain Nidever's own lips several years before his death. The writer was personally acquainted with him from 1874 until his death which occurred about 1886. He was much respected in Santa Barbara, where he lived more than fifty years. We never heard his integrity called in question by anyone. . . . The account may also be found in the archives of the Santa Barbara Mission, preserved by the Mission Fathers. We secured a translation of their record of the event by a competent Spanish scholar fifteen years ago." Bancroft corroborates what Mr. Bowers says of Mr. Nidever; but the last statement regarding the presence in the Mission Archives of a paper or document containing the story of the Lone Woman we cannot verify. We found no such account among the numerous papers in the Mission Archives nor anywhere else.

title: "Story of a Woman Crusoe. Unlike Defoe's Hero, Her End Is Pathetic in the Extreme"
tropes: Girl Crusoe; Noble Savage; Wild Child
author: [Frank Gassaway]
transcripts: STORY OF A WOMAN CRUSOE. Unlike Defoe's Hero, Her End Is Pathetic in the Extreme. Beginning due west of Point Conception on the California coast and continuing at irregular intervals as far south as the bay of Todos Santos, in Lower California the lie the Channel Islands. In this ideal region for the yachtman, the fisherman and the hunter, one comes to fell like a new Crusoe on his primitive isle. And in very truth Crusoe'ssemi-mythical story was enacted upon oneself these same islands, though minus the man Friday and the happy ending. The castaway in this case was a woman, a Danish imigrant left ashore through some mischence by the crew of a vessel that had sought shelter behind San Nicholas during a storm in the early '50s. For over seventeen years the lone creature lived unsought and forgotten, though the time at length came when, on the days the mist-clearing north wind blew, she could climb to the island's highest point and view the ranchers' herds grazing upon the mainland. And at last, when hope and reason had both long died, the poor, wild, gibbering creature was found in her wolf's burrow among the hills by the advance guard of the otter hunters' fraternity, who had long wondered at the mysterious footprints they marked upon the lonely sands.—Field and Stream.

title: "Alone For Eighteen Years. Indian Woman, Abandoned on Desert Island, Finally Found by Party of Otter Hunters"
tropes: Discovery; Wonder; Girl Crusoe; Wild Child; Jump Overboard
transcripts: <hi rend="bold">ALONE FOR EIGHTEEN YEARS</hi> <hi rend="bold">Indian Woman, Abandoned on Desert Island, Finally Found by Party of Otter Hunters.</hi> On San Nicholas island, which is uninhabited, a party of sea-otter hunters, landing to chance their luck, found, to their amazement, the imprint of human feet on the sandy shore—imprints freshly made. They scattered in search. But, the wind shifting and commencing to blow hard, they had to regain their vessel before the maker of the marks could be found. It was undeniable, however, a human being lived on this bleak, wind-blown island of sand and tall brushwood. On returning to the mainland they reported the strange discovery, but nothing was done until a Roman Catholic priest was so moved by the news that he persuaded the captain of a small schooner to sail with him for San Nicolas. After two days' searching he discovered this lonely Crusoe—the first of a new kind. For he found inside a low hut of driftwood a woman more like a beast than a person. She was clad in otter skins, and the feathered skins of the sea-fowl, and her companion was an otter, which she had caught very young and tamed. The priest with difficulty got her story, for she had almost forgotten how to speak. Many years previously the small tribe of Indians to which she belonged—inhabitants of San Nicolas from time past—had been shifted by the government to the mainland. As they were being taken on board, her baby had fallen into the sea, and she had leaped after him, and in the dusk had been given up as drowned. She reached the shore, however, to find the child was dead. In utter loneliness she had lived there for 18 years.

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">A Female Crusoe.</hi> A correspondent of the Newburyport <emph>Herald</emph>, tells the following tale: SANTA BARBARA, CAL., September 11, 1853.} We have now at Santa Barbara a great curiosity, it is an Indian woman who has lived for 18 years alone upon the Island of San Nicholas, a small island about 45 miles from this place, during which time she has not seen the face of a human being. This island was once peopled by a tribe of Indians, to whom the Northwest tribes were hostile. To preserve the remnant of this tribe from destruction, as well as with a view to christianize them, the Padres induced them to come to the mainland 18 years ago. After they were all on board the vessel sent for them, this woman swam ashore to look for her child which had been left; and a storm springing up in the night, the vessel was compelled to put to sea; on returning she could not be found. She was known to be alive by those who at times visited the island, for the purpose of hunting otters, from the marks of fires and from foot-prints in the sand. On being approached the other day she manifested much joy which she betrayed by signs of the most significant character, and at once commenced packing up her few articles of furniture. Whether the sounds that she uttered are words or not has not yet been ascertained. The man who found her is familiar with five or six Indian languages, but he was unable to understand a single expression; it is more than probable that she had forgotten her native tongue entirely. Her clothing consists of skins of birds, sewed together with the fibres of some tree or plant. Her food has been shell-fish, seals, and a small bulbous root, similar in appearance to an onion, but wholly tasteless. The needles with which she stitched her garments are made of the sharp bones of a fish. She had two hooks made of a bent nail and sharpened by the friction on a stone. Her lines were beautifully twisted from the sinews of some animal, probably a species of fox which abounds on the island. Her age, as near as can be estimated, is about 55 or 60. Her features are quite masculine, and her hair of the color of dark brown, and very fine. This is very remarkable for an Indian; their hair you know, is always jet black and coarse. In some future letter I will give you a more extended account of this marvel of the 19th century. She is truly an object for the reflection of the philosopher and the inspection of the curious. Yours, &c. C.

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">The Tragedy of San Nicholas Island</hi> <hi rend="bold">By MRS. F. H. DUDLEY, Ventura, Cal.</hi> <hi rend="bold">An Honorable Mention in the Storiette Contest.</hi> The story of the Indian Woman left alone on the island of San Nicholas for nearly twenty years, has been written by a number of romancers, who gave but little heed to facts and free reign to the imagination. From occurrences that have passed into history and are known to be authentic, this tale is drawn. The aborigines of San Nicholas Island were supposed to be of Aztec or Toltec origin, a peaceable people like all tribes indigenous to the tropics. War with the savage Alaskan Indians had nearly exterminated the Indians of San Nicholas, when the Catholic fathers who founded the Missions on the mainland, desired to bring the few remaining natives across the channel that they might teach them the Christian religion. Accordingly, after repeated efforts to accomplish this, a schooner was sent to the island in 1836 for this purpose. Some time was consumed in gathering together these people and their effects. As the last boat was leaving the strand, a woman with a young babe in her arms, sprang on shore. Her little girl, a child of eight years, had slipped from her side in the confusion—gone possibly in search of some remembered trinket dear to her childish heart—or perhaps overcome with terror at the unusual migration of her people. The woman besought them to await her return, and hastened over the hill, calling as she went. The moments passed—the white man is ever impatient, and he grumbled at the delay. An hour went by, but the woman had not returned. The wind was rising rapidly, and a storm was imminent. The schooner had signaled them twice in the last half hour. The waters about the island were shoal and there was no safe anchorage along its shores. The waves were running high upon the ledges surrounding the little bay, and their crests were white with the foam of action. The ship signaled again, and with a muttered imprecation and a gruff command, the boat pushed off to join the tossing vessel. As soon as all were on board, Captain Hubbard weighed anchor and stood away for deep water. When the relatives and friends learned that the woman had been left behind, they besought the captain with many tears, and with pleadings in their own tongue, to return and bring her away. The gale increased in fury and containued [continued] unabated for the space of a week. The heavy laden schooner labored hard, and disaster threatened. When San Pedro Harbor was finally reached, the San Nicholas Indians were distributed between Los Angeles and San Gabriel Missions, and Captain Hubbard departed for Monterey, where he had orders to take on a cargo of lumber for Port San Francisco. On reaching the Golden Gate in rough weather, the improperly laden craft capsized and was eventually blown out to sea and is supposed to have been taken by a Russian vessel. The crew reached shore in safety, and it was always Captain Hubbard's intention to return to San Nicholas for the lost woman. There was now no craft of any description except open boats and Indian canoes from San Francisco to San Diego, and no one could be found willing to risk a voyage to San Nicolas in one of these. It was generally known along the coast of California that an Indian woman and her children had been left upon the island of San Nicholas,—but as time passed and they were not rescued it came to be generally believed that all had perished, and thus they were left in their cruel isolation. The white man sat at his own fireside, and said complacently, "They are dead. If not, what matters it? 'Tis only an Indian woman and her savage progeny." Fifteen years slipped by, and in the spring of 1851, Captain Nidever, of Santa Barbara, with one other white man and a small crew of Mission Indians, visited San Nicolas in a schooner in search of otter. They made a landing at the eastern end of the island, and walked along the southern shore a distance of five miles or more. Captain Nidever discovered footprints of a human being soon after landing. These were no doubt made when the ground had been soaked by the previous winter rains, for the impressions were deep and quite dry and hard. The footprints were small, and the captain felt convinced that they were made by a woman. A short distance from the shore were found several circular, roofless huts made of brush about six feet in height and the same in diameter. These enclosures were fully a mile apart, and near them were stakes of drift wood driven into the ground, from which were suspended pieces of seal's blubber out of the reach of wild animals. The blubber was comparatively fresh, and had no doubt been placed there but a few weeks previous. Captain Nidever had landed upon San Nicolas early in the morning, intending to remain during the day to search for seal and otter, but near noon a northwester began blowing, and he hastened back to the schooner. Here they remained at anchor for eight days in the lee of the island, the sea being at times so rough and the wind so fierce that he expected momentarily to be driven from his anchorage. When the storm abated sufficiently, Captain Nidever returned to Santa Barbara without again landing upon the island. The next year he once more visited San Nicholas for game, landing near the same place as on his previous voyage. He and the ship's mate explored the island nearly to its western extremity. The blubber found on the previous visit had been replaced by a fresh stock. In the crotch of a tree near the west end of the island they found a basket containing a garment made of the skins of the cormorant, cut in squares and neatly pieced together, with the ends of the feathers all pointing downward. There were shell hooks, bone needles, a rope of sinew, and various trinkets in the basket with the robe. These things Captain Nidever scattered upon the ground, thinking if they were replaced on his next visit to the the tree, it would be conclusive evidence that the woman was still alive. After several days spent in securing seal and otter upon the ground already explored, another wind storm came on, and the spot containing the basket was not re-visited, and, as on all previous voyages, the woman was left to her fate and the schooner crossed to San Miguel island without her. In July, 1853, Captain Nidever again went to San Nicholas, determined to rescue the woman if she could be found. Before, he had gone to find otter and seal; now he had a nobler quest. He anchored midway of the northwestern shore of the island, near Corral Harbor, where the natives had embarked in 1836. At this point and at the western extremity of the island is found an abundance of good water, seal and fish. Here Captain Nidever made camp, and with his men began a systematic search. On the second day a hut was discovered upon the ridge, and on approaching it, piles of ashes and bones were seen at its entrance. Within the enclosure, sat the object of their search, talking aloud to herself, and with a rude knife, manufactured from a piece of rusty iron hoop, washed up by the waves, she was diligently scraping blubber from a piece of seal skin. She watched the approach of the men with interest, but made no attempt at flight. She was clothed in a garment of cormorant skins, which reached nearly to her ankles, and her throat and arms were bare. Her hair was yellowed by the sun and tangled, and her skin where exposed, was brown, but where protected by her robe, it was quite fair, showing her to be of Aztec or Toltec origin. She received her visitors with the quiet dignity of a queen, greeting each with a bow and smile. She talked incessantly, but no word of hers could be understood, although the Indians of the rescuing party spoke several dialects. In her hut was a fire, and when the Captain and his men were seated, the woman roasted roots, termed "carcomite," by Californians, which she served to the company on abalone shells. One day she took her new comrades to a deep hidden grotto, where bubbled a cool spring from whence she drew her supply of water for cooking. Here they found several unique water jars woven by her of the island grasses and lined with asphaltum, which is plentiful on the western shore. The water jars resembled wide-mouthed bottles, and would hold from two to six quarts. It was interesting to watch her make baskets water tight. She would drop into them, bits of asphaltum and hot pebbles, whirling them deftly as the asphaltum liquified. It required skill and patience, but when they were thoroughly glazed with a thin coating, the jars were both light and durable. A second spring near the above mentioned grotto, she used as a lavatory, and would frequently visit it for she was very cleanly in her habits. At the expiration of a month, when the schooner was ready to depart, she was made to understand by signs that she was to go on board. She evidenced the pathetic struggle she had waged with want in the years of solitude, by gathering together every fragment of food in her possession. In the crevices of rocks and in other spots secure from the depredations of the wild dogs which infested San Nicholas, she had laid up stores of bones and other refuse in anticipation of some future "starvation time." These she insisted should be carried with her. Once on board, and the firebrand she had bought burned to ashes, she clung closely to the stove, showing that she had often suffered from cold as well as hunger. Captain Nidever conveyed the Indian woman to his home in Santa Barbara, where she lived in his family until her death. She was supposed to be about fifty years of age when rescued. She had a docile, loving nature and was of a peculiarly happy disposition. How she had retained these qualities in her years of lonely life, is a mystery. She became much attached to her new friends, and they in turn gave her a most cordial affection. She was naturally intelligent and full of resources, and soon learned to communicate with those about her. She told of her sorrow at the death of her oldest child, who was devoured by wild dogs on the day her people were taken from the island by Captain Hubbard. The young babe met a similar fate later when the mother, driven by hunger, was forced to leave it unprotected to go in search of food. Strange to say, this woman had formulated an apparently fluent language of her own, which no one was able to understand. Three of the Mission fathers, versed in every Indian dialect on the California coast, were quite unable to make themselves understood. Some of the former inhabitants of San Nicolas were brought from San Gabriel and Los Angeles, but they also were unable to converse with her or interpret her language. But few of her words have been remembered. Man she called "noche," the sky, "toygwah," a hide, "tocah." Possibly the Alaskan Indians, who overran San Nicolas in in the early part of the last century, left upon her memory an indelible impression of their nomenclature, which superseded her native tongue in the years when human association was denied. This is a question that mght [might] be settled from the meager vocabulary she has left by some enthusiastic, painstaking student of philology. Travelers abroad who visit the Vatican in Rome, and are permitted to view the priceless relics from many lands that have been gathered there, will find among the collection a basket woven of island grasses, and within it a wonderful feather robe made of the soft breasts of the cormorant. This garment was fashioned by the deft fingers of Morenita, the lndan [Indian] woman, when she dwelt alone upon the island of San Nicolas.

transcripts: Notes and Queries [The editors will welcome as contributions to this section of the <emph>California Folklore Quarterly</emph> either small items of traditional materials or inquiries designed to elicit information about such materials. In general, discussion of the materials here offered will be brief. Records of facts likely to be lost or overlooked, and inquiries which our readers may be able to answer—such items will be the typical ones.] [...] <emph>The Wild Girl of the Santa Barbara Channel Islands</emph>.—I wonder if any of the readers of <emph>California Folklore Quarterly</emph> has heard versions of the following or similar story of the wild girl of the Santa Barbara Channel Islands? It was first told to me by Joseph Henniger, Los Angeles artist, as we were driving along the coast highway between Ventura and Santa Barbara, while one of the islands was in full view. That was in January, 1942. The present version was taken down stenographically from a second account given by Mr. Henniger in November. The story is so typical of the primitive animal-fed-child stories, of which the legends of Zeus and of Romulus and Remus are famous examples, that it deserves the attention of folklorists everywhere. The man who told this story was just loaded full of California folklore. He knew California history as well as anyone with whom I have come in contact. He was telling us one night that there was a very curious story told about a wild girl who was found here in California. All of this was apropos of the stories of children raised by wolves in India. A group of sportsmen living up at Santa Barbara decided to go over to hunt wild goats on one of the islands off the coast. No one had gone to this island for a number of years because it was very hard to reach. These men finally made the island, anchored the boat offshore, and went ashore in a small boat. They hunted for the day and in returning to the boat came across this curious creature who was running along the beach stark naked and tore up the side of the mountain as fast as a goat could go. One of the men asked the fellows if they had noticed this thing running along the beach; he would have sworn it was a young woman completely nude. The other fellows hadn't noticed it, but the man was so insistent that they climbed up the side of the mountain and found a cave and with their lights went in. They found this cave loaded full of bones—goats' bones, rabbits', etc. In the back of the cave they found this wild young girl. They tied her up and took her back to the boat and took her to the mainland. She couldn't speak any English. When they got to shore they put her in the hands of medical authorities who said she had been wild for several years. They delved back into the records of missing persons and [found that] in the year 1901 or 1902 a sailboat had set out from Santa Barbara with a man, his wife, and daughter a little over two. Several weeks later pieces of the boat were washed ashore but there were no signs of the bodies, and so these men concluded that what had happened was that this child had survived the storm. She had been old enough to walk and apparently had existed since that time on the island. She was removed to a hospital and the authorities did everything they could to cover up her predicament and hide her from the curious. The man who told Henniger the story was named Waddie, a certified public accountant. AUSTIN E. FIFE <emph>Santa Ana, California</emph>

"An Earthly Paradise. A Stranger's View of Santa Barbara, and Her Surroundings"
author: G. F. M.
transcripts: AN EARTHLY PARADISE. A Stranger's View of Santa Barbara and her Surroundings. (Correspondence of the Clinton[,] Mass., Courier.) SANTA BARBARA, Cal., Jan. 1881. At Point Conception the [co]ast of California makes a sudden turn from a southerly to an easterly direction, and runs east and west for fifty miles. About midway on this coast facing toward the south and entirely surrounded by mountains lies Santa Barbara. The cold winds have no chance to get at this little valley, protected as it is by the Santa Inez range. [sic] which rises 4,000 feet above the sea. The normal southerly direction of the coast line is continued from Point Conception to below Los Angeles by high and mountainous islands, on one of which, San Nicholas, an Indian woman spent eighteen years alone. The story of this woman's solitary confinement was given in full in <emph>Scribner's</emph> for September last. These islands form a barrier against all storms and soften the asperity of all winds blowing from the sea. There we see that nature has done all in her power to make the climate perfect. The mean winter temperature is 58¡ F. and the difference between the Winter and the Summer is only 15¡; then it is never cold in the Winter or hot in the Summer. It is very seldom that a frost is experienced, and therefore the flowers bloom the year through. Formerly nearly all the houses were made of adobe, but since the Americans have come, neat little cottages and elegant dwellings have sprung up, and fine business blocks have been built. A great many of the old adobes still exist, however, and add a picturesque appearance to the town. They are built of sun-dried bricks and retain their muddy color; the roofs are covered with tiles. Imagine a red earthenware drain-tile cut in halves longitudinally, making a semi-cylinder; these are placed in rows on their convex surfaces, lapping over like shingles; then to cover the cracks between two tiles, a third is placed over them on its concave face. The whole makes a heavy and not very protective, but yet a very picturesque covering. The main business thoroughfare is State street, and extends back two miles, directly from the steamboat wharf. The smaller streets branch off to the right and left like lesser arteries. THE ARLINGTON I[s] the principal hotel, and is unequalled south of San Francisco. The grounds are filled with choice varieties of semi-tropical plants and deer captured in the mountains. Nearly every little cottage has its pretty garden patch, and the people seem to vie with each other [in] keeping their grounds neat and inviting. In many of these gardens can be seen from seventy-five to ninety varieties of roses, geranium hedges, heliotrope, and fuchsias trained over the piazzas and full of blossoms, calla lilies four feet high and almost as common as weeds. The streets are shaded by the peculiar eucalyptus and the pepper tree. The eucalyptus or blue gum is a native of Australia, and grows straight and spindling to an immense height. The pepper has all of the grace of the willow, and is in addition an evergreen which in the Winter is covered with long panicles of bright red berries. In this country these trees grow so fast that in five years they will shade a house. In short, the whole town is one continuous garden. On Thanksgiving day one of the local preachers delivered a sermon in which he showed that his congregation had cause to be profoundly thankful for their good fortune in having such a place as Santa Barbara to live in, discoursing to some length on the different advantages of the same. Then, thinking he had dwelt long enough on earthly matters, he proceeded to say that the best of things must have an end, that they all must die some time and go to another world. He then endeavored to describe the abode of the blessed, and exhorted his listeners to so live that they should go there after death. In short the general impression left on the minds of his hearers was that heaven was really a very good place to go if—if they could not live in Santa Barbara. It is needless to say that the inhabitants of this earthly paradise thought it a remarkably fine sermon. Among the foothills, about 300 feet above the sea level, stands THE OLD MISSION built by the Spanish padres, one hundred years ago. It is built of adobe and sandstone in the Moorish style of architecture, is painted white, and with its two towers is a land mark [sic] for the country around. This Mission is a curious and interesting place. It is still kept up and there are five monks residing there at the present time. The walls are eight feet thick, and are covered on the inside with pictures, some of which were painted in Spain, long before the Mission itself was built. There are also a great many carvings in wood, marvelously well done; these were executed by the Mexican Indians. We made the acquaintance of Padre Francoir, who showed and explained to us the many interesting features of the place. In the vestry room we saw the antique vestments of the Church heavily wrought in gold and silver by the Spanish nuns; huge solid silver candlesticks and golden anchors. Then with great care Father Francoir unlocked a little gold casket, and lying beneath a glass plate was disclosed a bit of a bone formerly belonging to Santa Barbara herself. Away up in the old tower is a chime of bells, not especially musical, but "Like sweet bells jingled, out of tune and harsh." They seem to think it is necessary to ding them at all hours of the day and night, and they certainly do make a most infernal racket. At a little distance in the rear are the Mission water works, which furnish the city with water. The water is brought from a mountain caon and is exceedingly hard. REMARKABLE EQUESTRIANISM. The amusements prevalent here are, first, horseback riding—every one [sic] rides—they use the little broncho ponies and the great Mexican saddles, which almost cover up diminutive steeds. But to see riding, one must see the Mexicans themselves. Imagine a swarthy skinned, black-haired individual in a white sombrero and fiery red necktie, galloping along a little "calico" horse, with long flapping stirrup leathers, a Mexican bit and bridle, with the lines ending in a lash, which is twirled in the right hand of the rider. How they can ride! Not according to our severe method in the East, but easily and gracefully. It is said they can spread a blanket on the ground, run a horse onto it and turn him there. I have seen them ride along at full speed and pick a hat from the ground. They are like Centaurs. So much for the "Greaser." He can ride and throw the riata. These are his only accomplishments. The town is fast becoming a New England settlement. The Mexicans are being pushed to the wall and very bitter they feel toward the Americans, who are taking possession of their beautiful country. Another amusement is picnicing [sic] on the beach and surf bathing; the water is so warm that one can go in any season of the year. A ride of six miles up into the mountains takes one to the Hot Sulphur Springs, where one can take a bath in different springs in the rocks with the temperature varying from 115 degrees F. to 50 degrees; 115 degrees is fully hot enough, and just about as much as one can stand. These springs are said to be a sure cure for all rheumatic complaints. A ride of fifteen miles takes one to the big ranches of Hollister, Cooper and Stow. The first two men raise almonds, English walnut, [sic] (which are grown in their perfection here), apricot s [sic], limes, etc. Cooper raises the same variety, but devotes the greater part of attention to olives and to the production of olive oil. He is now producing an immense quantity, and although his price per bottle is 25 cents more than that of the French oil, he cannot begin to supply the market. These ranches were formerly over-run with grasshoppers, which came over from the <emph>mesa</emph> (table-lands) opposite, in clouds. Now the farmers go over in the breeding season and plow all of the eggs under ground [sic]. In this way they avoid the huge swarms. The farmers here cannot afford to raise vegetables for the market, the Chinese gardeners being their competitors. It is astonishing to see how cheaply they can afford to sell. A family can get all they can use in a day for five cents; for example, one can get two bunches of celery, two quarts of tomatoes, some turnips and a carrot, for the regular sum of five cents. They raise as a general thing six crops a year from a single piece of ground. In the character of any one [sic] who has lived any time in California, cordiality is the first thing noticed; the ability to tell big yarns is the next; (by the way I hope the readers of the <emph>Courant</emph> will not think that I have lived here long enough to be influenced.) Every where [sic] the stranger is welcomed and made to feel at home immediately. It is so different here in this respect from cold New England. I suppose it is all due to the climate. In my next letter I hope I may have something interesting to say of a journey on horse-back from Santa Barbara to Los Angeles. G. F. M.

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">ALONE FOR EIGHTEEN YEARS</hi> <hi rend="bold">Indian Woman, Abandoned on Desert Island, Finally Found by __group__Party of Otter Hunters.</hi> On San Nicholas island, which is uninhabited, a party of sea-otter hunters, landing to chance their luck, found, to their amazement, the imprint of human feet on the sandy shore—imprints freshly made. They scattered in search. But, the wind shifting and commencing to blow hard, they had to regain their vessel before the maker of the marks could be found. It was undeniable, however, a human being lived on this bleak, wind-blown island of sand and tall brushwood. On returning to the mainland they reported the strange discovery, but nothing was done until a Roman Catholic priest was so moved by the news that he persuaded the captain of a small schooner to sail with him for San Nicolas. After two days' searching he discovered this __person))lonely Crusoe—the first of a new kind. For he found inside a low hut of driftwood a woman more like a beast than a person. She was clad in otter skins, and the feathered skins of the sea-fowl, and her companion was an otter, which she had caught very young and tamed. The priest with difficulty got her story, for she had almost forgotten how to speak. Many years previously the small tribe of Indians to which she belonged—inhabitants of San Nicolas from time past—had been shifted by the government to the mainland. As they were being taken on board, her baby had fallen into the sea, and she had leaped after him, and in the dusk had been given up as drowned. She reached the shore, however, to find the child was dead. In utter loneliness she had lived there for 18 years.
