transcripts: FOREWORD The reason men have always followed the setting sun, moving, for the most part, always in a westerly direction as if they are searching for the gold that the sun's rays so closely resemble, is hard to explain. Historians and sociologists have tried to explain this phenomena [sic] in volumes too numerous to mention. Frederick Jackson Turner, in his monumental thesis, "The Frontier in American History," has left his imprint permanently on American history in explaining this movement. Until the frontier was definitely depleted and the ocean reached, the United States could be called an agrarian civilization. This type of civilization affected the American way of life as well as making this country the mecca for the oppressed and downtrodden from other parts of the world. They came here with their meager possessions and a light shining in their eyes to be absorbed into an ever-changing culture. The area covered in this study goes from one ocean boundary of the United States to the other, and it extends into the Pacific Ocean a total of fifty miles. It is related to American history with the first settlement along the Atlantic coast. From that frontier settlement it then moved in a westerly direction over and around seemingly insurmountable obstacles. To follow the wanderings of one man across the uninhabited areas of the United Sates is almost impossible. To add to the difficulties, he entered what was then part of a foreign country. He traveled across more than two thousand miles of this area, and he never returned, as many of the earlier wanderers were prone to do from time to time. Those who returned left letters and other accounts in the headquarters of the fur traders, mainly St. Louis. These accounts are highly prized by the research worker; in some cases such accounts are very valuable in tracing our early history. As members of migrating parties were inclined to keep diaries and accounts, we have a much clearer picture of these later groups. Isaac J. Sparks belonged to the earliest of those groups known as the independent fur traders and trappers. He traveled, trapped, and lived with a group of men whose exploits and daring have become a legend in the history of the west. To enumerate a few of the men with whom he associated in his wanderings will make the rest of this paper more readable. Jedediah Smith was one of his co-workers. Sparks was present when Smith met his death at the hands of hostile Indians. Kit Carson and Moses Carson were associated with Sparks in the fur trade. Ewing Young was Sparks' chief on one of his major trapping expeditions into the Colorado region. His California associates will be only enumerated; they were: J. J. Warner, owner of Warner's Ranch, a stopping place for early settlers coming into California; Isaac Williams, fur trapper and trader, who settled near the present site of Los Angeles with his Indian wife; Captain Williams G. Dana, of Santa Barbara, the uncle of Richard Henry Dana of "Two Years Before the Mast" fame, and a prominent early Californian; George Nidever, of Santa Barbara, fur trapper, owner of the Santa Barbara Channel Islands, and an early California pioneer; Benjamin Foxen, of Los Alamos, associated with Fremont in his capture of Santa Barbara; John M. Price, pioneer Englishman, who settled in California and became part of this new country. These are only a few; but from the names mentioned, the reader can draw some conclusions of what is to come in more detailed form in the paper. As the early immigrants into California, in nearly all instances, married into the Spanish families, their descendants show the racial mixture. This was not true of Sparks. Although he married a woman who had been born in California and who had a Spanish name, no Spanish blood ran in her veins. This episode constitutes a romantic chapter which will be dealt with in chronological order. Unlike most of the early settlers, Sparks did not give up his citizenship to become a Mexican subject, and for the first thirteen years of his life in California, he was a fugitive from justice; for he had escaped from the jail in the Pueblo of Los Angeles, and he never returned to face the charges of being a spy, which had been brought against him. He also obtained land grants later, to the chagrin of the American courts, who could not understand how an American, who was not married to a Spanish woman and who was a citizen of the United States, could obtain two large land grants and other major holdings from the Mexican government. This caused a great deal of trouble, and his claims were not recognized until after his death. The religion of all the people in the Spanish colonies at this time was Roman Catholic, and no other religion was allowed to exist; but the facts indicate that Sparks could have been a much better church member. Although his entire family became Roman Catholic and some of them had the honor of being buried within the Santa Barbara Mission, Sparks' remains lie in a cemetery of all faiths outside of Santa Barbara. In this study the author will endeavor to treat each detail of Isaac Sparks' life to the extent of the available material. CHAPTER IV REMOVAL OF THE INDIANS FROM SAN NICOLAS ISLAND In California the islands off the coast of Santa Barbara are one of the area's most interesting phenomena. They have repeatedly figured in the exploration and conquest of California as they are one of the first stopping places for ships returning from the Pacific Islands. When the sailors who were dying from scurvy and suffering the indescribably agonies which accompany this disease, the curse of earlier mariners, sighted these islands, prayers of thanksgiving were offered to the Virgin Mary. These islands were of particular importance to the early trappers. During the summer months the sea otter migrated south, and these islands were breeding grounds for them. The otter skins were extremely valuable. Even the great Russian-American Company sent from the north trappers to obtain these skins. As Isaac Sparks and George Nidever were associated in the business of fur trapping, they had something more than a casual interest in these islands. To clarify the difficulties and hardships involved in the later removal of the Indians from San Nicolas Island, a description of the island and its people is appropriate. About eighty miles south of Ventura is a wind-swept island which has the appearance of being gently lifted from the depths of the ocean. The island's altitude is about 800 feet above sea level. It is surrounded by comparatively low banks; there is a gradual acclivity which terminates in abrupt escarpments. The surface of the island is relatively level.<hi rend="superscript">1</hi><note n="1" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">1</hi>Ventura, <hi rend="underline">Observer</hi>, December 20, 1892.</note> This island has a mean length of about nine miles and an average width of about four miles. The longer axis is nearly east and west. From the geological viewpoint, the island is of recent origin. The fossils, which are numerous in some places, are of quaternary period except some found in the southeastern portion of the island; these latter may probably be classified as Pliocene. At the time of the removal of the Indians, the island was treeless.<hi rend="superscript">2</hi><note n="2" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">2</hi>According to Nidever and Sparks there were no trees.</note> There was on it neither tree nor shrub except a small species of thorn and cactus, neither of which obtain a height of more than two or three feet. However, this has not always been the case; for there are existing evidences to indicate that the island was once covered with timber. Nidever mentions scrub trees and moss in 1850, but there was not enough to give any protection. Much of the surface is covered with dead land shells—-helix, trionix, and helix gabbi.<hi rend="superscript">3</hi><note n="3" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">3</hi>Ventura, <hi rend="underline">Observer</hi>, December 20, 1892.</note> When they flourished, there must have been a great deal of vegetation on the island. Their large size and numbers are noticeable to even the casual observer. These shells were used by the Indians as money. Shells from this island have been found in the region of the San Joaquin Valley where they were identified by the engraving on them as having originated on this one island, which has led to the belief that there was a trade carried on all over the central region of California by the Indians.<hi rend="superscript">4</hi><note n="4" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">4</hi>There is a display of these shells, the engravings, and their approximate value at the Southwest Museum.</note> Although the island was characterized as being wind-swept, this is true only at certain seasons of the year; at other times the sea and the climate are calm and serene. During the season in which the wind prevails, it is difficult to land and more difficult to remain at anchor. The writer spent a week on the island in the month of September. Several times during this week the sea lashed furiously, while the waves and spray were flung thirty feet high to dash against the rocky shore. The noise made by the tumultuous ocean closely resembled thunder, and the entire island seemed to shake when each wave broke upon the rocks. Even after living all my life on or near the ocean, never before had I witnessed such a natural phenomenon. When Cabrillo sailed up the coast four hundred or more years ago, he seems not to have discovered San Nicolas Island; nor was it seen by Vancouver during his voyage years later. The earliest recorded voyagers who visited the island named it "Sea Otter Island," because of the great number of sea otters found there. At the present time there are numerous aquatic birds, land birds, and a small fox on the island. Numerous skeletons of two species of dog are to be found on the island. These dogs were living as late as 1853; they had been domesticated by the Indians.<hi rend="superscript">5</hi><note n="5" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">5</hi>John Price, <hi rend="underline">Diary</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">Year</hi> <hi rend="underline">1860</hi>, 16.</note> The relics found on the island display a workmanship superior to that of relics found on the other islands and on the mainland. This indicates contact with the northern tribes. The barbed spear points used in fishing are not found on the other channel islands.<hi rend="superscript">6</hi><note n="6" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">6</hi>Ventura, <hi rend="underline">Observer</hi>, December 20, 1892.</note> The island aborigines fashioned many implements from stone and bone, but the use of these implements is a puzzle to archeologists. The opinion is held that there was on this island a comparatively higher civilization found than on the mainland and on the other islands. The inhabitants seemed to have been of superior physical mould; the women were tall, handsome, and of a lighter complexion than the other natives of this region.<hi rend="superscript">7</hi><note n="7" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">7</hi><hi rend="underline">Ibid</hi>.</note> Between 1803 and 1840 the Russians habitually visited San Nicolas Island in their search for the valuable fur of the sea otter. They brought with them natives of Alaska to whom they had taught the use of firearms. It is said that the Russians left some of these natives on the island to continue the work of capturing otters after the Russians' vessels had sailed north. While the Russians were absent, these Alaskan Indians took possession of the women on the island. In the conflict which followed all the men and male children were killed. When the Russian ships returned and removed the Alaskans, the women were abandoned to their fate. In some way this news reached the mission fathers; and the story which follows tells of the Indians' removal and the story of the lone woman of San Nicolas Island. George Nidever's statement regarding the old Indian woman of San Nicolas Island, the manner in which she was left, and the circumstances of her rediscovery is, in substance as follows:<hi rend="superscript">8</hi><note n="8" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">8</hi>George Nidever, <hi rend="underline">The</hi> <hi rend="underline">Indian</hi> <hi rend="underline">Woman of</hi> <hi rend="underline">San</hi> <hi rend="underline">Nicolas</hi> (MS).</note> In the month of August, 1835,<hi rend="superscript">9</hi><note n="9" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">9</hi>The exact date as taken from John Price's <hi rend="underline">Diary</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">1835</hi> was August 21.</note> to the best of Nidever's memory, Isaac J. Sparks, an otter hunter of Santa Barbara, Bill Williams<hi rend="superscript">10</hi><note n="10" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">10</hi>"Bill Williams" should not be here confused with the "Bill Williams" of Rocky Mountain fame; it was Isaac Williams a member of the <hi rend="underline">first</hi> Ewing Young expedition. The rest of the crew was Charles Hubbard and nine Kanakas, members of Sparks' otter hunting group.</note> of the Rancho Chino, and others to make twelve all together, went over to San Nicolas Island in a schooner called the "Peores Nada" to remove the Indians who then inhabited the island.<hi rend="superscript">11</hi><note n="11" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">11</hi>"Peores Nada" was a ship of 20 tons, constructed in Monterey by Joaquin Gomez. With Captain Hubbard, the chief pilot, it was chartered by Isaac Sparks. She capsized at the entrance of San Francisco Harbor.</hi> Sparks' group assembled the Indians and brought them all, about 17 or 18 men, women, and children down to the beach. At this point one of the women asked permission to return to the interior of the island for her child, which, she said, had been left behind. She was allowed to leave, but during her absence a heavy wind sprang up which compelled the assembled Indians and their guardians to leave the island and run before the wind, for the San Nicolas Island is on the outer rim of the channel and it affords no shelter whatever for vessels in a storm. The "Peores Nada" arrived safely at San Pedro where she landed the Indians who went up to the San Gabriel Mission. It was the intention of Sparks' group to return to San Nicolas Island for the lone Indian woman, but the owner of the "Peores Nada" ordered the ship to Monterey where she was loaded with lumber for San Francisco. At the entrance to the Golden Gate she ran into a storm and capsized. As there was no other large craft on the coast, no attempt was made to rescue or to learn the fate of the Indian woman.<hi rend="superscript">12</hi><note n="12" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">12</hi>The small boats used in otter hunting would not reach the island because it was at the closest point 50 miles from the mainland and 155 miles from the Santa Barbara Harbor.</note> About a month after the removal of the Indians, Nidever joined Isaac Sparks in an otter hunting trip to the islands of Santa Rosa and San Miguel. It was during this trip that Nidever learned from Sparks the facts of the Indians' removal from San Nicolas Island; but he did not learn the reason for their removal, by whose authority they were removed, or he could not recall these facts.<hi rend="superscript">13</hi><note n="13" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">13</hi>Isaac J. Sparks, <hi rend="underline">Diary</hi>, <hi rend="underline">Year</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">1835</hi>, 14. Sparks states that the removal was ordered by the mission fathers at San Gabriel. Also, the reason given for this was the depredations of the Northwest Indians in this area. George Nidever, <hi rend="underline">Reminiscences</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">Scenes</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">Early</hi> <hi rend="underline">Santa</hi> <hi rend="underline">Barbara</hi>. In this manuscript Nidever states that he wanted to establish a sheep ranch on the island.</note> He recollects quite clearly, however, that Bill Williams was with them and was evidently interested in the Indians' removal as Williams afterwards took one of the Indians to live with him.<hi rend="superscript">14</hi><note n="14" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">14</hi>Nidever, <hi rend="underline">ibid</hi>., 1. Sparks and Nidever had a brush with the Indians on this occasion. Sparks killed three of them.</note> It was 1852 before any effort was made to learn the fate of the Indian woman who had been left on the island, although it was well known throughout the coast that she had been abandoned on the island. In the fall of 1851, Nidever went to San Nicolas in search of sea gull eggs; there he found footprints, which from their size, he concluded were those of a woman. Their appearance indicated that they had been made but a short time before, which led him to believe that the Indian woman still existed.<hi rend="superscript">15</hi><note n="15" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">15</hi>All thought she had perished.</note> When he returned to Santa Barbara, he reported his discovery of the footprints to the mission fathers, who urged him to make a thorough search on his next visit to the island. However, he did not return to the island until the fall of 1858 when he went to the island on an otter hunting expedition. On his trip he was accompanied by Charley Brown and Sparks. The first day they went on shore they found a large woven basket made of grass in a crotch or fork of a large bush; in the basket were several shag skins cut into regular shapes, a dress made from the skins of the same bird, a sinew rope, a bone knife, abalone fish hooks, and several of these with a seal skin. Sparks and Nidever scattered the things about on the ground an left the basket lying there so that they might have some proof of the Indian woman's existence if, on their next visit, they found the things replaced in the basket or removed. During the next few days they were busy with their hunting, for they intended to resume the search as soon as their hunting would permit. On the third or fourth day a heavy gale sprang up which prevented their coming ashore and finally forced them to leave the island. On the next trip to the island in the summer of 1853 Nidever and Charley Brown went without Sparks to the island, again in search of otter. When they went ashore to find where the otter lay, Brown discovered footprints on the northwest side of the island. They then decided to make a thorough search of the island on the next day.<hi rend="superscript">16</hi><note n="16" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">16</hi>Nidever, <hi rend="underline">op</hi>. <hi rend="underline">cit</hi>., 2.</note> Accordingly, on the following morning, they took their men ashore. First they searched over a low, sandy flat, which was covered with dunes and bushes and which stretched across the island about a mile and a half below its head. Nidever took no active part in the search, but Brown went across with the men. When they found nothing, he sent them back with instructions to search carefully along the edges of the flat.<hi rend="superscript">17</hi><note n="17" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">17</hi>Ventura, <hi rend="underline">Observer</hi>, December 20, 1892.</note> He remained on that side of the island and proceeded towards its head until he struck the footprints which had been discovered the previous evening. When he followed them over the banks, he traced the tracks until they were lost on the soft carpet of moss with which the ground was covered. Between the sand flat already mentioned and the head of the island there is a long, high ridge; it was up the northwest side of this ridge that Brown had followed the footprints. From this point he saw, further up the ridge, three huts. Upon reaching them, he found they were constructed of whale bones which had been covered with brush.<hi rend="superscript">18</hi><note n="18" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">18</hi>Mr. Aruther Woodward, of the Los Angeles Museum in Exposition Park, while on an archeological expedition to San Nicolas Island, reconstructed one of these huts; it can be seen in the museum.</note> They were open all around and within the grass was growing thickly, which indicated that they had not been occupied for some time. When he looked about over the ridge from this point, he discovered a small, black object which appeared to be moving and which looked very much like a crow seated on a bush. As he went towards it, he soon discovered it to be the Indian woman. She was seated crosslegged on the ground within a small, low, circular enclosure of sage brush, a type of wind break; she was engaged in separating the blubber from a piece of seal skin, which she held across her knee with one hand. In the other hand she held a rude knife, the blade of which was a piece of iron hove and the handle a piece of wood. Within the enclosure or wind break, a fire was smouldering, and without was a large pile of bones and ashes; evidently this enclosure had been her abode for a long time.<hi rend="superscript">19</hi><note n="19" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">19</hi>Nidever, <hi rend="underline">op</hi>. <hi rend="underline">cit</hi>., 4.</note> Blankets woven of grass, water bottles of the same material made in the shape of a flagon and lined with asphaltum, knives of bone, and other articles lay scattered about. There were no stone mortars or earthen vessels, but there were several shovel or scoop-shaped vessels of wood, the use of which Brown did not learn.<hi rend="superscript">20</hi><note n="20" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">20</hi>These had been left by the Indians when they were removed. She moved from the huts because the dogs on the island killed her child and attacked her. It was learned later that she used fire to protect herself. All of the above-described things were collected by the priest at the Santa Barbara mission and sent to Rome. According to the soldiers who visited the Vatican, they are still on display there in the museum.</note> Stretched between two upright stakes at some distance from the ground was a sinew rope from which were hanging strips of seal blubber. The windbreak was situated on the northeast side of the island about half way up the ridge, so that it received the full force of the morning sun. The Indian woman was dressed in a robe or gown of bird skins sewn together with the feathers out and pointing downwards.<hi rend="superscript">21</hi><note n="21" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">21</hi>The feathers were from the Shag which is dull black in colour.</note> This was her only covering. Her feet were bare as was her head, which was covered with a thick growth of matted hair. This was bleached to a reddish color and hung down to her shoulders.<hi rend="superscript">22</hi><note n="22" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">22</hi>Nidever, <hi rend="underline">op</hi>. <hi rend="underline">cit</hi>., 4.</note> Her features were quite regular, complexion fairer than the Indians of the mainland and, although she must have been about fifty years old, her face was free of wrinkles. Her teeth were worn down to the very gums much like an Eskimo of the same age from eating dried seal meat. When Brown approached her it was from the rear so that she did not see him, although the wild dogs nearby began to growl when they saw him. These she yelled at and they went away. From the elevator where he stood he signalled to the men who could be seen on the sand flat below, and they came towards the enclosure in a circle so she could not escape. As soon as they were near enough, Brown stepped around in front of her and was surprised by her smile and bow to him instead of becoming alarmed or startled.<hi rend="superscript">23</hi><note n="23" place="bottom"><hi rend="superscript">23</hi>Charles Brown, <hi rend="underline">Early</hi> <hi rend="underline">History</hi> <hi rend="underline">of</hi> <hi rend="underline">Santa</hi> <hi rend="underline">Barbara</hi>, 3.</note> As the other men came up she smiled to them, talking rapidly all the time but no one could understand her. Nidever then came up and they sat in a circle around her while she roasted some roots and invited them to share with her. Nidever feared that force would be necessary to take her with them, but Brown differed with him. After going through the motions of putting all the things in her baskets and walking off with them towards the beach and saying in Spanish "let us go" they had the satisfaction of seeing her face brighten up and she began to put all her things in the basket. When she had finished doing this she went with them down to the beach. They found a spring near the beach and left some of the things she had brought here. Farther on they came to a second spring where she stopped and worked. They had no difficulty at all in taking her on board the ship. They gave her some food on board the ship and she accepted it readily. That afternoon Brown made her a dress and a skirt of canvas to which was added a man's shirt, black necktie and an old cloak. These she continued to wear while on the island. The following day they went ashore and camped, remaining here for almost a month. Near the camp they constructed a small hut to shelter her and here she remained most of the day, while all the men except the cook were off hunting otter. She was free to come and go but took only infrequent walks about the island and never made any move towards deserting her rescuers. She spent most of her time in weaving baskets, and brought wood and water for the cook. She showed at one time she desired to return to her former food. A sea otter was killed by the hunters and dragged up near the camp to be skinned. After this operation had been performed the carcass was being dragged to the water so that it would not contaminate the camp. At the sight of this she gave the hunters to understand this was a wasted of meat. She then rushed down and seized it by the flipper and hauled it back. After it began to smell she showed her disgust for it, and her preference for the other food, and did not object to its being taken away. On their way to the mainland she knelt in the bottom of the boat and made odd signs when the weather became rough and a storm was encountered. As they reached shore, an oxcart and a man on horseback came in sight and her delight was unbounded. She was taken to Nidever's home where she remained until her death about seven weeks later. She was allowed to eat too much fruit and vegetables which brought on dysentery. The mission fathers sent for Indians from San Gabriel, San Fernando and Santa Ynez, besides those of the Santa Barbara Mission and San Buenaventura, in hope of finding someone to converse with her, but did not succeed. She would dance, smile and jabber for all, and when Sparks visited she would carry on a little chat and rock her arms as if her baby should be in them. Her dresses, baskets and other materials were collected by Father Gonzalez by whom they were sent to Rome. She is buried in the mission garden in Santa Barbara and the gravestone is entitle "Juana Maria."

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">The Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island</hi> <hi rend="bold">Foreward</hi> When I started this paper, I was a second year Electrical Engineering Major at Cal Poly Pomona. As a part of the requirements for Dr. Urcia's English 105 Class, we were assigned a research paper, complete with footnotes. I had just seen the movie, "The Island of the Blue Dolphins," and I thought that this might be a good subject for the paper. Little did I know where this simple English 105 assignment would take me. Among other things it instilled in me a love and fascination for the history of our country and, in particular, our great state of California. All of this could not have been possible without the help and assistance of the staff of the Southwest Museum in Los Angeles, California. Allowing a nineteen-year-old college student to physically touch and read through their priceless manuscripts was an act unheard of at other historical libraries. Reading through these old documents brought the story to life for me. However, having access to all of the documents did not make the task any easier. Many times there were conflicting statements from the various sources. Sometimes they were minor points, while at other times they required even more searching to discover or learn the truth. I hope that all of my efforts bring the story of Juana Maria alive for you as it has for me. <hi rend="bold">The Islands</hi> Of all the stories that can be found about the Channel Islands off the coast of California, there is one that goes far beyond all others in its strangeness and mystery. It is the account of the Indian woman who has been referred to as the "Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island." The story is something of a mystery because all of the facts are not known and never will be. For this article, all reliable information that could be found has been studied and compared in the hope of obtaining a clear picture of what actually happened on San Nicolas Island. Some nine miles long and three and a half miles wide, the island is located approximately seventy miles from Port Hueneme, California. Robert M. Norriss described it as "a faulted asymmetric anticline, composed of Pleistocene sediments lying uncomfortably on Eocene sandstone and shale."<hi rend="superscript">1</hi> In simplier terms, the island has a 907 foot peak toward the ocean side and south of the center. It is made up of varying layers of cracked rock and sediments that are bent in opposite directions from the peak. Because of the high winds and storms that bombard the island, it is slowly wearing away and will probably disappear in time. The island is surrounded by reefs and shallow water. The sea is extremely rough in this area, and the only time that one can safely land or leave the island is around six o'clock in the morning.<hi rend="superscript">2</hi> There are no good harborsfor a ship to find refuge from wind or storm. It is a bird island, once being covered with thousands of ravens, cormorants, sea gulls, blue herons, bald eagles, larks and robins.<hi rend="superscript">3</hi> Other occupants of this desolate land were seals, otter and sea lions. The first European to see San Nicolas Island was Bartolome Ferrer who sailed past it in 1543. Sebastian Vizcaino sailed past the island in 1602, but neither Ferrer nor Vizcaino set foot on it.<hi rend="superscript">4</hi> On December 6, 1602, Juan Cabrillo was the first European to actually land on the island.<hi rend="superscript">5</hi> According to Cabrillo, the island was densely populated by a superior race of Indians which A. L. Kroeber classifies as of the Gabrielino or Shoshone stock.<hi rend="superscript">6</hi> Cabrillo' s report states that the men wore loose cloaks while the women wore petticoats and capes of sealskins, heavily fringed and handsomely ornamented with shells and stones. If a woman wanted to look different from others and was very industrious, she embroidered her garments with pearls and small pink shells. A semi-caste system existed on the island. The higher a woman rated on the social scale, the more ornamentation she had on her garments. She might also wear stone necklaces and iris-hued abalone earrings.<hi rend="superscript">7</hi> The Indian inhabitants of San Nicolas Island were described as a peaceful tribe because no warlike weapons have ever been found.<hi rend="superscript">8<?hi> "The children had light hair and ruddy cheeks. The women had fine forms, beautiful eyes, and a modest demeanor."<hi rend="supsercript">9</hi> They lived on abalone, fish, sea lions, sea elephants and birds.<hi rend="supsercript">10</hi> In order to be in the best location for the food of the season, they moved from one site to another. This is demonstrated by the fact that some sixty-eight sites have been found where villages existed, but not all of these were inhabited at the same time. It is estimated that, at their peak, these villages supported over one thousand Indians.<hi rend="supsercript">11</hi> The Indians manufactured water-tight baskets and soapstone vessels for cooking. They also made needles, awls, ollas (pottery water jars) of stone and other useful utensils. Their canoes were made long and deep with both ends elevated at the same degree to allow travel in both directions. According to Mons de Cessac, an archaeologist for the French government, all of these products showed evidence of superior workmanship and had excellent form.<hi rend="supsercript">12</hi> Not a great deal is known about the islanders or what happened to them from 1602 to around 1800. During this period the population began to fall in great numbers. This was probably due to diseases carried by the white men who stopped at the island for hunting. In the year 1811, a ship belonging to Pope and Boardman of Boston and commanded by a Captain Whittemore<hi rend="supsercript">13</hi> brought twenty-five to thirty Kodiaks from the Russian camp at Sitka to San Nicolas Island for the purpose of hunting otter and seal. After the Kodiaks were supplied with guns and provisions, they were left on the island while the ship sailed off to other business, with Whittemore's promise to return at the end of the year to pick them up.<hi rend="supsercript">14</hi> During the time that the ship was away, a feud broke out between the Indians and the Kodiaks. The feud had to do with the seizure of the island women by the Kodiaks. In the battle that ensued, a majority of the island men were massacred, both young and old alike,<hi rend="supsercript">15</hi> and the island women were forced to live with the Kodiaks for the remainder of their stay. At the end of the year the ship came to remove the Kodiaks and the skins which they had collected during the year but that is, in fact, all they did. "The islanders were left to their fate." <hi rend="supsercript">16</hi> <hi rend="bold">Removing the Survivors</hi> From that time to about 1830, there are no records of what happened to those who were left on the island. Because of the extremely poor living conditions on the various Channel Islands, the Franciscan Mission Fathers decided to bring all of the Indians from the islands to the mainland. This was to be done in order to preserve the races from extinction as well as to improve their conditions.<hi rend="supsercript">17</hi> By 1835, the task had been carried out on all of the islands except San Nicolas. This island was left until last because it was the most distant and there were no ships available for the long voyage. In 1835, the Mission Fathers of Santa Barbara were able to charter a twenty-ton schooner with the aid of Isaac J. Sparks, Lewis F. Burton and Bill Williams of the Chino Ranch of Los Angeles.<hi rend="supsercript">18</hi> The ship <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> or "Better Than Nothing," was commanded by Captain Charles Hubbard. These men along with about twelve crew members sailed to the island on August 1, 1835, to remove the Indians.<hi rend="supsercript">19</hi> It is interesting to note that, at one time or another, each one of the men was credited with having been captain of the ship. However, records indicate that Charles Hubbard was the captain.<hi rend="supsercript">20</hi> The evacuation was carried out under the direction of Captain Bill Williams, the Collector of the Port of San Pedro.<hi rend="supsercript">21</hi> By the time the rescue party arrived, the number of Indians found on the island is uncertain. The high figure is around forty men, women and children.<hi rend="supsercript">22</hi> The low figure is two women and one man who was without all of his faculties because of a blow over the head sustained during the Kodiak battle.<hi rend="supsercript">23</hi> The more widely accepted, and more reasonable figure, is around seventeen or eighteen men, women and children.<hi rend="supsercript">24</hi> In the confusion of moving from the island, a child was misplaced or became lost. When this was discovered, the launch which was to take the Indians to the larger vessel was thoroughly searched. Since the child was not found in the boat, the rocks and beach were searched. There was no child or any sign of a child anywhere. The mother pleaded to be allowed to return inland to continue the search. The captain reluctantly gave his permission.<hi rend="supsercript">25</hi> Not long after the woman went inland, the winds began to increase in velocity. The sea became rough and storm clouds appeared. The captain and the crew began to grow anxious because of the woman's delay in returning to the boat. The storm grew in intensity and finally reached a point where it was no longer safe for the launch or the schooner to remain in the area. At this time, they set out for the safety of the mainland and left the woman alone on the island.<hi rend="supsercript">26</hi> The woman was described as a widow between twenty and thirty years-of-age, of medium height, fine in form, light in complexion and with dark brown hair.<hi rend="supsercript">27</hi> This would mean that she was a child at the time of the Kodiak affair or was an offspring of one of them. There is a great deal of confusion about how the woman was left on the island. Some say that the woman reached the schooner before she discovered her child missing. When she found that they were going out to sea in the storm instead of remaining in the area to continue the search for her child, she jumped overboard and swam back to the island for her child.<hi rend="supsercript">28</hi> Another story is that she was inland and not with the other Indians when the ship arrived; thus, she was left behind.<hi rend="supsercript">29</hi> While her diving from the boat makes a nice story, it is highly improbable that this event actually occurred. The original story is substantiated by George Nidever who talked with Isaac Sparks, and by other first-hand accounts. Furthermore, the launch used at the time was not a large craft and it would have been rather difficult to lose a child of nursing age in a small boat without someone knowing it. An investigation of first-hand accounts and interviews that have been recorded shows that the Emma C. Hardacre's story about the Indian woman diving from the ship is inaccurate, as are her reports of several other events. When the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> reached San Pedro, some of the Indians were sent to Los Angeles and others to the San Gabriel Mission. Two of the women soon married wealthy men in the Los Angeles area, one of whom was Bill Williams of the rescue party.<hi rend="supsercript">30</hi> The man who was injured in battle, and who was supposed to have been without all of his faculties, remained in San Pedro among the hunters. It is said he was strong enough to do the work of three or four normal men.<hi rend="supsercript">31</hi> Captain Hubbard intended to return to the island after the storm to find the woman and her child. However, before he could do so, he had two other commitments to fulfill. The first of these was to take George Nidever to the islands of Santa Rosa and San Miguel for otter hunting in September, 1835. Among those present on the hunt was Mr. Sparks, who told Mr. Nidever of the Indian woman.<hi rend="supsercript">32</hi> It is ironic that George Nidever, who was, in a way, responsible for the woman's being left on the island, was so influential in her finally being found. Captain Hubbard's second task was to take a load of lumber from San Pedro to San Francisco. On this voyage, the ship capsized at the Golden Gate, was washed out to sea and captured by the Russians.<hi rend="supsercript">33</hi> After the loss of the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph>, it was impossible to make any effort to rescue the woman because there was no other ship available that was large enough to make the trip safely.<hi rend="supsercript">34</hi> By this time, the woman was given up for dead because of the wild dogs that roamed the island.<hi rend="supsercript">35</hi> It is interesting to note that these wild dogs, which were so troublesome, had once been the prized animals of the Indians. However, over the years, the dogs grew in numbers to a point where they were no longer welcome. After California became a State, some interest was aroused again in San Nicolas Island but it did not have to do with the woman. Everyone had forgotten about her except Father Gonzales of the Santa Barbara Mission. When a European, Tom Jeffries, obtained a ship and expressed a desire to explore the island, Father Gonzales offered him $200 to bring the woman or her child or both back alive.<hi rend="supsercript">36</hi> When Jeffries' ship returned to Santa Barbara, people lined the shore waiting for the signal to indicate he found the woman, but no signal was given. The woman was soon forgotten again, but the trip was not. The otter and seal that had once populated the island had returned, and hunting there would once again be excellent. <hi rend="bold">The Search</hi> As California grew, the size and number of ships on the coast increased. The Gold Rush in 1849 undoubtedly had some influence on this. Finally, with larger ships available, George Nidever went to San Nicolas Island in April, 1852, and he took Mr. Jeffries along with him on this trip. They planned to collect sea gull eggs which were in great demand at that time. The landing party, made up of Mr. Nidever, Mr. Jeffries and two Indians, set foot on the island six or seven miles from the southern tip. About two-hundred yards from the beach, they found human footprints. They were small in size and could not have been those of a man. Because the intact prints were sunk into the dried and cracked ground, it was concluded that they had been made shortly after a rainstorm when the ground was soft. A few hundred yards, still farther from the beach and about two miles apart, the group found three small circular huts made of sage brush. These huts stood about five feet high, six feet in diameter and showed signs of lack of use for some period of time. There were several poles, four-to-six feet high outside each hut. Seal blubber, which appeared to be at least three months old, had been stuck on the top of each pole and out of the reach of the dogs. Upon seeing these signs, the group was convinced that someone was on the island, as Isaac Sparks had said. Before any further searching could be done, a gale came up and forced them to return to their ship. Even though they were on the southern side of the island, they were blown about a great deal. After eight days, they sailed to Santa Barbara Island for shelter and returned to the mainland of Santa Barbara when the gale subsided.<hi rend="supsercript">37</hi> Upon hearing of the discovery of the footprints, Father Gonzales asked that they make every effort to find the woman. After taking a load of lumber to Santa Cruz, Nidever returned to Santa Barbara and outfitted his ship for an otter and seal hunt on San Nicolas Island. On this trip, Nidever had a man named Carl Dittman, alias Charles Brown, and two Indians along with him, in addition to the regular crew. They landed on the island at the southern end and Nidever, Dittman and the Indians went ashore to see where the otter lay. They found nothing of the woman on this landing. On the third day, they landed toward the northern end of the island. The Indians were left to watch the boat while Nidever and Dittman started toward the headland. About one-half mile from the headland they came upon a wide, low, sandy flat that extended from one side of the island to the other. They started across on the edge of the flat (which side is not known). In the crotch of a small Malva Real tree they found a small basket woven out of grass, about threefeet long, one-and-a-half feet wide, and some fourteeninches deep. It was covered with a piece of sealskin.<hi rend="supsercript">38</hi> They removed the basket from its perch and uncovered it. Inside they found a dress made of cormorant shag (skins of birds sewn together with the feathers pointing downward). The basket also contained several square pieces of shag, bone needles and knives, fish hooks made of abalone shell, and a rope made of sinews which was a half-inch in diameter and about 25-feet long. Dittman noted that the rope compared with the best of its day on the mainland. The men concluded that the rope had been used to snare seals for food.<hi rend="supsercript">39</hi> All of these items were neatly placed in the basket. Nidever wanted to spread the articles around and then return to see if the woman had replaced them. Dittman was opposed to disturbing the things, but finally agreed to having them spread about. The next two or three days were spent hunting. Then a strong wind came up and soon increased to a gale. The men remained on the island about a week hoping that the storm would blow itself out and allow them to go ashore and check on the basket. However, since the storm showed no signs of abating they left for the safety of the mainland. Dittman reported that Nidever was so excited about finding the basket he almost ran the ship on a reef at San Miguel Island where they stopped and found shelter.<hi rend="supsercript">40</hi> Once again, there is some confusion about this second trip to the island. Dittman's story seems to make the most sense. In three different reports by Nidever, he has varying stories. In one case, it appears that the report could be in error. This discrepancy has to do with the finding of footprints and a piece of driftwood. Dittman and Nidever both reported this on the third trip<hi rend="supsercript">41</hi> but, in one of Nidever' s reports, he said it occurred on the second trip<hi rend="supsercript">42</hi> This point is rather minor. The important thing is that they all agree on finding the basket. Another point of controversy arises in the reports concerning the dogs on the island. They were said to have looked like coyotes, but they were white and black.<hi rend="supsercript">43</hi> If they actually had been coyotes, they would have been mottled light brown, white and grey. Both men agree on seeing the dogs but they disagree on which trip, the second or third. It is possible that since these dogs roamed the entire island, they could have seen them both times. Nidever reports that seven or eight dogs were seen on the second trip in 1852.<hi rend="supsercript">44</hi> Dittman mentions seeing only two or three on the third trip in 1853.<hi rend="supsercript">45</hi> There is some discrepancy in the reports regarding the starting date of the third trip. Was it June, July or August? All sources consulted state that the Indian woman lived only three months from the time that she was found. In the book of Burials of Santa Barbara Mission, entry Number 1183 records the burial of the Indian woman (Juana Maria), and it is dated October 19, 1853.<hi rend="supsercript">46</hi> This would mean that she had to be found sometime in late July or early August, 1853. The exact date is not known or, at least it could not be found in any of the primary sources. During the summer of 1853, Nidever refitted his ship for another otter hunt on the Channel Islands. The men hoped for better weather this time since it was summer and they did not expect storms. First, they went to San Miguel Island, but there is no record of how long they stayed there. If they remained there a week or two, the reports of starting the trip in June, 1853, would be very plausible.<hi rend="supsercript">47</hi> After leaving San Miguel Island they headed toward San Nicolas Island, arriving there in the early afternoon. Again, there is no record of how long the trip took. However, since it was seventy miles from San Pedro, and still farther from Santa Barbara, it can be assumed that the trip took one or two days. They landed on the northeast, or inland side, at about the middle of the island. As soon as they anchored, Dittman, Nidever and two Indians went ashore to see where the otter lay. When they reached the shore, the Indians were left to watch the boat while Dittman and Nidever went on ahead. They started off toward the head of the island and Dittman reported seeing several dogs. They were very wild and ran away as soon as they saw the men.<hi rend="supsercript">48</hi> When they reached the head of the island, Nidever wanted to sit down and rest while Dittman went on ahead along the shore on the seaward side of the island. After walking for some distance, he found footprints leading from the beach, up over a bank and toward the ridge above. He followed them until they disappeared in a thick moss that covered the ground. Nidever reported that there was a matted area in the moss that looked as if the woman had sat down to rest before going on.<hi rend="supsercript">49</hi> Dittman returned to Nidever and told him what he had found. At first, Nidever thought that the footprints must have been made by the Indians they had brought with them, but changed his mind when he saw the size of the footprints. They were too small for either of the Indians. Furthermore, it would have been impossible for the Indians to have gone ahead of them without being noticed. Because of the dogs they had seen earlier, Nidever did not think that they would find the woman alive or even find her remains. In spite of this belief, he decided to search that end of the island thoroughly the following day. Since it was getting late, they started toward the boat and discontinued their search for the day. The following morning after they had finished breakfast, the entire crew, except for the cook, went ashore to search. Dittman took three Indians and an Irishman named Colorado and started out for the sandy flat. Arriving there, they spread out in a straight line and walked from one side of the island to the other. This pass brought no results. Dittman then sent the men back to search the edges, and especially the area where the basket had been found on the previous trip. Dittman headed toward the spot where he had found the footprints the night before. When he located them, he followed them up over the bank and up the side of the ridge until they ended. He continued up the ridge in the same direction as the footprints until he found a piece of driftwood which, he concluded, the Indian woman had probably dropped on her way back to her camp. From this point on the ridge, Dittman could see three huts farther up the ridge. On closer investigation, he found that the huts were made of whale's ribs and covered with brush. Grass was growing inside them and there were other signs that the huts had not been used for a long time. From the huts, Dittman could see all of the men moving about below him. He looked around the area and, at some distance on the northeast side of the ridge and about half way up, he saw what appeared to be a crow moving about in the brush. As he came closer, he found that it was the woman with her head and shoulders showing over the top of an enclosure like those previously described. Dittman was able to get within several yards of the woman because she was facing the other direction and did not notice him. As he came closer, two dogs that were by the hut began to growl. As soon as they started to growl, the woman yelled and they ran away. From this vantage point with the men still in sight, Dittman placed his hat on the ramrod of his rifle and raised and lowered it to attract the attention of his men. When they finally saw his signal, he motioned for them to come to where he was standing. As the men were closing in, the woman saw them. She shaded her eyes and looked every few minutes, all the while talking to herself very rapidly. As he waited for his men to come closer, Dittman had a chance to observe the woman and her surroundings. <emph>.... She was seated cross legged on the ground and was engaged in separating the blubber from a piece of seal skin which was lying across one knee and held by one hand. In the other hand she grasped a crude knife, a piece of iron hoop thrust into a rough piece of wood for a handle and held so that the back of the hand was turned down, scraping and cutting from, instead of toward her. Just outside of the enclosure there was a high pile of ashes and bones showing that she had lived in this place for some time. Baskets of grass and vessels of the same material made in the shape of a flagon and lined with asphaltum, used to hold water, were scattered about. On a sinew rope stretched between two poles, several feet above the ground were hanging pieces of seal blubber, while near her was the head of a seal from which the brains, already putrid were running. Her covering consisted of a single garment of the shag's skin, the feathers out and pointed downward, in shape resembling a loose gown. It was sleeveless, low in the neck and was girded at the waist with a sinew rope. When she stood up, as I afterwards observed, it extended nearly to the ankles. She had no covering on her head; her hair which was thickly matted and bleached a reddish brown, hung down her shoulders.</emph> <hi rend="supsercript">50</hi> As soon as the men had come close enough for Dittman to signal to them, he ordered them to circle the woman to prevent her escaping. When they were still some distance away, but not so far as to allow the woman to escape, Dittman stepped out in front of her. Instead of running, as he thought she might, she seemed very happy to see him. She began talking and gesticulating, but none of this was intelligible to him. As each of the men approached her the woman bowed in greeting and started talking to them. During this time Dittman signaled to Nidever who was below on the beach and took no great part in the search.<hi rend="supsercript">51</hi> When all of the men had arrived at her camp, the woman had them sit down. Then she took two types of roots and placed them in the fire to roast. When they were done, she took them out and passed them around to the men and made signs for them to eat. According to both Dittman and Nidever, one of the roots was called a <emph>carcomite</emph> by the Californians.<hi rend="supsercript">52</hi> All of the Indians in the group tried to converse with the woman, but all proved unsuccessful except in sign language. Nidever asked the Indians if they thought that they could handle the woman if they had to remove her forcibly. They said that it would be no problem but Dittman said that force would not be necessary. Nidever tried to show the woman in sign language that she was to go with them back to the mainland, but she was not able to understand Nidever and was confused. Dittman attracted her attention by tapping her on the shoulder. Then he took one of her baskets and went through the motions of packing and the woman understood this very well. She understood even better when Dittman said, "Vamoose." When she heard this word she quickly went to work packing all of her things including the seal's head.<hi rend="supsercript">53</hi> When everything was packed, she picked up as much as she could carry and the men picked up the rest. She started off toward the beach but Nidever, still not trusting her, had two Indians lead with Dittman and himself following the woman to prevent her escape. They stopped to rest at a pool of fresh water near the beach and noticed that the surface of this pool always seemed to be rippled as if a breeze were blowing over it. Dittman observed the strange phenomenon on this occasion and on several future stops at the pool.<hi rend="supsercript">54</hi> There were several poles around the pool on which the men hung the articles they had been carrying. They made signs for the woman to do the same thing. She did so without hesitation. They noticed that there were bones in the cracks and fissures of the rocks around the pond. The men concluded that the woman had left the bones there because she carried bones in one of her baskets and occasionally she would suck on a bone and then put it back in the basket. From time to time she took bits of food from her basket and ate it. Dittman says that she never ate much at one time but that she ate several times during the day.<hi rend="supsercript">55</hi> After they rested the party continued along the bank until they came to another pool. At this point the woman made signs that she wished to bathe. The crew went on ahead to the boat and Dittman and Nidever withdrew until she was finished. When she returned they proceeded walking on to the beach. She understood their signs telling her to get into the boat. After boarding, she went to the bow and sat down, placing one hand on each side of the boat. Arriving at the schooner, the woman climbed aboard and went to the galley where she made signs to indicate that it was warm and it seemed to please her. At dinner time the crew gave the woman some of their food which she ate without any signs that it disagreed with her.<hi rend="supsercript">56</hi> That afternoon, Dittman made the woman her first "civilized" clothes in order to preserve the unusual cormorant feather gown she was wearing. Her new outfit consisted of a petticoat made of ticking, a man's a black necktie and an old cape which Nidever gave to her. While Dittman was making her petticoat she laughed at his method of sewing. About this time, Nidever gave her the cape which was badly in need of mending. Since her eyes seemed to be weak, she could not see to thread the needle and Dittman threaded it for her so that she could mend the cape. Her method was rather unusual. She placed the cloth between her legs, then thrust the needle through the cloth with one hand and then pulled the needle the remainder of the way with the other hand. In spite of its crudeness, her method proved to be successful. She was very pleased with her new clothes and wanted everyone to notice her wearing them.<hi rend="supsercript">57</hi> The next day the crew went ashore in the same location to set up a camp for otter hunting. They put up a tent for themselves and a hut-type shelter for the woman. They remained on the island for nearly a month. During this time, the men were gone nearly all day, but the woman kept busy collecting firewood and water for the camp. She did this willingly and without ever being asked. She always wanted to help in any way that she could. While working, she talked, laughed and sang. If she wasn't helping out in the camp she was weaving baskets. She worked on several baskets at one time, going from one to the other. As a result, she never finished any that she had started.<hi rend="supsercript">58</hi> The woman seemed to like the type of food the men prepared. Only once did she show any sign of returning to her old source of food. On this occasion Dittman killed a female otter and dragged it ashore to skin it. After it was skinned he was going to dispose of the carcass. The woman stopped him and scolded him for the waste of meat. She dragged the carcass up the beach and left it. After a few days, however, the carcass began to smell, and when the crew went to dispose of it, the woman made no objections. In fact, Dittman says, she made signs to get rid of it because of the smell.<hi rend="supsercript">59</hi> The otter was within a few days of giving birth when it had been shot. The unborn otter was removed from the female, skinned and stuffed, and given to the woman. She hung it by a string in her shelter and played with it for hours, hitting it to keep it in motion.<hi rend="supsercript">60</hi> Having completed their hunt, the group packed to leave the island. After their departure, such a violent storm arose that they thought they would have to return to the island for safety. During the storm the woman made signs that she could stop the wind. She knelt down on the deck facing the wind and seemed to be praying. She did this a number of times during the day, and when the wind stopped that afternoon, she smiled and made signs that her prayers had been answered. The night was spent on the lee side of Santa Cruz Island and the next morning they set out for the Santa Barbara mainland.<hi rend="supsercript">61</hi> As they sailed into Santa Barbara harbor, the woman saw an ox-cart on the shore. She pointed to it and danced and laughed the entire time it was in sight. One of Nidever' s sons had come on horseback to greet them as they came ashore and the woman ran around the horse pointing, laughing and dancing.<hi rend="supsercript">62</hi> After his arrival in Santa Barbara, Nidever took the woman to stay at his home. While she was there she often went into town, but she never came home without some gifts for the children. Many people stopped at Santa Barbara to see her; some brought gifts which she accepted but did not open. After the people had gone, she would take great delight in giving the gifts to the children of the house. The woman was always in good spirits and sang and danced when people came.<hi rend="supsercript">63</hi> In an effort to find someone who could speak the woman's language, the Mission Fathers sent for the Indians from surrounding areas. It is not clear if they were unable to find a translator or, if those who came could not converse with her. It is not unlikely that, over the period of eighteen years, she had developed a language of her own. She must have heard the language of the hunters who came to the island during those the years, because she used such words as pickininy in referring to her child, and <emph>manana</emph>.<hi rend="supsercript">64</hi> In sign language, the woman told Nidever and others that, " .... she did not find her child, that she wandered for days without tasting any food or drink, sometimes sleeping but [a] little, until her clothes were torn, and her feet and legs bleeding."<hi rend="supsercript">65</hi> The fact that she did not find her child is recorded in several different accounts by Nidever, and it can be assumed to be true. The stories about her finding the child and its being partially devoured by the dogs came from sources that have proved to be erroneous in several instances. The fact that the woman did not find her child would tend to discount the claim of Arthur R. Sanger of Los Angeles who says that he has the skeleton of the child.<hi rend="supsercript">66</hi> With regard to the child, Nidever continues in his report: <emph>After a time she forgot her child and sang and danced. She also told that she was very sick at one time; that she had seen vessels passing two [sic] and fro but none came to take her off; that she saw us on the island before we found her .... About 5 weeks after she was brought over, she was taken sick from eating too much fruit and 7 weeks from the day of her arrival died.</emph><hi rend="supsercript">67</hi> While the Indian woman was ill, Mrs. Nidever cared for her. She cooked some seal blubber for her but the woman would not eat it and pointed to her worn teeth. Before she died, the Mission Fathers baptized her <emph>sub conditione</emph> (conditionally, because they did not know if she had been baptized before) and named her Juana Maria. She was buried in the Mission cemetery on October 19, 1853. The burial record is Number 1183 on Folio 13 of the Register of Burials of the Presidio of Santa Barbara. The woman's possessions were great curiosities. One of her two water-tight baskets was given to some unknown person who reported this along with a picture of the basket to <emph>Hutchings' Californa Magazine</emph>.<hi rend="supsercript">68</hi> Her dress and several other articles were reportedly sent to Rome's Vatican Museum, but there have been no reliable reports of their ever having been seen. The remainder of her things, and probably the dress, were sent to San Francisco, where they were lost in the 1906 earthquake.<hi rend="supsercript">69</hi> In 1928 a plaque was erected on the church wall in the Santa Barbara Mission Cemetery. It reads as follows: <hi rend="bold">JUANA MARIA</hi> <hi rend="bold">INDIAN WOMAN ABANDONED ON SAN NICOLAS ISLAND EIGHTEEN YEARS FOUND AND BROUGHT TO SANTA BARBARA BY CAPT. GEORGE NIDEVER IN 1853</hi> <hi rend="bold">SANTA BARBARA CHAPTER DAUGHTERS OF THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION 1928</hi> It is almost beyond the grasp of a normal person to imagine how a human being could be left alone for eighteen years on an island and still remain as happy and cheerful as did Juana Maria and all of the time hoping and waiting for her rescue. <hi rend="bold">Epilogue</hi> One might wonder what has happened to Juana Maria and to San Nicolas Island since 1853. No one knows where the remains of Juana Maria, or most others, are buried in the Santa Barbara Mission Cemetery. The practice of that day was to dig up the bones of all of those in an area and re-bury them in a common grave when the cemetery filled up. For this reason, the plaque to Juana Maria is on the wall of the Church in the Mission Cemetery and not on any particular plot of ground. At one time or another, sheep were run on many of the Channel Islands, totally destroying any natural vegetation on the islands. As a result, they are slowly being worn away. In a conversation with the Navy's Ecologist, Mr. Ron Dow, in October of 1982, I learned that there were no otter on San Nicolas Island, but there were large numbers of sea lions and sea elephants. The island is indeed wearing away and Mr. Dow and others spend considerable time investigating areas where the elements have exposed burial sites from the Indian inhabitants. Once the sites are researched, the remains are carefully re-buried where, it is hoped, they will remain undisturbed by the elements in future years. <hi rend="bold">San Nicolas Island Today</hi> San Nicolas is one of the eight Channel Islands off the southern California coast and contains over 20 square miles of gently rolling terrain accented with steep sea cliffs. These steep cliffs are perfect nesting habitat for seabirds such as cormorants and western gulls. Atop the island the tiny island fox reigns as the largest land mammal. The isolated beaches provide resting places for three species of pinnipeds (seals and sea lions )--northern elephant seals, harbor seals and California sea lions. Dense undersea kelp forests surround the island providing food and shelter for many species of fish, invertebrates, and once again--for sea otters. Pristine tidepools ring the island's rocky shores where crabs, abalone, sea urchins and sea snails have adapted to their ever-changing homes. San Nicolas Island is typical of the islands in the Channel Islands archipelago--but it is also unique. <hi rend="bold">A Military Presence</hi> Since 1933, San Nicolas Island has been under the jurisdiction of the U. S. Navy. Approximately 400 people work and staff the island. San Nicolas is part of the Pacific Missle Test Center's Sea Test Range. Navy personnel work on projects such as missle tracking and weapon system testing. A 10,000 foot runway accomodates supersonic target aircraft and planes from the mainland during operations. Facilities for island personnel include a bowling alley, cafeteria and a hobby shop. Because of the military operations, visitation by the general public is prohibited. The natural resources of San Nicolas Island are managed by a joint agreement between the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Interior and California's Department of Fish and Game. The U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service is currently working on a sea otter recovery program on the island. Once abundant around all the Channel Islands, sea otters were hunted to extinction for their valuable pelts. Biologists working on the sea otter project relocate animals from the Monterey Bay population in hopes that a colony of otters will be established once again in Southern California. <hi rend="bold">About the Author:</hi> <hi rend="bold">John P. transcripts: OWNERSHIP BY CAPT. GEORGE C. NIDEVER Capt. George C. Nidever came into possession of the property in 1840 or 1841. Nidever came to Santa Barbara in 1834 from West Virginia, having taken eight years to cross the continent, hunting, trapping and fighting by turn. At Santa Barbara he followed otter hunting by profession. He was the first man to stock San Miguel Island. He was the principal in the rescue of the "lone woman" of San Nicolas Island. He married Sinforosa Sanchez in 1841. Slow of speech and movement, of unblushing integrity, and a dead shot, he was a terror of evildoers. He resided at the mound for some 10 years and added two outbuildings to the adobe house; one was used as a warehouse for furs, the other as a gristmill. It is said that Nidever made improvements in the grounds, setting out trees and gardens. To the Bancroft Library of the University of California we are indebted for the following excerpts from a manuscript entitled "Life and Adventures of George Nidever, Recollections furnished by himself to E. F. Murray for the Bancroft Library, 1878." In this interview Nidever tells of his purchase of the mound property from Joseph Chapman in 1840, and of his hiding out in the old adobe house on the mound at the time of the invasion of California by the Americans. He says: I was born in 1802, Dec. 20, in Sulivan Co., East Tenn. My father, also named George, was a native of Penn.; I do not remember the town. . . . In the fall of 1840 I bought what is now known as the Burton Mound property from Joseph Chapman, who had purchased it from the mission. It had formerly been used to store hides in by the Fathers.

transcripts: <hi rend="underline">NEWBERRY [NEWBERY] AWARD</hi> <hi rend="bold">O'Dell's Early Life Aids 'Dolphin' Story</hi> <hi rend="bold">By Jean Hedger</hi> JULIAN — Scott O'Dell of Stoneapple Farm drew from a life spent along the California coast instead of books for material for his 1960 Newberry [Newbery] Medal winner. The history of the Lost Woman of San Nicholas Island is the base of "Island of the Blue Dolphins." O'Dell learned of the Indian girl he called Karana in 1956 while researching for his "Country of the Sun," a history of Southern California. What is known of the lost woman can be told in a few words. Records of a ship's captain show that when the Indians left the island she leaped into the sea and returned because her brother was left behind. She lived alone on the island of perpetual winds for 18 years after her brother was killed by wild dogs and was found by a Captain Nidever in 1853. <hi rend="bold>Narrative</hi> This historical fragment is elaborated by the author in a first-person narrative that firmly orients the reader. The narrator is a person rather than male or female, but it was necessary that she not be a repetition of Dafoe's [Defoe's] "Robinson Crusoe," O'Dell said. Inventive methods of survival were taken from a combination of coastal lore and the author's imagination. Lamps were made by the girl from the dried bodies of little fish called "sai-sai". These silver fish come swimming out of the sea in schools so thick you can almost walk on them "on nights when the moon shines full", [sic] says the girl. This is an example of the sense of reality and time placement the adventure story gives. The girl could not call the fish grunion, as we know them, or the story would be out the window, said O'Dell. <hi rend="bold">Time Measured</hi> She measured time by suns and moons, and first marked the seasons, then only the years, and at last made no record at all. The girl avoids the easy label of "earthquake" by saying "the earth rose and fell like a great animal breathing." The newspaperman, intensely conscious of his craft, has an effortless style in the story designed for both adults and children. "The book wrote itself," he said, "and this is the only time it has ever happened." O'Dell has been book editor of the Los Angeles Mirror last fall after five or six years there. He is an authority on California history, and wrote "Hill of the Hawk," a regional novel. An uninteresting area is likely to be dismissed by O'Dell as "a 10,000 word topic." Only Anglo Saxon words are used in the lyric prose of "Island of the Blue Dolphins." Good writing has been defined as talk written down and O'Dell's language sounds well read aloud. <hi rend="bold">Classic Simplicity</hi> There is a classic simplicity in this story of the sea. Few sea stories can afford to meander down unnecessary literary paths; something fundamental in the sea rejects unessentials. The object of speaking or writing should be to make something clear. If this does not happen, the story is pointless no matter how pretty the prose. O'Dell's prize winning novel is as clear as the poster on the corner illuminated by innate good taste. He visited the four by eight mile island (typically measured archaically as "leagues" in the book) about 30 years ago when with the technical department of Paramount Pictures which sought a location for Stevenson's "Ebb Tide." (San Nicholas Island was not chose because of its lack of a harbor and landing dangers. The force of pounding waves and furious winds are expected to sweep the island back into the sea someday.) <hi rend="bold">Coastal Living</hi> The ways of coastal living and knowledge of plants and animals set down in a book by O'Dell were not gained from one. Great mounds of abalone shells shining in the sun were seen by the author when he was a boy watching the harvesting of the sea near Palos Verdes in the days before there were conservation laws. "You could chew on a dried abalone all day," he remembered. The trays of dying meat destined for China covered 25 or 30 acres. The sights and sounds of these years led to Karana's fanciful scarecrow of abalone shells on the island. The shells were hung on poles. Their insides were bright, they caught the sun, and turned one way and another in the wind. It is doubtful that anyone could grow too old to be delighted by the ingenuity of a whale rib fence to rebuff wild dogs. "I just wondered how one could be protected on an island with no wood," said O'Dell, "and this seemed logical." "it was important to me to say the things in the book," said O'Dell, "we are in danger of losing the qualities of independence and self-reliance." <hi rend="bold">Specialization</hi> He speaks unhappily of an age of specialization when lawyers can speak only of torts, and admires his Julian neighbors who have practical, diversified knowledge. One neighbor has built a 5,000 square foot house by himself, including plastered ceilings and electrical wiring. Another invented a nasal spray. "Writers should write, not talk," said the writer who doesn't complain of a lack of literary neighbors. O'Dell, despite his admiration of self-reliance, would rather write than tend his 30-acre apple orchard or split wood although he does this occasionally. "Wood is $35 a cord, but can be split at $7 a cord," he remarked. O'Dell has cancelled previous contracts to clear the decks for another two-level book. This one will concern a vain Spaniard who had five or six suits of armor and discovered California in 1540 two years before Cabrillo came. He was named Alar Con and called himself the "son of the sun," thereby impressing early California residents considerably. The book[,] which won the Newberry [Newbery] Award[,] also is entered in the Hans Christian Anderson international contest. "Island of the Blue Dolphins" will be around a long time. The highly regarded Newberry [Newbery] award insures the life of a book; the story's topic had wide general interest for all ages; and it is beautifully written.
