title: "A San Nicolas Island Twined Basketry Water Bottle"
publication: Reports of the University of California Archaeological Survey, No. 50
tropes: Vanishing Indians
author: Robert F. Heizer
permission_acknowledgement: Respone 2/4/15 saying public domain a far as known. Webform to Hearst Museum of Anthropology at UC-Berkeley, 1/30/15
transcripts: ﻿76. A SAN NICOLAS ISLAND TWINED BASKETRY WATER BOTTLE Robert F. Heizer ABSTRACT Concerning the few possessions taken by the last surviving native of San Nicolas Island to the mainland in 1853, published records are scarce or non-existent. The basketry analysis presented here is based upon a photograph, reproduced herewith, of a San Nicolas Island twined specimen which finally came to the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, but which was destroyed in the fire following the 1906 earthquake. In 1836 the Franciscan missionaries effected the removal of the last survivors of the Nicoleño tribe<hi rend="superscript">1</hi> to the mainland. In the confusion of the transfer a woman was left on the island who remained there alone until 1853 when George Nidever brought her to Santa Barbara mission where, after four months, she died. The several published and manuscript accounts of her life alone for eighteen years on San Nicolas Island are being prepared by me for seperate publication. The few personal possessions which she brought with her to Santa Barbara in 1853 are said to have been sent to Rome except for one piece described as a "water bottle made of rushes and covered with asphaltum." This water bottle was reported in 1904 by Eisen as in the possession of the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, and the illustrations of that same basketry piece shown here (Fig. 1) are reproduced from photographic prints found in the C. Hart Merriam files at the University of California. The photographs were secured by Merriam's efforts, and are of particular value because the basket was destroyed, along with the building and other collections of the Academy, in the fire following the 1906 earthquake. <note type="end" place="bottom">1. The Nicoleño group is classified by Kroeber (1925:633-34) as Shoshonean. This classification rests upon analysis of four words recorded from the old woman. The words (after Eisen, 1904:15) are: <hi rend="underline">tocah</hi>, hide; <hi rend="underline">nache</hi>, man; <hi rend="underline">toygwah</hi>, sky; <hi rend="underline">puoochay</hi>, body.</note> Dimensions of the bottle are not recorded, but its height may be estimated at about 10 inches (ca. 25 cm.) and its diameter at about 6 inches (ca. 16 cm.). The base of the bottle has a surface coating of asphaltum and there are small spots randomly distrubuted on the outer surface of the basket which apparently are daubs of asphaltum applied over leaks. Since the old Nicoleño woman is known to have followed the customary Chumash-Gabrielino trick of coating the interior of baskets with asphaltum by means of lumps of asphalt and hot stones which melted the asphalt and distrubed it over the inner walls, it seems unlikely that the basket was, as Eisen (1940:15) states, "asphaltum covered." The basket is made by the twined technique and the accompanying diagram (Fig. 2a) of technique has been kindly provided by Dr. M. A. Baumhoff. In the diagram the dotted lines represent weft elements which have disappeared through rotting away. The disintegrated wefts may have been of buckskin, fur strips, feathers or hair. Two main areas, the body just above the center, and the neck, once held the decorative bands which have now disappeared. The ordinary warp appears to be of bundles of fibers rather than a single vegetal element, and this type of warp according to Mr. L. Dawson, who has made a particular study of Southern California basketry, is also the ordinary Chumash technique. The alternately spaced wefts, now disappeared, probably were decorative elements. The alternating pitch of single pairs of weft elements to form a chevron has not been noted by Mr. Dawson as a Chumash basketry trait, but he has observed this in two baskets attributed to Salinan manufacture, and this feature has been also noted by Dawson on some of the basketry fragments from Isabella Meadows Cave, Monterey County (Meighan, 1955). Beyond this not much can be said. Any basket from the Southern California coastal area is of interest because we know so little about the textile art of such groups as the Chumash and Gabrieliño. The uniqueness of the San Nicolas specimen lies partly in the circumstances surrounding its history and preservation of this bare record in the form of a photograph now over half a century old. That such water bottles were commonly used by the Shoshonean tribes of Southern California seems probable since the mainland desert groups are otherwise reported to have used such forms, and there is a Chumash record for a large asphalt-sealed water bottle of basketry (Heizer, 1955, p. [102]) as well as one for the Costanoans (<hi rend="underline">ibid</hi>., p. 163). That there remain as yet undiscovered baskets dating from the eighteenth century is a practical certainty, and in the course of time museum collections in Mexico and Europe will probably yield such treasures to the seeker. Father Font on the Anza expedition in 1776 says that he saw no baskets being made on the Santa Barbara Channel coast and quotes some religious colleagues who told him that baskets were made on Santa Cruz Island and traded from there to the mainland people. Anza collected a number of baskets from the Chumash on the way north with the intention of taking them back to Mexico, and it is these pieces which may ultimately turn up in Mexico if a search is made for them. Font remarked on the return trip a few months later that no baskets were to be seen in the Channel villages because the expedition had already collected them-- [—]presumably the supply was not yet replenished. While speaking of unusual baskets, reference should be made to the two remarkable early ninteenth century specimens, one of which is now in the University of California Robert H. Lowie Museum of Anthropology and described by Zelia Nuttall (1924) and to the unusal seedbeater (?) from a cave in the Manzana region, Santa Barbara County, described by Irwin (1946) and illustrated by Heizer (1951, Fig. 3E).

title: "A Feminine Crusoe. Eighteen Years on a Desert Island"
tropes: Origins; Discovery; Indian Queen; Noble Savage; Wonder
author: [Fred Spalding Witter]
transcripts: <hi rend="bold">A FEMININE CRUSOE.</hi> <hi rend="bold">Eighteen Years on a Desert Island.</hi> Seventy miles from the shore is San Nicolas Island, the sixth of the group that cluster around the Bay of Santa Barbara, California. It is celebrated for having been the residence for eighteen years of "The Lost Woman of San Nicolas." As her name is famous and as her story has been told in romance I will give the bare facts about her as I found them to be without any added ornament, and leave the fiction to the pen of the novelist. The Island of San Nicolas was once densely populated. This is attested by the skulls aud bones and other evidences of human abode that are found there. The Alaska lndians frequently visited the island to hunt for the furs of the sea otter. They took their women with them on these hunts, and on returning after the hunt was over they left them on the island to their fate. By order of the government in 1885 the Indians were removed from the island. Just before they were to embark, and carry away every human inhabitant, as it was supposed, a white Indian woman begged for the privilege of going ashore for her child, which she had accidentally left. She was gone a long time in a fruitless search for her offspring. The wind blew a gale, the water was shallow, there was no one who was seeking the lost one. They set sail, intending to return for the lost woman of San Nicolas, but the boat becoming she was left to her fate. It was generally known that there was a woman abandoned on the island, but no attempt was made for her deliverance. As the world soon forgets, so the woman of San Nicolas was forgotten and the year passed away. After a lapse of sixteen years a man who landed on the island found that it was inhabited by some one. The footprints of a human being sunk deep in the ground were seen. The hardness of the ground was an indication that they had been made a long time. From their size they evidently belonged to a woman. Circular enclosures made of brush six or seven feet through, were seen, where some one had lived. Near the huts were sticks driven in the ground and dried blubber hanging on them, thus prepared for food. In 1852 San Nicolas was visited again and another hunt was made for the long-lost woman. The huts were seen that had been seen before, but the old blubber had been taken away and new food of the kind hung in its place. Wild dogs were found which ran away at the approach of civilized man. In a basket covered with seal skins that they found in a bush heap was a dress made of shag skins, cut in square pieces, a rope made of sinew and several smaller articles, such as fish hooks and bone needles. The discoverers of these proofs that there lived on that island a human being scattered them on the ground, and on their return they found them gathered together and placed in the basket again. The Catholic fathers of the "Old Mission," the foremost in every good word and work, offered a reward to anyone who would find tbe lost woman, and a third effort was made in 1853 to discover the prodigal about whom there was such a mystery and in whom the world of this coast was beginning to take an Interest. "Fresh tracks of the woman were found. They belonged to very small feet, and were like those that were seen in the first attempt to find the woman. Huts made of whale ribs and covered with brush were discovered. At length an object was seen in the distance that appeared to be moving. Going towards it they saw the woman that for eighteen years had reigned Queen of San Nicolas, her subjects being the wild animals, her robe a dress of bird skins she had made and her throne the hut she had built. She was seated in an enclosure, so that only her head and shoulders could be seen. Two or three dogs were about her that disappeared at the command of their sovereign. She was seated on some grass that covered the ground and served her as a bed. Her dress was neatly made of bird skins, extending to her ankles, the feathers of which pointed downward. Her head was covered with a thick mat of yellowish brown hair and her shoulders were bare. She was occupied in stripping blubber from a piece of sealskin which she held across her knee and using for that purpose a knife made, of an iron hoop. In her hut was a fire, beside which she sat talking to herself and, occasionally shading her eyes with her hand, looked at the men that were in search of her. She received them with much courtesy, bowing and smiling and showing that this lost child of nature had much of the politeness of a true woman. She took some roots in the bag, roasted them in the fire and gave them to the men to eat. She gathered up all her food, which was her chief concern, owing to the famines she had experienced, washed herself at the spring, and followed the men cheerfully to the boat. On being taken to Santa Barbara she manifested great delight on seeing the sights of civilazation. She became a universal favorite and was presented with many gifts. Passengers on the Panama steamer that landed there all wanted to see the lost woman of San Nicolas. She related by signs her experience on the island as she spoke a language that none of the Indians knew and none of the Spanish fathers, versed in Indian dialects, could understand. Civilization, which prolongs the life of some, shortened that of the woman of San Nicolas. An excessive love of fruit led to her death in Santa Barbara at the age of fifty. She was buried with the honors of the Catholic Church by the Franciscan Fathers, and her dress and trinkets were sent to Rome and placed in that receptacle of the world's curiosities. The story of the lost woman of San Nicolas will always remain a wonderment. Her ingenuity is seen in the pails she made of grass, made to hold water by smearing them with melted asphaltum, and in her bird-skin dresses, her bone needles, her knife of iron hoop and the langunge she invented and spoke. It is inexplicable to all who have learned her story how a woman could live, eighteen years on an island around which the waves were beating a requiem to hope, getting her food aud cooking it without even those facilities which are common to the savage, and making her dresses neatly without the aid of needles except what she carved out of bone. She laid aside one dress for eighteen years, to be worn when the white men should come, of which she had a presentiment. She built her own house, protected herself from the cold, gained supreme control over the wild beasts about her and preserved her love for men and women for well nigh two decades of human life alone in the wilds. With no previous knowledge of civilization, solitude appeared to have educated her for it. An ordinary woman would have perished with despondency in such a desolate, hungry, naked, shelterless outlook.

transcripts: Chapter IX SAN NICOLAS ISLAND Screeching missiles scorch offshore skies in daily tests from Point Mugu on the mainland south of Ventura to barren, windswept San Nicolas, outermost of the Channel Islands. San Nicolas is also the pinniped capital of the United States, the home of some of nature's most amazing and amusing sea creatures. It's a 9-mile long, 30 1/2-mile wide mountain of sand, 76 miles out to sea from Los Angeles Harbor, that boasts a fascinating history highlighted by the tale of Juana Maria, one of the most astounding true stor[i]es of one person's fight for survival ever recorded in the annals of time. The saga of this mysterious woman brought the curtain down on the centuries-old Channel Island Indian culture that thrived through five distinct civilizations. San Nicolas is a bird Island, populated by thousands of ravens, cormorants, sea gulls, blue herons, bald eagles, canaries, larks and robins. It's also a rocket base for solar studies by International Geophysical Year scientists. Discovered by Cabrillo, the Island was named by Vizcaino in honor of St. Nicolas, the saint's day celebrated December 6, 1602, when the Spanish explorer's ship sailed by the Island. Some 68 prehistoric Indian village sites have been identified on San Nicolas by UCLA anthropologists Clement Meighan and Hal Eberhart who estimate that well over 1,000 Indians lived on the Island at its peak population period. These aborigines, a more peaceful people than those who dwelled on the mainland or other Channel Islands, as evidenced by the scarcity of arrowheads unearthed, existed on a seafood and bird economy, deriving their food supply from abalone, fish, sea lions, sea elephants and birds. The Island apparently never supported a great deal of plant life in the time of man's existence on it. Plundered by early 19th century otter hunters, by 1835 but a score of Indians was left on San Nicolas. That year Franciscan Mission fathers decided to remove the last of the San Nicolas Indians to the mainland. The schooner <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> was chartered to bring the aborigines to San Pedro. Charles Hubbard, captain of the small vessel, and his crew went to the Island, conveying word to the Indians there that they no longer need be subjected to the cruel forays by otter hunters. They were told by Captain Hubbard that they would be taken to the mainland where there was plenty to eat and life was much better. As the Indians piled their frugal belongings into the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph>, Captain Hubbard made haste to leave. A sudden gale churned up the sea and threatened to hurl the boat against the Island's rocky shores. One of the Indian women discovered that her child had not been brought aboard the schooner as she had expected and cried out that she had to go back for her baby. She leaped into the water and swam ashore. It was impossible for Captain Hubbard to wait any longer. The <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> set sail across the choppy channel leaving the Indian woman and her child alone on the isolated Island. At Los Angeles Harbor, the last of the San Nicolas Indians were met by Franciscans who set about to assimilate them with the other Indians at the San Gabriel Mission. Captain Hubbard explained the unfortunate experience on the Island. He could not return immediately as he had a commitment to transport a group of otter hunters led by George Nidever to Santa Rosa Island and then continue on up the coast to San Francisco. Captain Hubbard expressed the hope of returning to San Nicolas for the Indian woman. But neither he nor the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> ever had the opportunity. Less than a month later the boat with Captain Hubbard aboard sank in San Francisco Bay. Nor did anyone else return for the abandoned Indian woman on the lonely desolate Pacific isle. That is, not for 15 years. Through the long interval the story was often told, but few believed the woman or her child survived for long. San Nicolas at the time was overrun with packs of vicious wild dogs, descendants of animals loved by the Indian woman's forefathers. It was difficult enough for the small band of the Island's last Indian community to ward off the wild animals, but a young woman alone—impossible, thought those on the mainland who knew the story. At least that was the general feeling about the matter until 1850 when Thomas Jeffries and George Nidever with a crew of Indians sailed to the distant Island in a small boat. They went there to hunt otter and to find, if at all possible, the remains of the Indian woman. For six weeks they stripped otter and seal of hides, salted the skins and stowed them in the boat. Then one night an Indian who had been on a hike around the Island returned to the Island camp flushed with excitement. He told of seeing a figure running in the distance. He said he tried to catch up with the Island phantom, but failed. Truly, it did not seem possible. Could it be the lost woman? Several trips and three years later—on another otter hunting excursion to the Island—Nidever and his companion, Carl Detman, ever on the alert now for the possibility that the Indian had actually seen the lost woman of San Nicolas, spotted a basket containing a robe sewed of birds' plumage. Now they were convinced. Incredible as it seemed, they knew the Indian woman who swam back to the Island 18 years earlier to find her misplaced child was still there and very much alive. Nidever abandoned his hunt for otter. He ordered his men to join him in searching the Island, canyon by canyon, cave by cave, never quitting until the mysterious woman was found. It was Detman who made the discovery a few days later. He traced her footprints to a grass shelter on one of the Island peaks. She was seated in her hideaway, observing members of Nidever's party searching the beach below for her. A pack of dogs, trained to answer the wild woman's instant command, was at her side. Two pet ravens were also in the roofless enclosure. Surprised by Detman, she accepted his presence calmly, ordering the dogs away. Despite the fact that Detman was the first person she faced in 18 long difficult years, she did not become alarmed. The woman was dressed in cormorant feathers, a garment identical to the one found earlier by Detman and Nidever. She was in excellent physical condition. There was a large supply of food in her grass hut. When Detman summoned Nidever and the entire party confronted the woman, she told them the story of her 18-year existence on the Island, not by word of mouth, for none could understand her dialect. But through sign language, she explained how she hid when boats came to San Nicolas on rare occasions. Her child was found dead when she swam to the Island the day the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> left without her. She knew every inch of the Island, had walked its length and breadth through the years with her dogs ever at her side. She never wanted for food, living off birds, fish, abalone and seals' blubber. Water was easy to obtain from the many existing springs. Her life was lonely. But in time she came to accept it and fled in fear from every visitor. When Nidever returned to the mainland he brought the Indian woman to his Santa Barbara home where his wife cared for her. The story of her discovery spread afar. The curious came from miles to see the strange wild woman, who, in reality, was a quiet, shy person amazingly attractive despite her unique ordeal. Mission padres searched without success for one of the Indians taken from the Island in 1835. But no one could be found who spoke the woman's language. Civilization proved to be a greater challenge than life alone on San Nicolas. Despite her new diet of proper food, or perhaps because of it, she failed rapidly. In a short time she became too weak to walk. Within three months of her discovery, the last of the Channel Island Indians died. With her also died the great culture of the Islands that had thrived for centuries. On her death bed one of the priests from the Santa Barbara Mission baptized her, giving her the name Juana Maria. Her robe of cormorant feathers was sent to the Pope in Rome, where it now rests in the Vatican Museum. She was buried in the Mission graveyard, where a plaque erected to her memory in 1928 reads: <floatingText> <span/> <body> <lg type="trope-group" n="1"> <l>Juana Maria</l> <l>Indian Woman Abandoned on</l> <l>San Nicolas Island eighteen years</l> <l>Found and brought to</l> <l>Santa Barbara</l> <l>by</l> <l>Captain George Nidever</l> <l>in 1853</l> <l>Santa Barbara Chapter</l> <l>Daughters of the</l> <l>American Revolution</l> <l>1928</l> </lg> </body> </floatingText> Archeologist Arthur R. Sanger of Los Angeles believes he has the skeleton of the Indian woman's child. Sanger has searched the Channel Islands for 30 years collecting Indian artifacts for the Museum of the American Indian, New York, and the Los Angeles County Museum. He is convinced his skeleton, one of thousands of Indian relics he has collected and catalogued from the Islands, is that of Juana Maria's infant. One reason for his conviction is that the skeleton was buried deeper than most on the Island, which is being blown to sea by cyclone-like storms that buffet San Nicolas continuously. Another item that supports his belief is that beads buried with the child were imported there in the 19th century. Sanger's Indian collection includes many skeletons, and novel whale and sea turtle effigies, apparently used by the Indians as good luck pieces. Four years after Juana Maria was removed from San Nicolas, Captain Martin Kimberly introduced sheep to the already badly eroded Island. He and a continual succession of Island lessees sowed salt grass on the sandy terrain to provide nourishment for the thousands of sheep that roamed its hills and canyons for 84 years. Others who ran sheep on San Nicolas included William Howland, the Vail brothers, L. P. Elliott and Roy Agee. The latter ended this phase of Island activity in 1941 with the activation of San Nicolas during World War II, first as an Army base and later as a Navy station. During the thirties the Navy maintained a weather station there. Total population of San Nicolas then was 15, including Navy and sheep ranch personnel. Miss Alma R. McLain was employed on the Island as a school teacher for a time. Her student body consisted of Frances Agee and John Scrimiger. San Nicolas Elementary School was known as the smallest school in the country boasting a full time, fully accredited school teacher. Since 1945 San Nicolas has served as one of the nation's most important guided missile proving grounds. In fact, Point Mugu, the Navy's giant Naval Air Missile Test Center on the California coast south of Ventura, was established solely because of the presence of San Nicolas Island 70 miles to the southwest. In the past 10 years a $5,000,000 labyrinth of electronic networks has been scattered about the sand-encrusted Island hills of San Nicolas. Theodolite, telemeter and radar towers speckle Island peaks, knolls and sand-swept mesas. The sea between San Nicolas and Point Mugu provides missile scientists with a perfect testing range. Instruments at Point Mugu, Laguna Peak behind the Ventura County Navy station, at the Santa Cruz Island facility and at San Nicolas record data which enable scientists and engineers to evaluate operations of the various missiles in flight. Some missiles are fired into the sea between San Nicolas and the mainland or beyond the Island. Others such as the Regulus are actually put through their paces, guided to and landed on the San Nicolas airstrip and then shipped back by boat to Point Mugu for future test flights. From the moment a guided missile is placed into its launcher until it is landed, destroyed or dragged dripping from the Pacific, it is the subject of at least one and often as many as 40 cameras. These photographs provide scientists with proof positive why the weapon did or did not react as anticipated. The 250 Navy and civilian technicians stationed on bleak San Nicolas are all vitally involved in the study and development of guided missiles. "Welcome to the poor man's Catalina," declared the officer in charge of the San Nicolas Station, as we disembarked from one of the two Navy four-engine Douglas DC4s that make daily runs between Point Mugu and San Nicolas. Swarms of sea gulls and raucous ravens soared above and about the Island operations tower, which also serves as administrative headquarters for the San Nicolas Island base. A gust of wind ripped across the airstrip and several giant ravens perched on wires by the operations tower were blown upside down and were having a time righting themselves. Jim, the station's pet raven, buzzed us as we walked toward operations, and then gave chase to the Island's three dogs, Cecil, Rusty and Oscar, all males. "Women are verboten here. That holds true for the dogs, and Sam, our pet cat. This is strictly a man's island," exclaimed the operations officer. "And a haven for ravens," he added, as Jim landed at our feet, tugged at the officer's pants cuffs and then nipped him playfully on the leg. There are thousands of the big, black birds on the Island, descendants of the same birds considered sacred by San Nicolas Indians. Ravens exist on mice that also thrive on the Island. "Jim hurt his leg more than a year ago," we were told, "and some of the fellows at operations took him to sick bay and patched up the injury. Now he's everybody's friend." After being assigned quarters in one of the Island's concrete barracks, we rejoined the operations officer at Operations on the 502-foot airstrip. San Nicolas, ringed by cliffs averaging 500 feet in height, rises to a peak elevation of 890 feet. We climbed aboard a powerful wagon for a trip to Lands End, an amazing stretch of sculptured rocks that extends to a needle-nose point into the sea. Here, abalone and lobster abound. Station personnel need not be skin divers to pry pink, blue and black abalone by the hundreds off weird shaped, eroded, sponge-like rocks during low tide. All that is necessary is to walk out on the rocks and pull them off. You don't even get your feet wet ... At night San Nicolas missile men drive to Lands End and catch lobster with bare hands. It's a great Island sport. Saucer-like pockets of clear water nestled in rocks at Lands End were filled with gorgeous ocean life—deep purple sea grass, sea urchins, brown sea moss, sea lettuce, black snails, hermit crabs and sea anemones of various sizes and colors. A 15-foot, jet black whale, victim of a vicious sea battle, washed ashore a day or two before our arrival, lay on a nearby sand spit. The operations officer checked his lobster traps and shouted with glee as he removed a half dozen tempting red snappers. Although unauthorized personnel are not allowed to land on the Island, Dick Probert's Avalon Air Transport amphibian line flies chartered groups to waters off the Island coast. This is Probert's skin divers' special. He anchors his amphib for four hours while sportsmen dive from the plane exploring the fascinating sea depths and bring up abalone and lobster for the flight home. From Lands End we drove across five miles of sandy waste, by-passing evidences of kitchen middens and innumerable fossilized tree stumps, indication of the presence at one time of small forests on the now barren Island. Shrapnel, 20 mm. shells and live 100-pound bombs littered a large section of sand hills—souvenirs of the Thirties and Forties when San Nicolas was used as a Navy firing range. At one point we paused on the sandy roadbed to descend to a half-hidden cave where an Indian artist had scrawled drawings of ocean waves and sharks in various forms of motion. We wondered if Juana Maria had lived in this cave, if perhaps it was she who made the lasting impressions on the walls. A short distance from the cave a tremendous thundering discordant symphony suddenly rent the air. We had arrived at the beginning of the five-mile stretch of sea lion beaches, inhabited by more than 5,000 of the peculiar pinnipeds. As we walked gingerly toward the sea lions, perched on rocks above the breaking surf, to get close-up pictures, the playful pinnipeds became aware of our presence and stirred up a storm—howling, barking, sneezing, yawning, squealing as they wriggled to the edge of the rocks and flipped into the water. "Go away!" they seemed to be shouting as they splashed about in the sea. The Island has the largest number of sea lions found anywhere in the nation and one of the few herds of sea elephants in the world. More than 300 sea elephants, cows and their offspring have been counted on San Nicolas. The ugly mammal gets its name from its proboscis, a grotesque trunklike snout more than a foot long. The sea elephants, sea cows and baby sea elephants put on an even more hilarious show than did the sea lions. Too lazy to care, these tremendous sad-eyed wrinkled beasts hardly moved as we walked about their herd. Except for the king bull. In the colony we visited there were about 50 mouse-faced cows, each seven to 10 feet long and weighing more than a ton. There were almost as many babies in the colony as cows. A short distance from the herd were a half-dozen bulls lying on scattered rocks. Whenever one of the bulls outside the herd would try to move in near a cow, a battle royal began. The king bull flopped over cows and rocks to the interloper, making the distance in jig time considering his size, 12 to 18 feet, and weighing in excess of 2 1/2 tons. Ripping into the invader with his tusk-like teeth, the king bull in each instance of battle swiftly drew blood and chased off his challenger. During repeated battles, cows and babies yapped, screamed, bellowed and barked, constantly curling their flippers that resemble giant-sized hands across their backs and scratching their skin. It was equally entertaining to observe the cooperation among the various wildlife on the Island—cooperation, that is, in some instances and downright thievery in others. Cormorants, sea lions, sea elephants and sea gulls sounded alarms for each other, with the arrival of indigenous Island fox or wild cats that roam the Island in large numbers. They also "blew the whistle" as we approached one beach after another. The sea gulls took to the air. This alerted the cormorants. And when they swarmed into the air the rush of their wings alarmed the sea lions and sea elephants who subsequently took to the water. However, at times when cormorants took flight, sea gulls rushed to their nests and promptly chomped away on cormorant eggs, while ravens invaded sea gull nests and devoured sea gull eggs. We also saw ravens ground an Island eagle as they protected their centuries-old reign as sacred rulers of their Island domain. Sea elephants and cows were a major source of oil during old whaling days and were almost hunted to extinction. They are now making a comeback and increasing in numbers from year to year at San Nicolas. Taking them in captivity is prohibited in United States waters. Later, back at the base, we sat in on a yarn-swapping session between Lincoln L. Jackson, 67, from Van Nuys, California, and C. W. Sanders, 36, boatswain's mate 2nd Class of Marion, Illino[i]s. Jackson, area supervisor of range instrumentation, came to San Nicolas in 1946 when the missile base was activated. He has lived on the Island longer than anyone else now there. San Nicolas' highest hill has been named Jackson Hill in his honor. Sanders is the veteran Islander among Navy men. They were discussing the winds that continuously sweep the Island. "Our prevailing northwest winds average between 35 and 50 m.p.h. nearly every day of the year," Sanders related. "But it blows much faster than that several times during the week," Jackson added. "We have no half-way weather out her[e]. Sandstorms can be expected at all times. Fine sand seeps into everything and plays havoc with our machinery." "Everybody learns to lean into the winds," Sanders continued. "When we go ashore, we can always spot someone from the Island by the way he walks—with a San Nicolas tilt." "The wind blows so fierce out here," Jackson noted, "that we'll build a road with a bulldozer on Friday and by Monday there won't be a sign of the road left." There are 10 miles of paved road on the Island. The rest is constructed, as Jackson indicated, quite frequently. San Nicolas has its own fresh water supply. Tapped from Thousand Springs in the heart of the Island, it has a mineral taste, but those who live on San Nicolas swear by it, favoring it over mainland drinking water. Jackson and Sanders, like most of the personnel on the Island, enjoy hiking and fishing. They're both Island authorities and have unearthed four complete skeletons. Noteworthy feature of the skeletons are the teeth—none missing and not a pinpoint of cavity. But the teeth, in each case, were worn down by the rigorous chewing habits of their owners. Popular pastime on the Island is baseball—when the winds aren't blowing. "This place grows on you," one of the men declared. "We get ashore regularly, if we want. And we can save money over here. No one can say that San Nicolas with its crazy ravens, sea elephants and good fishing is a dull Island. And, of course, the missiles keep us busy." In this International Geophysical Year 1957-1958, San Nicolas is playing an important role. At the dawn of the IGY year a mighty Deacon rocket with a Nike booster roared skyward from San Nicolas as a team of scientists began a study of solar rays in their relation to radio waves. The rocket was fired to penetrate the ionosphere, 50 miles above the earth, where radio waves are reflected back to earth. However, during solar flareups instead of bouncing the radio waves back to the earth, the ionosphere absorbs them, causing a radio blackout. The rocket flights measure ultraviolet light and X-rays during solar flares. Valuable information about the explosions on the sun is being recorded at the IGY station. Methods too are being learned for forecasting radio blackouts. No mention of San Nicolas Island is complete without information about Begg Rock, eight miles northwest of San Nicolas Island. Begg Rock was named after the schooner <emph>John Begg</emph> which crashed and sank on the 15-foot high rock that rises abruptly from a depth of 50 fathoms. The <emph>John Begg</emph> ran head-on into the tiny pyramid of guano-capped land in 1824. A reef extends northward and southward of the rock a little over 100 yards in each direction. A lighted whistle buoy marks Begg Rock 500 yards northward of its peak. The Navy has several lighted floats each about 10 feet long and four feet wide in its vicinity. No mention of San Nicolas is complete either without a buried treasure story. For there are legends galore about buried treasures here as well as on almost every one of the other Channel Islands. This story is but a year old. Two of the Navy men found an old weathered parchment which captured the imagination of mainlanders from California to New York and all points in between. The parchment, barely legible, was discovered beneath the floor boards of an abandoned sheepherder's cabin. It read: <floatingText> <span/> <body> <l>At Christmas time when gifts are sent</l> <l>They're from the saint, a kind old gent.</l> <l>On an isle which bears his name</l> <l>Is treasure, hid for you to claim</l> <l>In an iron chest so strong</l> <l>Buried where the land is long.</l> <l>If you walk where the tides do meet</l> <l>You will find it at your feet.</l> <l>Coins so rare, coins so old</l> <l>Coins of silver and of gold.</l> <l>If he who finds it is my friend,</l> <l>All my fortune he may spend.</l> <l>If he who finds it is my foe,</l> <l>Curses, misery and woe.</l> </lg> </body> </floatingText> If the person who composed the ditty actually knew of a buried treasure, then it is or was at Lands End "... where the tides do meet."

transcripts: ﻿<hi rend="bold">Indian Woman Lives 18 Years Alone on Island</hi> One of the most fascinating stories about California's Channel Islands is that of Juana Maria, the mysterious woman who brought down the curtain on the centuries-old Indian culture that thrived on the eight offshore islands. It is one of the most astounding true stories of one person's fight for survival ever recorded. UCLA anthropologists Clement Meighan and Hal Eberhart identified 68 prehistoric village sites on San Nicolas Island and estimated that well over 1,000 Indians lived on the island at its peak population period. They were a more peaceful people than the Indians who lived on the mainland and on the other Channel Islands, according to the two UCLA scientists, who came to that conclusion because of the scarcity of arrowheads unearthed. San Nicolas Island Indians existed on a seafood and bird economy, deriving their food supply from abalone, fish, sea lions, sea elephants and birds. The island apparently never did support a great deal of plant life. By 1835 only a handful of Indians were still living on San Nicolas Island. The Franciscan priests decided to move the Indians to the mainland. Capt. Charles Hubbard's schooner, <emph>Peor es Nada</emph>, was chartered to bring the Indians to San Pedro. The story goes that a storm moved into the island and the seas became turbulent as the Indians were being loaded aboard the boat. As Capt. Hubbard prepared to leave one of the Indian women discovered her child had not been brought aboard the schooner as she had expected. She jumped into the water and swam ashore. It was impossible for the boat to wait any longer as the stormy seas threatened to hurl the boat into the island's rocky seacoast. The <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> set sail across the choppy channel, leaving the Indian woman and her child alone on the island. The San Nicolas Island Indians were assimilated with other Indians at the San Gabriel Mission. Capt. Hubbard told the Franciscan fathers how the Indian woman and her child were left behind on San Nicolas Island. He had a commitment to transport a group of sea otter hunters led by George Nidever to Santa Rosa Island. From Santa Rosa Island the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> was to sail to San Francisco. "But just as soon as I return to Southern California, if no one has transported the Indian woman and her child to the mainland, I will sail to San Nicolas and pick her up," Capt. Hubbard promised the mission priests. Capt. Hubbard was never able to keep his promise. Less than a month later the <emph>Peor es Nada</emph> sank in San Francisco Bay with the sea captain aboard. Fifteen years went by before anyone returned to the lonely desolate nine-mile-long, three and a half mile wide island, 76 miles out to sea from San Pedro, to look for the Indian woman and her child. Few believed the woman and child survived for long. San Nicolas Island was overrun with packs of wild dogs. That plus the difficulty of a young woman eking out a living all by herself seemed to be an impossibility. In 1850, Thomas Jeffries and George Nidever sailed to the island with a crew of Indians to hunt otter. For six weeks they stripped otter and seals of hides, salted the skins and stowed them in a boat. Then one night an Indian who had been hiking around the island came running back where the otter hunters were camped. He told of seeing a human being running in the distance. He tried to catch up with the island phantom, but failed. Could it be the lost Indian woman of San Nicolas Island? But the shadowy creature was not seen again and the otter hunters returned to the mainland. Three years later on another otter hunting excursion to the island, Nidever and Carl Detman found a basket containing a robe made of birds' plumage. Now they were convinced. The Indian woman who swam back to the island 18 years earlier to find her misplaced child, or the child, now a young woman, or both, were alive on the island. Nidever abandoned his hunt for otter. He and his men searched the island, canyon by canyon, cave by cave, until they finally succeeded. It was Detman who made the discovery a few days after the search began. He had traced her footprints to a grass shelter on one of the island peaks. She was seated in her hideaway, observing members of Nidever's party searching the beach below. A pack of dogs, trained to answer the wild woman's instant command, was at her side. Two pet ravens were also in the roofless enclosure. Surprised by Detman, she accepted his presence calmly, ordering the dogs away. Despite the fact that Detman was the first person she faced in 18 years, she did not become alarmed. She was dressed in cormorant feathers, a garment identical to the one found earlier by Detman and Nidever. She was in excellent physical condition. There was a large supply of food in her grass hut. Through sign language, because none of the Indian otter hunters could understand her, she told how she hid on those rare occasions when boats came to the island. She was able to explain to the men that she found her child dead when she swam to the island the day the <emph>Poer es Nada</emph> left without her. She knew every inch of the island. She never wanted for food, living off birds, fish, abalone and seals' blubber. Water was easily available from the many existing springs. Her life was lonely. But in time she came to accept it and fled in fear from every visitor. The boat returned to the mainland and Nidever brought the woman to his Santa Barbara home, where his wife cared for her. The story of her discovery spread far and wide. Curious [sic] came for miles to see the strange wild woman, who, in reality, was a quiet, shy person. Mission padres searched without success for one of the Indians taken from the island in 1835, but none could be found who spoke the woman's language. Civilization proved to be a greater challenge than life alone on San Nicolas. Despite her new diet of proper food, or perhaps because of it, she failed rapidly. In a short time she became too weak to walk. Within three months of her discovery, the last of the Channel Island Indians died. With her also died the great culture of the islands that had thrived for centuries. On her death bed one of the priests from the Santa Barbara Mission baptized her, giving her the name Juana Maria. Her robe of cormorant feathers was sent to the Pope in Rome, where it remains to this day in the Vatican Museum. She is buried in the Mission graveyard, where a plaque erected to her memory in 1928 reads: Juana Maria Indian Woman Abandoned on San Nicolas Island eighteen years Found and brought to Santa Barbara by Captain George Nidever in 1853 Santa Barbara Chapter Daughters of the American Revolution 1928. Archeologist Arthur R. Sanger believed he had the skeleton of Juana Maria's child. Sanger searched the Channel Islands for 30 years collecting Indian artifacts for the Museum of the American Indian, New York, and the Los Angeles County Museum. He was convinced his skeleton, one of thousands of Indian relics he collected and catalogued from the islands, was that of the Indian woman's child. One reason for his conviction is that the skeleton was buried deeper than most on the island. Another reason was that beads buried with the baby were imported there in the 19th century. Sanger's collection included many skeletons and novel whale and sea turtle effigies, apparently used by the Indians as good luck pieces.
