transcripts: <hi rend="bold">ISLES OF MYSTERY</hi> MEMENTOES OF AN EXTINCT RACE IN THE PACIFIC OCEAN. DESERTED CHANNEL ISLANDS. THOROUGHLY EXPLORED AT LAST BY PROF. CHARLES FRED HOLDEN. SAN NICOLAS' LONE WOMAN. Remains That Tell of an Interesting Tribe of Quite Aesthetic Tastes. The deserted Channel islands of the Pacific, which lie some twenty miles off the southern coast of California, have at last undergone a thorough exploration by Prof. Charles Frederick Holden, with the result that much of absorbing interest regarding the extinct inhabitants of these lovely isles has been discovered. He visited San Nicolas, Santa Cataline and San Clemente and made many excavations and many rich finds. Giants once lived in the exquisitely lovely Channel islnds, for many skeletons have been found there more than seven feet high. Tradition has it that the warlike tribes of the Aleutian islands came down in boats more than a century ago and practically exterminated the Channel islanders. Certain it is that most of the unhappy wretches met death by violence, for nearly all the skulls discovered are crushed by blows from blunt instruments. The club is the weapon of the Aleutian savage, and this seems to fit the tradition. A few escaped, and up to about sixty years ago the remnants of the tribe were still living on San Nicolas. In 1835 the Franciscans of the Santa Barbara mission, learing [learning] that there were but sixteen of the strange Indian race then living, determined to rescue them. They went over in a sloop and succeeded in getting all on board. At the last moment an Indian woman returned for her child, and, one of the frequent storms of the Channel islands springing up, the sloop was driven away. It went on the rocks of Point Conception and all on board were lost. So only this woman was left, and she was soon forgotten. In 1851, however, Capt. George Nidever visited the island to hunt sea otter, and was amazed to find human footprints in the sand. Two years later he returned to investigate the matter, and succeeded in capturing the remaining Indian, now an old woman. She was dressed in birdskins, and was engaged in scraping blubber from a seal. They took her to Santa Barbara, where she lived for several years, and was known far and wide as "the lone woman of San Nicolas." But she never learned enough English to be able to tell anything of the life and the tradition of her strange race. Prof. Holden in his exploration just concluded found many large mounds in San Nicolas, one 300 feet long by 50 wide, composed of abalone shells, which were brought from the sea two miles distant, thus showing evidence of a large population. TELLTALE DISCOVERIES. He found objects of stone, bone and shell piled in heaps. There were pendants, rings and beads and curious objects in pearl among them, proving that the extinct peopel loved ornamentation. That they played games was shown by the finding of perforated and oval stones, and many small and peculiarly shaped instruments. Some of the mortars picked up were very high and narrow, others so heavy there was great difficulty in rolling them down to the ship. One showed evidence of ornamentation with abalone. Sculptured forms of miniature sea lions and whales carved from serpentine prove a love of art in the aborigines. According to Prof. Holden the islanders depended for food on abalone, fish and possibly roots. Consequently they belonged to an advanced period of the stone age. San Clemente, twenty miles long and three wide, Prof. Holden found, contained much evidence of ancient havitation. Possibly 300 years ago it had a large population. One square mile of its area was covered with skeletons, shells and ancient implements and mortars, some ones weighing 100 pounds. Santa Catalina is a high mountain ridge, the only landing places being the mouths of canyons. Up the canyons Prof. Holden located fifty sites which had been occupied by aborigines. Under a small summer resort hotel recently built there he found implements of all kinds. On San Clemente numerous bone implements were unearthed, and among them needles and awls for punching shells. Several mortars found there on San Cantalina [Catalina] show an aesthetic taste among the people, for they are highly decorated with mosaic of abalone. A sword handle was decorated with a plate made of abalone. Prof. Holden declares that the islands were inhabited for many centuries, for he found heaps of abalone shells on the seashore, covered with twenty feet of a deposit, which he calculates required centuries for its formation. The islands have been a mine of archaeologic treasure ever since 1872, when the first systematic exploration was made by Mr. W. G. W. Harford, of the United States coast survey, who subsequently exhibited his small but valuable collection to admiring scientific friends in the East. Dr. W. H. Dall, of the national Museum, paid a visit to the islands in the following year, and also secured some wonderfully interesting specimens of primitive art. In 1875 the Smithsonian institute sent out a party of scientific men, with Mr. Paul Schumacher in charge, and these gentlemen in their explorations discovered several very remarkable and extensive burial grounds, as well as large ancient village sites, buried deep under the castaway shells of edible mollusks. TELLS OF A DEAD PAST. From the grave yards weere unearthed a large number of skeletons, each surrounded by marvellous examples of the products and handiwork of the long past dead. The graves, as described by these investigators and others, make an interesting story of themselves. The skeletons lay crowded together in every conceivable position, sometimes super-imposed three or four feep, those below forgotten and unmarked, ruthlessly disturbed to make room for the last interment. Some of the graves had rude boxes constructed of the huge flat bones of the whales, in which the dead were deposited. The early sea captains related grewsome tales of the islands, where, within the yawning skeletons of whales, lay the grinning and bleached bones of men, exposed to view by the ceaseless shifting of the sands. In the department of prehistoric archaeology of the Smithsonian institution are to be found collected together all the results of the above expedition and that of a number of others, and the aggregate produces a startling revelation as to the possibilities of those faraway islands in valuable ethnologic finds. One type of the remarkable finds made in the graves is the gigantic soapstone, or steatite, pots, called ollas in the Southwest, which stand absolutely alone as monuments to the cleverness of the early inhabitants of these islands. Some of them are fully two and one-hald feet in diameter, almost globular in form, with very thin walls, and carefully polished over their entire inner and outer surfaces. It is astounding how these ancient peoples carved and modeled such symmetrical and fragile vases from this material, but nevertheless fully three-fourths of the vessels used for cooking and ceremonial purposes were adriotly fashioned from it. For most of the pipes, gorgets, mortars, anumal figures, pendants, net sinkers and the like the same stone was utilized. A shudderingly facetious use for sme of these colossal stone jars was as a headgear for the dead. Numbers of the skeletons were unearthed with skulls completely incased in the orifices of the vases. Beautiful haliotis shells, with their inner walls plated with pearly and shining nacre, were quite common finds with the burials, and some of them have been found partially filled with bitumen, a substance which seems to have had a very wide range of utility among the natives as a pitch for calking the wooden boats, as paint for decorating the body and earthenware vases, as handles for brushed and as cement for holding in place arrow and spear points. BEADS AND ORNAMENTS. An intensely interesting insight into the foibles and van weakness for personal adornment among these long past people is exemplified in a large and varied collection of shell beads, cut from the central shaft of big conch shells; shell disks, some slightly engraved with designs; shell plates, carved and pierced for suspension, and, the most interesting of all, the paint cups, of shell and steatite, half filled with bright red ochres and black shining asphalt, which were used in those ages, dimmed by time, to hideously decorate the faces and body of the shy and coy maiden, perhaps, as well as that of her sinister and warlike lover. Living upon an island home, the inhabitants necessarily obtained much of their sustenance from the surrounding waters, and, in evidence of these piscatorial proclivities, many remnants of carelessly constructed canoes have been unearthed from time to time by the various parties who have delved in the burial places, and it appears that many of these canoes became the last resting places or sepulchres for the dead. Stone net sinkers have been found in such profusion as to leave no doubt as to the persistent avocation of the fishermen, and in the Smithsonian collection appear numbers of finely cut shellfish hooks, carved out of the sea shells in almost complete semicircles, with sharp barbs, which would do credit to some of more modern manufacture. Half a dozen hairbrushed, examples of which are still to be seen in use among a few Southwestern tribes, were unearthed from graves. They are made from the fibre of the soap plant, or a species of yucca, bunched together in the semblance of a miniature whisk broom, the top, or handle, formed by heavily coating one end for several inches with bitumen. With such beautiful collections already gained from this garden spot for archaeologists, it is apparent that a vast amount of the richest and more valuable objective evidence obtainable in the United States must lie waiting for the hands of the enthusiastic scientist. Prof. Holden is the fortunate scientist who has availed himself of the rich field that has so long awaited a patient investigator. He has brought back with him a wonderland of curiosities, which he is now engaged in studying. A MELANCHOLY SPOT. San Clemente is the only one of the islands that is at all visited. A few sportsmen go there yearly for the magnificent bird shooting and unsurpassed sea fishing. The others are rarely ever approached. San Nicolar [Nicolas] is the most interesting of them all. It is partly covered with drifting sand now, but its grassy and wooded portions are the home fo thousands of wild sheep. Hundreds of immense white pelicans can be seen at almost any season promenading sedately on the narrow beach of Coral Harbor, the only safe approach to the island, a dilapidated shed, built by the Chinese, who came at intervals to gather the exquisitely lovely shells on the shore or to shear the wild sheep. The shell mounds, of which there are hundreds, are made up of astonishing varieties of mollusks, the bones of innumerable fish of all the species found in the neighboring waters and the bones of seals, sea elephants, whales, otters, birds and foxes. There must have been a time when the island was luxuriantly forested, for very many of the animals whose bones are found there could not live on the island in its present desolate condition. It is a melancholy spot for the visitor, for every acre of it has its tale or tales of an extinct civilization. That the people that once enlivened its shores and cliffs were peaceful is shown by the absence of weapons of offence [offense]. The weapons found there are those used in the household and the chase. These gentle savages are fishermen by choice, and they much have been sturdy and persistent whalers, judging by the myriad remains of these deep sea leviathans that Prof Holden found upon the islands. The great bones of whales are built into rudely artistic structures so compactly that they have withstood the ravages of storm and sand for centuries. The only actual record of this interesting savage race that we have previous to the disastrous attempt by the missionaries to remove the remnants of it, as told above, is the log of Capt. Juan Rodriquez Cabrillo, the Portuguese navigator, who sailed up the Californian coast in 1542. He stopped a day or two at each of the Channel islands and reported that they were inhabited by a "vigorour and lusty race of natives, who thronged the shores of the bays and headlands," and seemed mystified by the ship. The islands remain, but the natives are no more.

transcripts: AN INDIAN MOTHER. THE STORY OF A LONE WOMAN ON A DESERTED ISLAND. Jumped Into the Ocean and Swam Ashore to Find Her BabeFailing to Recover the Child, She Lived Alone on the Island For Eighteen Years. Off the coast of southern California lie the Santa Barbara islands. They look very near the mainland on the map, as if it would only be a pleasant afternoon's work to explore them in a rowboat, but in fact they are far enough away from the homes and haunts of men to have been the scene of a history stranger, lonelier and more pitiful than the one De Foe "made up" about Robinson Crusoe. These islands have been long uninhabited, visited only by grazers who keep sheep on some and by trappers after otter and seal. But Indians used to make their home on the larger islands, and it was when the last of the tribe were being removed to the mainland that an accident occurred which caused a woman to spend on San Nicholas 18 years utterly alone. In 1835 Spanish missionaries were busy in southern California civilizing, teaching and converting the Indiansnot such degraded beings as are now to be seen on the western coast, but a skillful people who learned well how to build and farm. The fathers had done much with the coast Indians and now turned their eyes to the little tribes on the rocky islands out at sea. They made arrangements to bring them one after another to the mainland. The Indians seem to have come willingly, but in one case the embarkation was effected with much difficulty on account of a storm. A schooner under the command of a Captain Williams had gone to San NicholasSan Nicholas lies 79 miles out at sea to bring away the Indians, about 20 of them, who lived there. A tempest fell upon the island as the schooner drew near, and to land was very difficult. All was wild hurry and confusion. The vessel was in danger, and the Indians were making a "flitting" for life. So it was not remarkable that as they were putting out to sea one young mother should find her child had been left behind. She thought it had been brought aboard by a sailor. When she discovered the truth, she was frantic. She prayed the captain to turn back, but he said the storm was too dangerous; they might all be shipwrecked and drowned. The poor girl grew desperate, and she did what many a mother would be driven to do in like casejumped overboard. She could swim, and the last that was seen of her she was striking out bravely, making her way back to her deserted home and her baby. But only a moment was she visible. No attempt was amde to rescue her. The schooner landed its exiles at San Pedro. At that time vessels were very few on the coast, and the schooner was engaged for two trips, which, it was considered, must be made before she could return to look up the lost woman. On the latter of these trips she was wrecked, and there was nothing bigger than canoes and fishing boats left on all the lower coast. Seventy miles in an open boat no man cared to undertake. Some said both woman and child must by this time be dead, some that the mother never could have reached shore. Father Gonzales, however, was one person who was not satisfied, but 15 years passed before he could get anything done. The details of the searches made cannot be given here, but Thomas Jeffries, a man who for $200 made the first effort, did not find her. But he found so many seals and otters that other schooners made several trips there in the next few years, carrying hunters and bringing home spoils. At last on one of these expeditions a Captain Nidiver found the print of [a] naked human foot in the sand. "There," he said, "has passed the lost woman." And he vowed he would not leave till he found here. He and his men now raked the island as with a comb. Soon they came on an unfinished dress of birds' breasts, a beautiful thing of wonderful workmanship. It was in a basket of rushes hanging in a tree. Near a spring dried fish and blubber were hidden in the rocks. At last Nidiver himself saw the woman, wearing a dress, low necked and sleeveless, like the one in the basket. When she saw him, she first started to run, then stopped and met him with friendliness. No one could talk to [he]r, but with the most touching hospitality she set about getting a mean for him and his men. She had various little neat pens and shelters in different places. The saddest thing is yet to be told. When they took her to the mainland, many Indians were brought to her, and she scanned each face eagerly, but no one who could even talk to her was ever found. Her little tribe was scattered and absorbed among other "mission Indians" as raindrops are lost in the sea. She was treated with all tenderness by Captain Nidever's Spanish wife, who kept her and would not allow her to be made a show of, but when no human souls caould be found who knew even her tongue she began to droop. She loved Mrs. Nidever's children devotedly and would tell over and over by signs how she had looked and looked for her baby and never found it. The lady came to love her much, and when she grew weak she sent for seal's meat to try to tempt her appetite with the food she was used to. The sick woman patted her hands for "Thank you," but she would not eat. She soon died. Her beautiful feather gowns were sent to the pope. The Nidever family still keep some of her water tight baskets, several of her bone needles are treasured by a lady in San Francisco, and the grave of this pathetic, wonderful heroine is still pointed out by the priests in Santa Barbara.  Youth's Companion.

title: "An Idyl of the Pacific. In Island White with Skeletons of an Extinct Indian Race"
tropes: Discovery; Wonder; Indian Queen; Vanishing Indians; Origins
transcripts: <hi rend="bold">AN IDYL OF THE PACIFIC.</hi> <hi rend="bold">In Island White with Skeletons of an Extinct Indian Race.</hi> On a lonely wind-swept Island of San Nicolas, eighty miles off the coast of Ventura County, where as far back as the memory of man runs hundreds of grisly white skeletons have dotted the valleys and hillsides, local archæologists are now busy gathering the relics of a strange, extinct race. The island ten miles long and oval in shape, being four miles across at the widest part. Strange utensils of serpentine, sandstone and steatite are found there among the human bones, and the island and its erstwhile inhabitants have a history so curious that it is difficult of comprehension. In 1835 the padres of Santa Barbara, learning that there were but sixteen of the strange Indian race then living there, determined to rescue them from the island. They went over in a sloop and succeeded, as they thought, in getting all on board. At the last moment an Indian woman returned for her child, and one of the frequent storms of the Channel islands springing up, the sloop was driven away without her. The sloop went on the rocks of Point Conception and all on board were lost. Sixteen years later Capt. George Nidever and two men went from the coast on a sloop to hunt otter off San Nicolas. On looking they were, like Crusoe, astonished to discover human footprints on the sand. They saw no one, however, and a storm compelled them to put to sea. It was two years thereafter that the adventurous captain, revolving in his mind the sight of the footprints in the uncanny island, determined to go and discover and bring over the lonely woman of whom he had vaguely heard. Men accompanied him, and at length they saw on the surf-beaten shore a woman with long tawny hair dressed in a queer garb of colored birdskins and scraping with a bone knife the blubber of a seal. They surrounded and approached her stealthily, and although suddenly confronted she did not appear in the least afraid, but smiled, and then falling on her knees prayed to the sun. The wild woman made no objection when by signs she was made to understand that she was to go with them in the boat. They reached Santa Barbara across the rough sea, and the first thing the Indian woman saw was Dr. S. L. Shaw, now eighty years old and yet living there, riding a horse. She had never seen nor heard of any object like it, and thought the man and horse were one, and she knelt on the shore and offered her devotions to it. Two weeks afterwards the last inhabitant of rock-ribbed tempest-tossed San Nicolas died from eating food to which she was unaccustomed, furnished by her rescuers, and the curtains fell on her strange race forever. Wild dogs had eaten her child. Her dress of red and blue features [feathers], a wonderful creation of barbaric hands, was sent to the Pope of Rome. Relic hunters have gathered mortars, pestles, ollas, toy steatite canoes and other curious things there for some years past and shipped them to various Eastern and European universities. Skeletons and parts of skeletons have also been collected, in large numbers, but today the bones of thousands of Indians are scattered about there. Some lie face down, indicating that they have fallen in battle. There are so many human relics there that San Nicolas is known as the "Isle of Skulls." "The lonely island, whose highest parts is [sic] but 1,040 feet above the sea," said a resident of Ventura last night, "is noted for the high artistic class of many of its relics. Had the woman rescued, then fifty-two years old, not died a story passing strange would no doubt have been told of the race so long hemmed in by the waste of waters about. As it is, much of the strange story is shrouded in mystery forever.["]—San Francisco Examiner.

transcripts: BEAUTIFUL SANTA BARBARA AN OUT-OF-DOOR PARADISE It Is the Riviera of the Great Pacific Coast, and Was Named For a Girl Killed By Her Father—Daughter of a Roman General Who Perished a Christian Martyr—California Found in 1542, and Explored Just Fifty Years After Columbus Discovered America—Santa Barbara Is the Place Where Tired People Come to Soak Up Sunshine—It Is Rich, But Democratic&#8212A Single Grapevine Covers an Acre, Produces Ten Tons of Grapes, Is Eight Feet in Circumference at the Base—Walnuts Yield $200 or More to the Acre. Editor Telegram: Please inform us how California compares in size with Pennsylvania? Ans.—There cannot be a comparison. California has 99,463,681 acres. To get a comparative idea you can take the states of Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware and Maryland, and spreading them all out together over California there would be an uncovered margin of 13,774 square miles, or more than enough in excess to make mroe than ten states like Rhode Island. California is "some" state. NUMBER VII. There is more than one outdoor paradise in California. In the list do not fail to include Santa Barbara. The climate has attracted invalids and persons in search of health and pleasure since the earliest settlement of the Pacific coast. While California was still a part of Mexico, many refined and aristocratic Spanish families made it their home and contributed to the charm of social life. A few descendants of the early Spanish settlers still reside there. They have become thoroughly Americanized, but may easily be identified by their names, their features and complexions and the graceful manners of their race. The mission of Santa Barbara is the best preserved in California, its monastery is the most extensive, it is an educational institution of high standard, and its influence is the widest of any in the state. Many people consider Santa Barbara the most desirable place of residence for families of wealth and leisure in the United States, if not in the world. The climate and environment are very much like those of the Riviera of France. It is the only place of resort in the United States which has a mountain range on one side of it, and an ocean on the other, and where the climate permits the population to live in comfort the year around. It is often called the Newport of the Pacific, but is more democratic and cosmopolitan than the queen of the Atlanic resorts. No social tyranny is recognized; the habits and customs of the people are not so artificial; everybody lives as nearly as possible to nature:[;] there is no rivalry in dress or dinner parties, or other forms of display; all classes spend most of their time out-of-doors, and the belle of Santa Barbara shows to the best advantage in a Khaki suit, astride a mustang climbing a mountain trail, rather than at a ball or garden party. The population is made up mostly of "remitters"—that is in this instance people who have retired from business, widows of large means, and others who are able to live luxuriously upon the proceeds of investments elsewhere. Many people from San Francisco spent part of the winters in Santa Barbara, owning or renting bungalows, which are of all sizes. There are colonies of people from the big eastern cities of Boston and New York.. The richest resident is a petroleum prince, who has figured in the divorce courts. Between the mission and the sea runs the main street of the town, a wide, well-paved thoroughfare, more than two miles long, which is lined on both sides with business blocks, banks, mercantile establishments, and the best bookstores and curio shops to be found on the Pacific coast. The high class of goods they keep is an index to the wealth and culture of the community. There is a line of trolley cars running from the beach to the mission[,] and a wide and beautiful boulevard follows the shore line for several miles. At the northern end are bath houses, and a bathing pier near a plaza, where a band plays every afternoon. There is sea bathing the year round, and one of the finest bath houses in the land. There are several sanitariums and hot medicinal springs at an elevation of 1,300 feet. One may spend an entire winter in Santa Barbara, and follow a different drive or trail every day. In fact, no city in California has so many beautiful drives and trails for motors, carriages and saddle horses. The Santa Ynez range of mountains is broken by innumerable canyons and gorges, and between them lie broad table lands, which are occupied as ranches, olive groves and walnut orchards. There is a drive or a trail through every canyon, and one of them known as La Cumbre trail, twelve miles long, offers a continuous panorama of glorious scenery. It crosses the mountains through a pass a little less than 4,000 feet above the seas. Another trail reaches the summit of the range by a climb of twelve to fourteen miles, and is equally attractive. The lowest pass is 2,224 feet, but it is possible to climb nearly 8,000[,] either on horseback or by motor. In Santa Barbara there is no rivalry in architecture or extravagance. The great competition is in flowers, plants and vegetable gardens. Most of the residences are of the villa type, simple and often severe. The ideal house is of shingles, stained brown, with wide porches hidden by climbing roses and other vines and furnished with hammocks and easy chairs. The fact that the temperature rarely varies more than twelve to fifteen degrees from one year's end to another, and is always moderatley warm, enables everybody to live in the open air, and is, of course, a blessing to the infirm and weary, and has a wholesome influence. People from the east go to Santa Barbara to be soaked in sunshine, and play golf 365 days in the year. The villa population is quite exclusive and has a society of its own. During the winter season the two great hotels, the Potter, probably as large as the largest on the coast, and one of the finest, and the Arlington, which has recently been erected upon the site of an old house of the same name, are filled with eastern people. During the summer middle west and western people take advantage at the hotels of the lower rates. The Potter hotel is very close to the ocean, where the sea bathers revel, and the great lawn on that side is in fact a perfect ocean of flowers. The Arlington hotel is also attractive. It belongs to E. P. Ripley, president of the Santa Fe railroad, and he is the man who controlled the contracting company which built the Lackawanna railroad from Binghamton to Buffalo about 1880. One of his subcontractors was the late John B. McDonald, who made fame and wealth as the builder of the New York city subway. Mr. Ripley in 1880, was in a way, Mr. McDonald's financial backer. The writer saw Mr. Ripley recently in Santa Barbara, and he looks almost as strong as he did over thirty years ago. His hotel is built of concrete and steel[,] and is after the mission style of architecture, has 300 rooms and cost nearly a half million dollars. The mission idea is carried out in every room and corridor, the woodwork being left in the rough and stained a dark brown by the use of petroleum. There are no ceilings. The heavy rafters are left uncovered; the walls are rough plaster, painted to match the woodwork; the floors are red tiles and even the bath tubs are of mission design. The mission style of architecture with its strong but simples [sic] lines, Moors and introduced into Mexico, was used by the Franciscan missionaries because they found it the best suited to the climate. That was the reason it was adopted in the south of Spain. The brick and tile did not reflect, but absorbed the glare of the sun. The cloisters are cool at noonday and the thick walls are proof agianst the dampness of the rainy season. It is being used more and more for public buildings, school houses, hotels, and nearly all the new schools and public edifices are being built after the mision design. The government architects planned the conventional granite for the federal post-office at Riverside, Cal., but to the end that a harmonious architectrure should prevail in the city, President Taft directed that the Riverside post-office should conform to the mission style. All about Santa Barabara is attractive. The entire amphitheater inclosed by the Santa Ynez mountains on the one side and the Pacific ocean on the other, is entirely taken up by rich ranchmen, who own large estates and keep most of their lands in natural parks. They visit in automobiles and on horseback; they wear sombreros and comfortable clothing; they take pride in their crops and orchards and brag about their walnuts and their olives. This is the walnut country par excellence, and it is the best paying crop. The trees require ten years to mature, but give no further trouble. It is only necessary to keep down the weeds and loosen the surface of the soil with plow and harrow. Walnut trees are not subject to diseases like fruit trees. The nuts require no refrigeration, cannot spoil on the hands of the grower, and sell for not less than twelve cents a pound on the cars. The average profit to the grower is $200 an acre. Walnut orchards are mostly limited in area. The largest in California has only 350 acres, and most of them are of less than twenty acres. But the business is extending rapidly. The walnut acreage will soon be increased when the entire Golita valley is irrigated. Irrigation will enable the farmers to extend the walnut and lemon groves and grow more beans, for these three are great staples. Santa Barbara has been boring a hold through the Santa Ynez range of mountains for a large and permanent water supply. The tunnel is seven by nine feet in size and 7,000 feet through the mountain. Aqueducts were designed for both sides and the aqueducts' supply of water for drinking, irrigation, etc., will be enough for a population of 250,000 people. No one dreams that Santa Barbara will ever have such a population. The new scheme is to irrigate the Golita valley. Writing of lemons, it is worth mention that the Crocker family have an enormous lemon ranch in the Montecito valley, just over a ridge from Santa Barbara, with a large stone packing house and all the appurtenances and ship their crops by the train load. It is the most extensive and complete lemon ranch in America, with 2,000 acres of trees. The crops are truly wonderful. In this temperature, and in a soil of surpassing richness, everything grows. All the plants known to the temperature and semi-temperate regions live happily together. The palm and the pine, the apple and the oleander[,] the maple and the magnolia grow side by side with equal vigor. Roses bloom and strawberry beds give ripened fruit every month. The cultivation of vegetables and small fruits for the local market, is the most profitable kind of farming, however, as hotels and boarding houses consume large quantities of both. The cultivation of flowers and plants is also a profitable business. On the main street of Santa Barbara is a concern which imports shrubs, vines, plants and trees from everywhere and acclimates them for California. You can see nearly a half hundred kinds of palms, camphor and cinnamon trees, papyrus, bamboos of all sorts and sizes, hibiscus, agavas, bread-fruit, and other strange plants that you read about in Robinson Crusoe, the Swiss Family Robinson and other tales of the South Sea islands. Out in Montecito park an oil and steel magnate named Gillespie has a great show place. It took eight years to construct the palace and surroundings at a cost of more than $3,000,000. It is first of all a palm park. But it is more. The home is copied after some Roman villa, and the grounds likewise. This palace and palm park is open to visitors at certain hours each day when Mr. Gillespie is away. The house has a great plunge like to the Roman baths. The water runs into high reservoirs, which as they are located along the descending hillside in front are tapped by pipes from which the palms are watered. Mr. Gillespie has been traveling the world over for many years looking for new varieties of palms[.] He now has about eighty distinct varieties and has sold single plants for as much as $500. A Buffalo man, the head of the Pierce-Arrow Automobile company, occupies the palace this winter. Some of the finest grapes in California are grown about Santa Barbara the vines having been imported from Spain in the early days by the Franciscan fathers who taught the natives how to make wine as well as olive oil. The largest grape vine in the world, it is said, grows in Carpintería valley, a few miles from Santa Barbara. It was planted in 1843 by a Spanish farmer and has yielded ten tons of grapes in a single season. It spreads over an acre of ground and is supported by seventy-eight posts. If it were not pruned so closely every season it would cover a much larger area. Six inches from the ground the trunk measures eight and one-half feet in circumference, and where it reaches the trellis and begins to spread, about six and one-half feet from the ground, the girth is five feet seven inches. There are several other very large vines int he same neighborhood. One of the largest ever known was cut down and sent to the Philadelphia centennial exposition in 1876, as a sample of California products and was a great advertisment for the state. It will be of interest to all who love the words and music of the song "The Rosary," to know the words were written in Santa Barbara by Cameron Rogers. He is an artist; he lives there and from his studio window there is a most entrancing view. It was set to music by Ethelbert Nevin. Nearby to the scenes of beauty in Santa Barbara one can find the greasy conditions of a rich oil country. Crude petroleum gushes up from the earth and sea at Summerland, a town near Santa Barbara. It is occupied by a colony of Spiritualists. It looks like one of the old fashioned oil towns of Pennsylvania. The first petroleum was discovered on the hillside, and the veins were followed down to the ocean, where what the Californians call "submarine wells" have been bo[r]ed and piped and are now flowing regularly. The oil comes up first through the sand, and then piped through the water and thence to the reservoirs on shore. The people of Summerland were the first to discover the adaptability of crude petroleum for making roads. It was an accident. The first man to use the crude petroleum on a road was so lazy that he shoveled the refuse from an oil tank into the street to get rid of it, when he should have carted it off to some dumping ground. The oil immediately absorbed the dust, and the heavy metal wheels which passed over it packed it down into a hard, smooth surface like asphaltum which shed the rains and was never muddy or dusty. His neighbors then put oil on the roadways in front of their houses to keep down the dust, and the practice finally became general and is now used effectively in every part of the country[.] The history of Santa Barbara is very romantic, but the town acquired its name from a tragedy, due to a father's killing of his daughter, and after her it was named. Santa Barbara was one of the early martyrs. She was born in Asia Minor, and was the daughter of a Roman general. She was convereted to Christianity when she was sixteen years old, in the year A. D. 233, during the reign of Alexander Severus, an emperor frindly to the Christians. His successor, Maximinus, was a thorough pagan and ordered all Christian converts put to death. The father of Barbara was Deoscorus, and he concealed her, hoping to persuade her to recant. When he was unable to do so he inflicted upon her cruel torments, which she bore with wonderful fortitude for a girl of seventeen, and he finally slew her with his own hand. Her piety, her steadfastness for the faith, and her example had great influence with the young Christians and caused her to be canonized by both the Greek and Roman Catholic churches. She suffered martyrdom at Nocomedia, Asia Minor about 235 A. D. It was not by a monk that Santa Barbara was named but by a Portuguese explorer, as will later apear. Off the coast of Santa Barbara is an archipelago of mountainous islands, the largest being called San Miguel, Santa Rosa and Santa Cruz. When the Spaniards first discovered the country they were all inhabited, but after the mission was established the island families were persuaded by the friars to move over to the mainland and settle near by. Juan Rodnguez [Rodríguez] Cabrillo, the discoverer of California, is buried upon the island of San Miguel, although no trace of his grave remains. He was the first European who is known to have explored the Pacific coast of what is now the United States. He was a navigator of enterprise, courage and tact, and although a Portuguese by birth, spent most of his life in the service of Spain like Columbus and Americus Vespucci, who were Italians. About the middle of October 1542, just fifty years after Columbus discovered America, Cabrillo landed on the beach of what is now Santa Barbara, and was met by natives in their canoes, who received him with demonstrations of curiosity and kindness, and exchanged presents with him. He remained some time, exploring the surrounding country, which in his reports to the viceroy of Mexico was described as of great attractiveness and fertility. He crossed to the islands of Santa Rosa, Santa Cruz and San Miguel and made the latter his headquarters, while he continued his explorations northward to a point many leagues north of the bay of San Francisco, although he never found the Golden Gate. It is difficult to determine how far north he went, but we know from his narratives that he was driven back by bad weather and returned to San Miguel to recover from a fracture of his right arm, but he grew worse instead of better and on January 8, 1543, he died and was buried on that island. Santa Barbara was given its name by Sebastian Viscaino, another Portuguese epxlorer, who set sail from Acapulco with three large caravels and a transport, carrying 200 soldiers and three Carmelite friars. Antonio de la Ascension, one of the friars, took copious notes of all they saw and heard along the coast, made a map of considerable detail and as directed by the explorer named each bay, cape, island and other conspicuous landmark after the particular saint whose festival occurred nearest to the day of discovery. On December 4, 1602, the party landed at Santa Barbara, and that being the anniversary of Santa Barbara, her name was given to the bay and the country that surrounds it. Although Viscaino was not the first discoverer of California, his voyage was the most important because of the maps of the coast and the authentic information which Padre Antonio and the other friars were able to furnish Europe in regard to that part of the world. The island of Santa Cruz recieved its name from the fact that one of the early explorers lost there a crucifix of great sanctity, which was found by the natives and restored as the vessel was about to sail. A romantic narrative relates how in 18[5]1 George Nidever, a ranchero, of Santa Barbara, found human footprints upon the sandy beach of the island of St. Nichalas, close to Santa Cruz, which was supposed to be uninhabited. He was reminded of a story that had been widely circulated about an Indian woman who had been abandoned there and made a thorough search. On the first day he wa unsuccessful; on the second day he found evidences of human existence, including a basket rudely made of reeds; on the [third] day he found three small huts [made] of the ribs of a whale and cove[red] with brush. In one of these huts [was] an Indian woman, with long hair fa[ll]ing over her bare shoulders, and we[ar]ing a single garmet made of [the] skins of birds. She showed no ala[rm] but when Mr. Nidever, and his co[m]panions, approached she offered th[em] roots and a piece of blubber to [eat.] She had entirely lost the faculty [of] speech. When Mr. Nidever told [her] that she was to accompany him to [the] mainland[,] she understood read[ily,] showed much pleasure and gather[ed] together her little belongings, wh[ich] consisted of baskets woven of gra[ss,] jars filled with pebbles and other [little] mementoes. Upon reaching Sa[nta] Barbara Mr. Nidever took her to [his] home, where she was kindly cared [for] until her death three or four ye[ars] later. Although she was never able [to] express herself so as to be under[stood,] she had not forgotten the art of ho[use]keeping, and performed the duties [of] a servant as long as her health p[er]mitted. Investigation developed the [...] that in the year 1835 the padres [sent] a schooner to the islands to collect [all] the Indians that remained there [and] take them over to the missions. Wh[en] they were ready to depart on of [the] women could not find her chid, [and] ran from the boat into the woods [...] search for her. Before her return [a] violent storm arose, and as there [was] no harbor and the anchorage was [...] secure, it became necessary to [...] out into the open sea[.] The cap[tain] intended to return for the woman, [...] for several days the ship was dr[iven] southward by the violence of the [gale] and finally landed its passengers [...] San Pedro, now the port of [Los] Angeles. A few days later the [cap]tain started northward with a [...] of lumber for Monterey, intending [to] stop at the island and take on [the] woman, but another gale capsized [the] schooner and all hands were lo[st. So] the woman was forgotten and re[main]ed for sixteen years alone, like Ro[bin]son Crusoe. It was believed that [the] child died shortly after the deser[tion,] from exposure to the weather. Until the discovery of gold in [Cal]ifornia, and the rapid development [of] San Francisco, Sacramento and o[ther] places farther north Santa Bar[bara] was second only in importance [to] Monterey, on the coast. The terr[...] occupied by the missionaries [was] divided into four districts, in each [...] which was a presido, or military [p]rison, and the officers exercised [...] civil and military jurisdiction. [Mon]terey was the official seat of the [gov]ernor, and the commandant at S[anta] Barbara was second in author[ity.] Thus it happend that after the d[eath] of Governor Arrellago, in 182[5, ...] Captain Arguello, commandant [of] Santa Barbara, exercised authority [un]til a new governor arrived. After [the] Mexican war Arguello remained [at] Santa Barbara, and became one of [the] most influential men of Cal[ifornia,] where he resided for thirty-four y[ears.] Another important commander [...] Santa Barbara was Lieutenant [Rom]mualdo Pacheco, and of a promin[ent] family. He left a son, Romualdo, [who] became governor of the state, and [a] member of the house of repre[senta]tives. His family still reside in [the] neighborhood. At the time of the arrival of Ca[ptain] John C. Fremont and his little [...] in 1846, Lieutenant Raimundo Ca[...] was commander at the presidio, [and] the misssion and the property [which] surrounded it were held by Nichola[s ...] Den and Daniel Hill, two Ameri[cans] under a lease from the Mexican [... gov]ernment for a yearly rental of $1,[...] The lease covered all the lands [...] buildings of the missionary except [the] church and the monastery. Some li[...] head of cattle, 1,700 head of sheep [...] many horses were also included. [The] bishop of the California diocese [en]deavored in vain to resist the a[...] of the government, and his death [was] hastened by his failure. He died [in] 1846 and is buried in the Mi[ssion] church. Daniel Hill, the lessee, was a [Cape] Cod sea captain who first visited [the] coast in command of a trading ve[ssel] in 1822, en route to the Haw[aiian] Islands, and was so much taken [with] the climate and surroundings of S[anta] Barbara, that he brought his [wife] and family and settled there in 1[...] starting a trading store, bought [...] and cattle and became the richest [man] in the community. Nicholas A. [...] an Irish physician, married H[ill's] daughter. He arrived in 1836 and [prac]ticed medicine while he raised ca[ttle.] Before his death he, too, had be[come] very rich and was the owner of [...] large ranches as well as 10,000 ca[ttle.] Several of the residences of [the] Spanish and Mexican colonial p[...] are still standing, although they [have] been considerably altered on mo[...] lines. The best description of life [in] Santa Barbara at that period may [be] found in Dana's "Two Years Be[fore] the Mast," which in the days of [...] youth was a universally popular [...] (To Be Continued.)

title: "A Feminine Crusoe. Eighteen Years on a Dessert Island—How She Lived and Dressed"
tropes: Origins; Discovery; Noble Savage; Wonder; Indian Queen
author: [Fred Spalding Witter]
transcripts: ﻿A FEMININE CRUSOE. Eighteen Years on a Desert Island--How She Lived and Dressed. San Francisco Correspondence Rochester Democrat. Seventy miles from the shore is San Nicolas Island, the sixth of the group that cluster around the Bay of Santa Barbara, California. It is celebrated for having been the residence for eighteen years of "The Lost Woman of San Nicolas." As her name is famous and as her story has been told in romance I will give the bare facts about her as I found them to be, without any added ornament, and leave the fiction to the pen of the novelist. The Island of San Nicolas was once densely populated. This is attested by the skulls and bones and other evidences of human abode that are found there[.] The Alaska Indians frequently visted the island to hunt for the furs of the sea otter. They took their women with them on these boats, and on returning after the hunt was over they left them on the island to their fate. By order of the government in 1835 the Indians were removed from the island. Just before they were to embark, and carry away every human habitant, as it was supposed, a white Indian woman begged for the privilege of going ashore for her child, which she had accidentally left. She was gone a long time in a fruitless search for her offspring. The wind blew a gale, the water was shallow, there was no one who was seeking the lost one[.] They set sail intending to return for the lost woman of San Nicolas but the boat becoming un[-]seaworthy she was left to her fate. It was generally known that there was a woman abandoned on the island, but no attempt was made for her deliverence. As the world soon forgets, so the woman of San Nicolas was forgotten and the year passed away. After a lapse of sixteen years a man who landed on the island found that it was inhabited by some one. The foot prints of a human being sunk deep in the ground were seen. The hardness of the ground was an indication that they had been made a long time. From their size they evidently belonged to a woman. Circular enclosures made of brush, six or seven feet through, were seen, where some one had lived. Near the huts were sticks driven in the ground and dried blubber hanging on them, thus prepared for food. In 1852 San Nicholas was visited again and another hunt was made for the long-lost woman. The huts were seen that had been seen before, but the old blubber had been taken away and new food of the kind hung in its place. Wild dogs were found which ran away at the approach of civilized man. In a basket covered with seal skins that they found in a brush-heap was a dress made of shag skins, cut in square places, a rope made of sinew and several smaller articles, such as fishhooks and bone needless. The discoverers of these proofs that there lived on that island a human being scattered them on the ground, and on their return they found them gathered together and placed on the basket again. The Catholic fathers of the "Old Mission," the foremost in every good word and work, offered a reward to anyone who would find the lost woman, and a third effort was made in 1853 to discover the prodigal about whom there was such a mystery and in whom the world of this coast was beginning to take quite an interest. Fresh tracks of the woman were found. They belonged to very small feet and were like those that were seen in the first attempt to find the woman. Huts made of whale ribs and covered with brush were discovered. At length an object was seen in the distance that appeared to be moving. Going towards it they saw the woman that for eighteen years had reigned queen of San Nicolas, her subjects being the wild animals, her robe a dress of bird skins she had made and her throne the hut she had built. She was seated in an enclosure, so that only her head and shoulders could be seen. Two or three dogs were about her that disappeared at the command of their sovereign[.] She was seated on some grass that covered the ground and served her as a bed. Her dress was neatly made of bird skins, extending to her ankles, the feathers of which pointed downward. Her head was covered with a thick mat of yellowish brown hair and her shoulders were bare[.] She was occupied in stripping blubber from a piece of sealskin which she held across her knee and using for that purpose a knife made of an iron hoop. In her hut was a fire, beside which she sat talking to herse[l]f and, occasionally shading her eyes with her hand, looked at the men that were in search of her. She recieved them with much courtesy, bowing and smiling and shosing [showing] that this lost child of nature had much of the politeness of a true woman. She took some roots in the bag, roasted them in the fire and gave them to the men to eat. She gathered up all her food which was her chief concern, owing to the fa[m?]ines she had experienced, washed herself at the spring and followed the men cheerfully to the boat. On being taken to Santa Barbara she manifested great delight on seeing the sights of civilization. She became a universal [f]avorite and was presented with many gifts. Passengers on the Panama steamer that landed there all wanted to see the lost woman of San Nicolas. She related by signs her experience on the island, as she spoke a language that none of the Indians knew and none of the Spanish fathers, versed in Indian dialects, could understand. Civilization, which prolongs the life of some, shortened that of the woman of San Nicolas. An excessive love of fruit led to her death in Santa Barbara at the age of fifty. She was buried with the honors of the Catholic church by the Franciscan Fathers, and her dress and trinkets were sent to Rome and placed in that receptacle of the world[']s curiosities. The story of the lost woman of San Nicolas will always remain a wonderment. Her ingenuity is seen in the pails she made of grass, made to hold water by smearing them with melted asphaltum, and in her bird skin dresses, her bone needles, her knife of iron hoop and the language she invented and spoke. It is inexplicable to all who have learned her story how a woman could live eighteen years on an island around which the waves were beating a requiem to hope, getting her food and cooking it without even those fealtles [faculties?] which are common to the savage, and making her dresses neatly without the aid of needles except what she carved out of a bone. She laid aside one dress for eighteen years, to be worn when the white men should come, of which she had a presentiment. She built her own house, protected herself from the cold, gained supreme control over the wild beasts about her and preserved her love for men and women for well nigh two decades of human life alone in the wild. With no previous knowledge of civilization, solitude appeared to have educated her for it. An ordinary woman would have perished with despondency in such a desolate, hungry, naked, shelterless outlook.

title: "A Feminine Crusoe. Eighteen Years on a Desert Island—How She Lived and Dressed"
tropes: Origins; Discovery; Noble Savage; Wonder; Indian Queen
author: [Fred Spalding Witter]
transcripts: <hi rend="bold">A FEMININE CRUSOE.</hi> <hi rend="bold">Eighteen Years on a Desert Island—How She Lived and Dressed.</hi> San Francisco Correspondence Rochester Democrat. Seventy miles from the shore is San Nicolas Island, the sixth of the group that cluster around the Bay of Santa Barbara, California. It is celebrated for having been the residence for eighteen years of "The Lost Woman of San Nicolas." As her name is famous and as her story has been told in romance I will give the bare facts about her as I found them to be, without any added ornament, and leave the fiction to the pen of the novelist. The Island of San Nicolas was once densely populated. This is attested by the skulls and bones and other evidences of human abode that are found there. The Alaska Indians frequently visited the island to hunt for the furs of the sea otter. They took their women with them on these hunts, and on returning after the hunt was over they left them on the island to their fate. By order of the government in 1835 the Indians were removed from the island. Just before they were to embark, and carry away every human inhabitant, as it was supposed, a white Indian woman begged for the privilege of going ashore for her child, which she had accidentally left. She was gone a long time in a fruitless search for her offspring. The wind blew a gale, the water was shallow, there was no one who was seeking the lost one. They set sail, intending to return for the lost woman of San Nicolas, but the boat becoming unseaworthy she was left to her fate. It was generally known that there was a woman abandoned on the island, but no attempt was made for her deliverance. As the world soon forgets, so the woman of San Nicolas was forgotten and the year[s] passed away. After a lapse of sixteen years a man who landed on the island found that it was inhabited by some one. The footprints of a human being sunk deep in the ground were seen. The hardness of the ground was an indication that they had been made a long time. From their size they evidently belonged to a woman. Circular enclosures made of brush, six or seven feet through, were seen, where some one had lived. Near the huts were sticks driven in the ground and dried blubber hanging on them, thus prepared for food. In 1852 San Nicolas was visited again and another hunt was made for the long-lost woman. The huts were seen that had been seen before, but the old blubber had been taken away and new food of the kind hung in its place. Wild dogs were found which ran away at the approach of civilized man. In a basket covered with seal skins that they found in a bush-heap was a dress made of shag skins, cut in square pieces, a rope made of sinew and several smaller articles, such as fishhooks and bone needles. The discoverers of these proofs that there lived on that island a human being scattered them on the ground, and on their return they found them gathered together and placed in the basket again. The Catholic fathers of the "Old Mission," the foremost in every good word and work, offered a reward to anyone who would find the lost woman, and a third effort was made in 1853 to discover the prodigal about whom there was such a mystery and in whom the world of this coast was beginning to take an interest. Fresh tracks of the woman were found. They belonged to very small feet, and were like those that were seen in the first attempt to find the woman. Huts made of whale ribs and covered with brush were discovered. At length an object was seen in the distance that appeared to be moving. Going towards it they saw the woman that for eighteen years had reigned Queen of San Nicolas, her subjects being the wild animals, her robe a dress of bird skins she had made and her throne the hut she had built. She was seated in an enclosure, so that only her head and shoulders could be seen. Two or three dogs were about her that disappeared at the command of their sovereign. She was seated on some grass that covered the ground and served her as a bed. Her dress was neatly made of bird skins, extending to her ankles, the feathers of which pointed downward. Her head was covered with a thick mat of yellowish brown hair and her shoulders were bare. She was occupied in stripping blubber from a piece of sealskin which she held across her knee and using for that purpose a knife made of an iron hoop. In her hut was a fire, beside which she sat talking to herself and, occasionally shading her eyes with her hand, looked at the men that were in search of her. She received them with much courtesy, bowing and smiling and showing that this lost child of nature had much of the politeness of a true woman. She took some roots in the bag, roasted them in the fire and gave them to the men to eat. She gathered up all her food, which was her chief concern, owing to the famines she had experienced, washed herself at the spring, And [sic] followed the men cheerfully to the boat. On being taken to Santa Barbara she manifested great delight on seeing the sights of civilization. She became a universal favorite and was presented with many gifts. Passengers on the Panama steamer that landed there all wanted to see the lost woman of San Nicolas. She related by signs her experience on the island, as she spoke a language that none of the Indians knew and none of the Spanish fathers, versed in Indian dialects, could understand. Civilization, which prolongs the life of some, shortened that of the woman of San Nicolas. An excessive love of fruit led to her death in Santa Barbara at the age of 50. She was buried with the honors of the Catholic Church by the Franciscan Fathers, and her dress and trinkets were sent to Rome and placed in that receptacle of the world's curiosities. The story of the lost woman of San Nicolas will always remain a wonderment. Her ingenuity is seen in the pails she made of grass, made to hold water by smearing them with melted asphaltum, and in her bird-skin dresses, her bone needles, her knife of iron hoop and the language she invented and spoke. It is inexplicable to all who have learned her story how a woman could live eighteen years on an island around which the waves were beating a requiem to hope, getting her food and cooking it without even those facilities which are common to the savage, and making her dresses neatly without the aid of needles except what she carved out of bone. She laid aside one dress for eighteen years, to be worn when the white men should come, of which she had a presentiment. She built her own house, protected herself from the cold, gained supreme control over the wild beasts about her and preserved her love for men and women for well nigh two decades of human life alone in the wild. With no previous knowledge of civilization, solitude appeared to have educated her for it. An ordinary woman would have perished with despondency in such a desolate, hungry, naked, shelterless outlook.

title: "The Isle of Skulls. A Woman's Lonely Life—Surrounded by the Bones of Her Tribe"

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">THE ISLE OF SKULLS.</hi> <hi rend="bold">A Woman's Lonely Life—Surrounded by the Bones of Her Tribe.</hi> On the lonely wind-swept island of San Nicholas, says the San Francisco Examiner, eighty miles off th coast of Ventura county, where, as far back as the memory of man runs, hundreds of white skeletons have dotted the valleys and hillsides, local archæologists are now busy gathering the relics of a strange extinct race. The island [is] ten miles long and oval in shape, being four miles across the widest part. Strange utensils of serpentine, sandstone and steatite are found among the human bones, and the island and its erstwhile inhabitants have a history so curious that it is difficult of comprehension. In 1835, the padres of Santa Barbara, learning that there were but sixteen of the strange Indian race then living there, determined to rescue them from the island. They went over in a sloop and succeeded, as they thought, in getting all on board. At the last moment an Indian woman returned for her child, and one of the frequent storms of the channel islands springing up, the sloop was driven away without her. The sloop went on the rocks off Point Conception and all on board were lost. Sixteen years later Capt. George Nidever and two men went from the coast on a sloop to hunt otter off San Nicholas. On landing they were, like Crusoe, astonished to discover human footprints in the sand. They saw no one, however, and a storm compelled them to put to sea. It was two years thereafter that the adventurous captain, revolving in his mind the sight of the footprints in the uncanny island, determined to go and discover and bring over the lonely woman of whom he had vaguely heard. Men accompanied him, and at length they saw on the surf-beaten shore a woman with long tawny hair dressed in a queer garb of colored bird skins, and scraping, with a bone knife the blubber from a seal. They surrounded and approuched her stealthily, and although suddenly confronted she did not appear in the least afraid, but smiled, and then, falling on her knees, prayed to the sun. The wild woman offered no objection when by signs she was made to understand that she was to go with them in the boat. They reached Santa Barbara across the rough sea, and the first thing the Indian woman saw [was] Dr. S. L. Shaw, now eighty years old, and yet living there, riding a horae [horse]. She had never seen nor heard of any object like it, and thought the man and horse were one, and she knelt on the shore and offered her devotions to it. Two weeks afterwards the last inhabitant of rock-ribbed, tempest-tossed San Nicholas died from eating food to which she was unaccustomed, furnished by her rescuers, and the curtain fell on her race forever. Wild dogs had eaten her child. Her dress of red and blue feathers, a wonderful creation of barbaric hands, was sent to the pope of Rome. Relic hunters have gathered mortars, pestles, olias, toy steatite canoes and other curious things there for some years past and shipped them to various eastern and European universities. Skeletons and parts of skeletons have also been collected in large numbers, but today the bones of thousands of Indians are scattered about there. Some lie face down, indicating that they have fallen in battle. There are so many human relics there that San Nicholas is known as the "Isle of Skulls." "The lonely island, whose highest part is but 1,040 feet above the sea," said a resident of Ventura, "is noted for the high artistic class of many of its relics. Had the woman rescued, then fifty-two years old, not died, a story passing strange would no doubt have been told of the race so long hemmed in by the waste of waters about. As it is, much of the story is shrouded in mystery forever."

title: "Story of a Woman Crusoe. Unlike Defoe's Hero, Her End Is Pathetic in the Extreme"
tropes: Girl Crusoe; Noble Savage; Wild Child
author: [Frank Gassaway]
transcripts: STORY OF A WOMAN CRUSOE. Unlike Defoe's Hero, Her End Is Pathetic in the Extreme. From Field and Stream. Beginning due west of Point Conception, on the California coast, and continuing at irregular intervals as far south as the Bay of Todos Santos, in Lower California, lie the Channel Islands. In this ideal region for the yachtsman, the fisherman, and the hunter one comes to feel like a new Crusoe on his primitive isle. And in very truth Crusoe's semi-mythical story was enacted upon one of these same islands, though minus the man Friday and the happy ending. The castaway in this case was a woman, a Danish emigrant, left ashore through some mischance by the crew of a vessel that had sought shelter behind San Nicholas during a storm in the early '50's. For over seventeen years the lone creature lived unsought and forgotten, though the time at length came when, on the days the mist-clearing north wind blew, she could climb to the island's highest point and view the ranchers' herds grazing upon the mainland. And at last, when hope and reason had both long died, the poor, wild gibbering creature was found in her wolf's burrow among the hills by the advance guard of the otter hunters' fraternity, who had long wondered at the mysterious footprints they marked upon the lonely sands.

title: "Miles of Human Bones. Discoveries of a Party Who Went to San Nicholas. The Island Entirely Destitute of Productive Soil—A Few Sheep Found There"
tropes: Origins; Jump Overboard
transcripts: ﻿MILES OF HUMAN BONES. DISCOVERIES OF A PARTY WHO WENT TO SAN NICHOLAS. The Island Entirely Destitute of Productive Soil—A few Sheep Found There. The party who recently went to San Nicholas island on a prospecting tour with a view to taking up goe[v]rnment [government] land, returned after a two days visit on the island. They concluded not to exhaust their rights on land so valueless. From Frank Fazzio, who took them over, some interesting details of the trip is [are] learned. The island is about four miles wide by twelve miles long and is located some 70 miles off this coast, almost due south of here. The soil has all been blown off and the rocks are almost entirely bare and destitute of soil, giving the whole island a very barren appearance. On the western side sand is about the only thing seen and this has been blown from the beach clear to the top of the island, 700 or 800 feet high. On the other side of the island, the east side, they found human bones for a distance of five miles, along the beach. They were very think and looked as if it has been a graveyard. They also discovered the remains of huamn bodies on the ridge which runs lengthwise through the island. In some places two skeletons were seen close together as if they had been buried together in the same grave. The wind had blown off what covering of soil that had been thrown over them and it looked quite ghastly. Bones were thickly strewn along this ridge for upwards of three miles. From appearances upwards of 3000 or 4000 Indians must have been buried there. A shanty which had been built on the west side was found buried clear to the roof in sand. There are now about 2000 sheep on the island and from a sort of rough grass they seem to keep fat. The party went into a cave which afforded an Indian woman, the sole occupant of the island, a home for seven years. It seems that when her party was leaving the island, that she jumped overboard and swam ashore in the night. Years went by before she was taken off. The party enjoyed the trip immensely, but say the island is not worth much.

title: "A Female Crusoe"
tropes: Discovery; Indian Queen; Wild Child
author: [Edwards Roberts]
transcripts: A FEMALE CRUSOE. The recent earthquake and electrical disturbances at San Nicolas island, near Santa Barbara, Cal., has revived interest in the story of the old Indian woman who led a Crusoe life on the island for many years and who was finally removed to Santa Barbara only to die from the effects of unaccustomed civilization. The following sketch of the female Crusoe is from "Santa Barbara and Around There" by Edward Roberts: On the smallest island was enacted the tragedy of the "Lost Woman of San Nicolas," which at Santa Barbara is a familiar tale. The story begins with the removal of a number of Indians from San Nicolas in 1836. Just as they were embarking one of the women discovered that her child had been left behind. Returning for it, she was abandoned by her companions, who were obliged by a coming storm to set sail for the mainland. It was intended to return so soon as the weather permitted, but years passed away and the woman in time was forgotten and left to her fate. Twenty years later, a hunter named George Nidever of Santa Barbara, visited the island for otters. While there he determined to look for the woman. After careful search he found three huts made of whale-ribs and brush, and from where they stood extended an open plain, in the center of which Nidever saw the object of his journey. The woman's dress was made of skins and feathers, and her hair hung in tangled masses from her bare head. When discovered, she was cutting blubber from a seal which she had killed, but on seeing her visitor she received him with every manifestation of delight, and readily accompanied him to his boat. Signs were made for her to enter it, and on her doing so, Nidever sailed for the bay, ad brought his charge to Santa Barbara. Her arrival there created great excitement and hundreds called at Nidever's house to see her. Although she could not have been more than fifty years old, she was gray-haired and emaciated. Her expression was one of blank ignorance and her skin was dry and wrinkled. Her language, strange as it may seem, considering the comparatively short time she had been lost, was unintelligible to all. Those who considered themselves masters of every Indian tongue could not understand a word that she said. Owing to this fact the story of her hermitage was never known. What became of the child she returned from the boat to find on that fatal day in 1836 is a matter of pure conjecture. How long it lived and where it was buried were facts that could not be discovered. The woman appeared to have lost all human instincts, and to every question asked made no answer that could be understood. In three months after her rescue she died and was buried by the Mission fathers.

title: "Expedition to Clear up the Mystery of the Wild Woman of San Nicolas Island: The Dress of Feathers Which Maria Better Than Nothing Sewed for Herself out of Skins of Birds Sent to the Propagandist Museum in Rome—Further Details Anxiously Sought of the Woman Who, for the Sake of Her Child, Lived Alone on California Island for Twenty Years—the Child Died Long Ago—the Mother, Crazed by Grief and Sufferings, Now Rests in Holy Ground"
tropes: Wonder; Wild Child; Jump Overboard; Noble Savage
image_description: Y--depiction of LW being found by GN
transcripts: ﻿EXPEDITION TO CLEAR UP THE MYSTERY OF THE WILD WOMAN OF SAN NICOLAS ISLAND. <emph>The Dress of Feathers Which Maria Better Than Nothing Sewed for Herself Out of Skins of Birds Sent to the Propagandist Museum in Rome—Further Details Anxiously Sought of the Woman Who, for the Sake of Her Child, Lived Alone on California Island for Twenty Years—The Child Died Long Ago—The Mother, Crazed by Grief and Sufferings, Now Rests in Holy Ground.</emph> AN expedition is being organized in Southern California for the purpose of exploring and making a scientific report on San Nicolas, the most remarkable island off the California coast. When this task is performed it may be possible to fill up the gaps in the meagre but marvellous story of Maria Better Than Nothing, the wild woman of the island. Maria's bones now rest in holy ground. She was buried by the mission in Santa Barbara, and the good fathers prayed over her body. If this was praiseworthy of the monks, there was in it also a certain appropriateness, for it was due to a particularly zealous group of Franciscan Fathers that Maria came to suffer her long and terrible isolation. Here is the Wild Woman's story precisely as any of the good people of Santa Barbara will tell it to you: Many years ago it came to the knowledge of the pious monks of the southern coast that on a barren island, twelve miles long and four wide, lying some seventy miles away, there dwelt a tribe of Indians who knew little of civilization and nothing of the Church. This desert spot, wind-swept, wave-beaten, with no harbors and sparse vegetation, seemed to the Franciscans ill-adapted for permanent missionary work. So they made the astonishing determination to carry off the entire population of the island and divide it among the missions of the coast. A ship was fitted up and set sail. In the face of almost hopeless obstacles the missionaries, having succeeded in anchoring their ship off the hilly side of the island, forced friendly overtures upon the desert tribe, and at length persuaded the hundred natives to leave their sterile soil and embark for the land of sunshine and abundant produce. On the day of embarkation a gale swept fiercely across the island. The ship heaved restlessly, tugging at her anchor. The captain was about to give the order to set sail when one of the women discovered that her child had been left on shore. It was too late. The vessel could no longer resist the gale and her anchor was hauled in with all haste. But the woman's maternal passion could not be thwarted. In a frenzy she leaped from the ship and swam back through the surf to the shore. Now for twenty years nothing was known of this poor creature. There was so little likelihood that she had survived that the responsibility of her rescue did not weigh heavily on the good fathers, who had, indeed, all that they could do in caring for and converting the Indians they had already imported. The captain who had been forced to abandon the young mother, had promised, it is true, to return for her, but his ship was afterward wrecked. After twenty years the oft-repeated story of the foresaken woman reached the ears of a warm-hearted and adventurous young priest. He enlisted the services of an otter hunter and several Indians, who, in a small schooner known as Better Than Nothing, set sail for the island, which had in the mean time been christened San Nicolas. There they found the woman. Not at first, because she had seen their approach and, timid as a deer, avoided them. A bunch of dried herbs and the smoldering ashes of a fire betrayed her presence on the island. And after a well-planned search they came upon the woman who had not seen a human face in twenty years. She was a startling picture, with staring eyes and unkempt hair and wearing the strangest costume ever seen on a woman. From neck to ankle she was decorously enveloped in a single, marvellously contrived garment of birds' skins, forming a brilliant patchwork of feathers. Her pitiful desire to be decently garbed, though abandoned and unseen, had been accomplished by years of painstaking labor. A dress of birds' skins is not made in a day. About her shoulders—for the winds of San Nicolas are chilly—was a garment of sealskin. Her slender, woman's hands had constructed the brush hut before which she was sitting when the sailors found her. With the cunning of a wild thing she had built this hut in a canyon and had placed about it a windbreak of whalebone and strong twigs. She smiled in unmeaning fashion when the men approached, and began to make strange wordless sounds. The Indians of the party, thinking her more than human, fell down to worship her. The others tried to communicate with her by sign, but the poor wild woman understood nothing. But although she had come to share many characteristics of a wild animal, she had retained a curious gentleness of disposition. Therefore, the adventurers were able to persuade her to leave her hut and board the ship with them, after consenting that she should bring with her a tame otter to which she clung with savage fondness. When they had brought her to Santa Barbara some Indians succeeded in drawing from the poor woman fragments of information about her appalling experience. But memory had almost left poor Maria Better Than Nothing, as they had named her, after the ship that rescued her. The baby for whom she had risked her life was shortly after torn to death by dogs, and doubtless the grief which the young mother suffered because of this wrecked her mind. For a long time she was ill and wanted to die, but instinct of self-preservation kept her alive and she lived on painfully year after year, making friends of the few animals on the island until the Better Than Nothing found her. Accustomed as she had become to a wild life, Maria could not resist the weakening influences of civilization. In less than three months the "wild woman" died, mourning to the very last the baby that had died a score of years before. Maria's remarkable dress of feathers was afterward sent to Rome for preservation in the great museum of the Propaganda.

transcripts: <hi rend="bold">A FEMALE CRUSOE</hi>. If De Foe had only known of a female Crusoe living on an ocean island, he might, perhaps, have wrought out a story superior to his Robinson Crusoe. Alexander Selkirk's brief life on Juan Fernandez was trivial, either in the hardships endured or the difficulties conquered, compared with that of a native woman on an island opposite Southern California. The Catholic Fathers at South [Santa] Barbara were transporting the natives of the Island St. Nicholas to the mainland. Among them was a mother who discovered that her babe had been left behind. She begged that the ship might be put back, but the captain refused. She leaped into the sea to swim ashore, but, as a storm prevailed, they all thought she was drowned. Eighteen years after, a company landed on the island. They found traces of life, and after long search discovered the woman, and took her with them. The poor mother never found her babe, but had managed to live in comparative comfort, though very lonely. After her long life chiefly in the open air, she could not bear the confinement of a house, and soon sickened and died.
